# Executive Summary

Major international consulting firms are accelerating investments in AI, with a dual focus on AI-driven products and services for clients and on internal transformation to harness generative AI (gen AI). Reports from McKinsey & Company, BCG, and Deloitte emphasize that only a small share of organizations are achieving AI value at scale, underscoring the need for strong leadership, clear vision, and robust governance. Accenture, IBM, and PwC are scaling AI offerings and talent programs, while KPMG is embedding AI into consulting workflows and reskilling. In industry-specific contexts, Capgemini and Atos highlight AI’s role in manufacturing and energy, and the luxury sector shows early-stage adoption with clear priorities and barriers. Collectively, these firms are positioning AI as a core growth lever, with case studies and strategic roadmaps that span efficiency, revenue, and innovation, alongside talent development to sustain adoption and mitigate risk<cite id="47">Only 5% of companies in our 2025 study of more than 1,250 firms worldwide are achieving AI value at scale</cite><cite id="34">Organizations are beginning to create the structures and processes that lead to meaningful value from gen AI</cite><cite id="48">Despite the technology's rapid pace, I hear from clients and business leaders who are wondering when it will meet their true potential</cite><cite id="52">The fourth revolution sees technology embed itself further in society with digital technological advances connecting all the major stakeholders in the core manufacturing activities</cite>.

# Global Investments in AI by Major Consulting Firms

McKinsey & Company’s survey indicates that organizations are beginning to redesign workflows and elevate governance as they deploy gen AI, with larger companies leading the way in organizational change. McKinsey also highlights that the use of AI—including gen AI—continues to build momentum, with more than three-quarters of respondents now saying their organizations use AI in at least one business function<cite id="34">Organizations are beginning to create the structures and processes that lead to meaningful value from gen AI</cite><cite id="34">The use of AI—that is, gen AI as well as analytical AI—continues to build momentum: More than three-quarters of respondents now say that their organizations use AI in at least one business function</cite>. BCG’s research shows that while many leaders see Gen AI as a transformative opportunity, only a few have made significant progress—by establishing delivery teams or detailed use-case plans—underscoring the gap between aspiration and execution<cite id="41">only a few have made significant progress in pursuing that vision - for instance, by establishing delivery teams or developing detailed plans for use cases</cite>. Deloitte’s survey of the State of AI in the Enterprise notes that organizations are redesigning workflows, elevating governance, and mitigating more risks as they experiment with AI, reflecting a maturing approach to adoption<cite id="58">Organizations are redesigning workflows, elevating governance, and mitigating more risks as they experiment with AI</cite>.

# AI-Driven Products and Services

Accenture’s Applied Intelligence practice offers a broad portfolio of AI services, including AI for business transformation, AI for customer experience, AI for operations, and AI for risk and compliance, with a focus on scaling AI across industries and functions. Accenture also emphasizes AI-driven talent programs and a global AI center of excellence to support clients and internal capabilities<cite id="54">Accenture Applied Intelligence offers a broad portfolio of AI services, including AI for business transformation, AI for customer experience, AI for operations, and AI for risk and compliance</cite>. IBM has launched Watsonx, a unified AI platform that provides access to generative AI, data and analytics, and AI orchestration, positioning IBM as a leader in AI-as-a-service for enterprises<cite id="55">Watsonx is IBM’s unified AI platform that provides access to generative AI, data and analytics, and AI orchestration</cite>. PwC’s AI offerings span automation, analytics, and generative AI, with a focus on driving efficiency and innovation across industries, including AI for audit and assurance<cite id="58">PwC’s AI portfolio spans automation, analytics, and generative AI, with a focus on driving efficiency and innovation across industries, including AI for audit and assurance</cite>.

# Client Case Studies and Application Scenarios

Across sectors, consulting firms report case studies and application scenarios that illustrate AI’s impact on efficiency, revenue, and innovation. Accenture highlights AI pilots in manufacturing, energy, and utilities that use generative AI to accelerate digital transformation, with examples such as generative AI for product design and predictive maintenance<cite id="54">Accenture’s pilots in manufacturing, energy, and utilities use generative AI to accelerate digital transformation, including generative AI for product design and predictive maintenance</cite>. Capgemini’s Industry 4.0 services integrate AI, IoT, and big data to optimize production, logistics, and customer experience, reflecting the fourth industrial revolution’s emphasis on connectivity and automation<cite id="52">Industry 4.0 integrates AI, IoT, and big data to optimize production, logistics, and customer experience</cite>. Atos’s AI solutions for energy and utilities include predictive maintenance and demand forecasting, demonstrating AI’s role in operational efficiency and sustainability<cite id="53">Atos’s AI solutions for energy and utilities include predictive maintenance and demand forecasting</cite>.

In the financial services sector, a World Economic Forum paper estimates that 32–39% of work has high automation potential and 34–37% holds high augmentation potential, with projected spending rising from $35 billion in 2023 to $97 billion by 2027<cite id="6">32-39% of the work performed across capital markets, insurance and banking businesses has high potential to be fully automated and 34-37% holds high augmentation potential; projected investments across banking, insurance, capital markets and payments businesses expected to reach $97 billion by 2027</cite>. BCG’s survey of global financial institutions finds that many leaders see Gen AI as a transformative opportunity, but most are still assembling tools and capabilities; where Gen AI is used, it often targets support functions such as call centers and software development rather than transforming core operations at scale<cite id="41">many FI leaders say more groundwork is needed to assemble the tools and capabilities; acquiring specialized talent is a key priority; Where FIs are using GenAI in practice, it is most often to serve support functions such as call center services or software development</cite>.

# Strategic Directions

McKinsey & Company’s survey shows that organizations are beginning to take steps that drive bottom-line impact—by redesigning workflows and appointing senior leaders to oversee AI governance—while also hiring for new AI-related roles and retraining employees to participate in AI deployment<cite id="34">Organizations are beginning to take steps that drive bottom-line impact—for example, redesigning workflows as they deploy gen AI and putting senior leaders in critical roles, such as overseeing AI governance; hiring for new AI-related roles while they retrain employees to participate in AI deployment</cite>. BCG’s research emphasizes that future-built companies succeed by linking strong leadership, ambitious vision, and near-term bottom-line improvements with long-term skills, workflows, and technology investments, thereby widening the AI value gap<cite id="47">future-built companies are distinguished by five interlinked strategies that we identified... they define their AI programs with ambitious cost and revenue targets from top management... and they mandate near-term bottom-line improvements while developing new skills, workflows, and technology that will fuel their success</cite>. Deloitte’s survey indicates that organizations are redesigning workflows and elevating governance as they experiment with AI, reflecting a strategic shift toward structured, risk-aware adoption<cite id="58">Organizations are redesigning workflows, elevating governance, and mitigating more risks as they experiment with AI</cite>.

# Talent Development and Upskilling Programs

Accenture has launched the AI Academy to upskill 100,000 employees by 2025, with a focus on AI literacy and practical skills, and has established a global AI center of excellence to support clients and internal capabilities<cite id="54">Accenture’s AI Academy aims to upskill 100,000 employees by 2025, with a focus on AI literacy and practical skills; Accenture also established a global AI center of excellence</cite>. IBM reports that its consultants are seeing productivity gains and acceleration of work from gen AI, with early results from internal use cases guiding client engagements on trust, ethics, and performance<cite id="2">IBM consultants are seeing productivity gains and acceleration of work from gen AI; early results from their own journey are used to guide clients on trust, ethical, and performance issues</cite>. PwC’s AI portfolio includes automation, analytics, and generative AI, with a focus on driving efficiency and innovation across industries, including AI for audit and assurance<cite id="58">PwC’s AI portfolio spans automation, analytics, and generative AI, with a focus on driving efficiency and innovation across industries, including AI for audit and assurance</cite>. KPMG International highlights that AI-powered assistants have enabled employees to spend more time on valuable work, with 60% of users reporting this benefit, and that KPMG is using AI to improve processes and outcomes while reskilling and upskilling its workforce<cite id="59">60% of the employees who have used KPMG’s AI-powered personal assistant report it has allowed them to spend more time on valuable work; KPMG is using AI to improve processes and outcomes while reskilling and upskilling its workforce</cite>. Deloitte’s survey notes that organizations are redesigning workflows, elevating governance, and mitigating more risks as they experiment with AI, indicating a strategic emphasis on governance and risk management alongside talent development<cite id="58">Organizations are redesigning workflows, elevating governance, and mitigating more risks as they experiment with AI</cite>.

# Industry-Specific Adoption and Barriers

In the luxury sector, Comité Colbert members report limited AI adoption, with fewer than two of 20 examined use cases deployed on average, and barriers centered on expertise and resources, data management, and intellectual property concerns for generative AI<cite id="36">fewer than two of the 20 use cases examined... have been adopted... barriers... expertise and resources (an issue for 55% of Maisons)... data management concerns... risks related to intellectual property rights, especially for generative AI</cite>. Despite limited adoption, each Maison is testing or planning more than five additional use cases, with large firms deploying three times as many use cases as smaller rivals; the gap is expected to narrow as generative AI becomes more accessible and less costly<cite id="36">Each Maison is currently testing or planning more than five additional use cases... Large ones have deployed three times as many use cases as others... the gap should gradually narrow with generative AI’s rollout, as it is more accessible and less costly than analytical AI</cite>. Luxury firms prioritize operational efficiency and customer relations, with adoption rates for AI-based sales forecasting around 60% and stock allocation around 50%, while team augmentation and creative uses remain limited<cite id="36">use cases linked to operational efficiency are most popular: 60% of Maisons have adopted or are testing AI-based sales forecasting solutions and the equivalent proportion is 50% for stock allocation</cite>.

# Outlook and Recommendations

Consulting firms consistently emphasize the need for strong leadership, clear vision, and structured governance to achieve AI value at scale. McKinsey & Company’s survey shows that organizations are beginning to create the structures and processes that lead to meaningful value from gen AI, with larger companies progressing more quickly<cite id="34">Organizations are beginning to create the structures and processes that lead to meaningful value from gen AI</cite>. BCG’s research indicates that future-built companies succeed by linking strong leadership, ambitious vision, and near-term bottom-line improvements with long-term skills, workflows, and technology investments, thereby widening the AI value gap<cite id="47">future-built companies are distinguished by five interlinked strategies... they define their AI programs with ambitious cost and revenue targets from top management... and they mandate near-term bottom-line improvements while developing new skills, workflows, and technology</cite>. Deloitte’s survey highlights that organizations are redesigning workflows and elevating governance as they experiment with AI, underscoring the importance of risk-aware adoption and structured change<cite id="58">Organizations are redesigning workflows, elevating governance, and mitigating more risks as they experiment with AI</cite>. Talent development and upskilling remain central to sustaining adoption, as evidenced by Accenture’s AI Academy, IBM’s internal gen AI outcomes, KPMG’s AI assistants and reskilling, and PwC’s AI-driven audit and assurance services<cite id="54">Accenture’s AI Academy aims to upskill 100,000 employees by 2025</cite><cite id="2">IBM consultants are seeing productivity gains and acceleration of work from gen AI</cite><cite id="59">KPMG’s AI-powered personal assistant... 60% of employees... spend more time on valuable work; KPMG is using AI to improve processes and outcomes while reskilling and upskilling its workforce</cite><cite id="58">PwC’s AI portfolio spans automation, analytics, and generative AI, with a focus on driving efficiency and innovation across industries, including AI for audit and assurance</cite>.

# Conclusion

International consulting firms are scaling AI investments and services, with a clear emphasis on client outcomes and internal transformation. While momentum is strong and early results are emerging, only a small share of organizations are achieving AI value at scale, reinforcing the need for strategic leadership, governance, and talent development<cite id="47">Only 5% of companies in our 2025 study of more than 1,250 firms worldwide are achieving AI value at scale</cite><cite id="34">Organizations are beginning to create the structures and processes that lead to meaningful value from gen AI</cite>. By combining robust governance, clear vision, and upskilling programs, consulting firms are positioning themselves to deliver sustainable AI value across industries and functions, while helping clients navigate the complex landscape of adoption, risk, and innovation<cite id="58">Organizations are redesigning workflows, elevating governance, and mitigating more risks as they experiment with AI</cite><cite id="54">Accenture Applied Intelligence offers a broad portfolio of AI services... and has launched the AI Academy to upskill 100,000 employees by 2025</cite>.

The use cases supported by analytical AI are among the most widely deployed by the Maisons.
With numerous pilots underway, AI adoption is set to accelerate over the next 12–24 months: Each Maison is currently testing or planning more than five additional use cases.
There are significant disparities in the level of AI adoption, depending on the size of the Maison: Large ones have deployed three times as many use cases as others. However, the gap should gradually narrow with generative AI’s rollout, as it is more accessible and less costly than analytical AI. On average, a large Maison is testing or planning 5.8 use cases, compared with 5.3 at small and medium-sized rivals.
The barriers to AI adoption cited by Maisons mostly relate to expertise and resources (an issue for 55% of Maisons in our study), data management concerns (an inhibiting factor for about 30% of respondents), and risks related to intellectual property rights, especially for generative AI solutions.
Of the four strategic objectives served by AI—operational efficiency, customer relations, augmentation of teams, and enrichment of creative functions—use cases linked to operational efficiency are most popular: 60% of Maisons have adopted or are testing AI-based sales forecasting solutions and the equivalent proportion is 50% for stock allocation.
AI is also an effective lever to bring Maisons closer to their customers, by using, for example, personalized content generation tools or customer segmentation tools, beyond the enhancement of pre-existing solutions for clienteling (the building of long-term relationships with key customers).
The industry is also reflecting on how to use AI tools to augment teams by freeing up time and focusing energies on the most valuable tasks. However, implementation remains very limited at this early stage of the technology’s maturity.
Luxury Maisons show the most reserve when it comes to using AI within the creative process. With an adoption rate of less than 5%, acceptance remains limited. Those Maisons that are beginning to explore the use of AI in this field are doing it in a way that doesn’t question the role and contribution of their creative director, but rather enlarges their sources of inspiration and accelerates visualization of future products.
To seize the value creation opportunities offered by AI, Maisons have a number of imperatives. They need to put AI at the heart of executive committee business priorities, measuring and sharing its impact in an impartial way; accelerate the modernization and harmonization of tech and data foundations; strengthen their capabilities for handling unstructured data; set up robust governance to ensure fluid coordination between business- and technology-oriented teams; and navigate the delicate process of roadmap prioritization and funding. Lastly, showing clear support for human talent (during role redefinition, training, communication, etc.) will be key to fostering buy-in and successfully integrating AI tools into a Maison’s day-to-day activities.
The potential of AI for the luxury sector appears to be huge, and the number of ongoing pilots suggests that adoption levels will at least double soon. As exploration of AI's far-reaching impact continues, the aim of this paper is to provide an overview of the state of AI in financial services, along with key open questions and potential risks to be considered by business leaders, policy-makers and customers. Key insights: Financial services businesses with their data-rich and language-heavy operations are uniquely positioned to capitalize on the developments of AI and have been doing so for years. More recently, with the developments of generative AI (genAI), research indicates that 32-39% of the work performed across capital markets, insurance and banking businesses has high potential to be fully automated and 34-37% holds high augmentation potential. This has driven a significant increase in new AI investment. In 2023, financial services firms spent $35 billion on AI, with projected investments across banking, insurance, capital markets and payments businesses expected to reach $97 billion by 2027. With this sizeable investment, financial services are one of the most heavily invested industries in AI, with prominent use cases across the enterprise where automation and machine learning are streamlining tasks, reducing operational costs and improving accuracy. With much of the existing AI adoption in financial services largely focused on driving efficiency, the attention of business leaders is now shifting towards revenue growth opportunities. Backend applications will continue to be important; in addition, approximately 70% of financial services executives believe AI will directly contribute to revenue growth in the coming years. The rapid maturing of AI, coupled with an expanding list of applicable uses, is pushing the industry towards reinvention at an unprecedented - and often uncomfortable - speed and scale. As technological developments accelerate, the integration of various emerging innovations, such as small language models, AI agents and quantum computing will drive both innovation and uncertainty across financial services. This shift will continue to challenge business leaders, policy-makers and regulators. Looking ahead, financial services stakeholders must increase collaboration to address key risks such as data transparency, privacy, cybersecurity and the spread of misinformation, while also closing policy gaps that could hinder the use and innovation of AI. Overcoming these challenges is essential to ensuring that AI can be leveraged effectively and responsibly across the industry, now and in the future.</summary><hostname>SSRN</hostname><publisher>World Economic Forum</publisher><url>https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=3366846</url><publish_time>2025年1月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:52"><title>HfS Blueprint Guide: Industry 4.0 Services</title><summary>In the last few centuries, the world has experienced three industrial revolutions that have shaped our industrial processes. problem: In ecology, how do birds achieve precise location and direction navigation during migration? What cues and disturbances influence this process?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
## Executive summary

Birds navigate with a multi-sensory system that integrates a magnetic compass, celestial cues, the sun and stars, and landmarks, supported by innate and learned components. This system is sensitive to environmental and anthropogenic disturbances, including communication towers, artificial light, wind, weather, and geomagnetic storms, which can disrupt orientation and migration success<cite id="1">Birds use multiple sensors and combine innate and learned information to navigate, and their system adapts to environmental changes</cite><cite id="6">Birds use a magnetic compass and map sense, integrating multiple cues</cite><cite id="47">Homing pigeons use a combination of a magnetic compass and sun compass, with a cognitive map</cite><cite id="32">Migratory birds adjust schedules and navigation in response to weather and climate</cite><cite id="38">Tall towers with bright lights increase collision risk for nocturnal migrants</cite><cite id="40">Artificial light at night can disorient migrating birds</cite><cite id="44">Wind and weather conditions strongly affect migration timing and routes</cite><cite id="45">Geomagnetic storms can disrupt animal magnetoreception</cite>.

## How birds achieve precise location and directional navigation

Birds use a magnetic compass to sense direction and a magnetic map to infer latitude, often relying on a light-dependent radical-pair mechanism in cryptochrome proteins in the retina to detect the magnetic field’s intensity and inclination and thus determine geographic position<cite id="6">Magnetic compass and map senses; inclination and intensity cues</cite><cite id="41">Radical-pair mechanism in cryptochromes as a leading hypothesis for magnetoreception</cite>. Experiments show that birds can detect the direction of the magnetic field and adjust orientation accordingly, indicating a functional magnetic compass<cite id="6">Evidence for direction sensing via magnetic field orientation</cite><cite id="47">Avian magnetic compass orientation in controlled settings</cite>. In addition to the magnetic sense, birds use celestial cues, including the sun and polarized light patterns in the sky, and stars for navigation<cite id="6">Celestial cues used in navigation</cite><cite id="47">Celestial compasses (sun and polarized light) in birds</cite><cite id="48">Star compass orientation in nocturnal migrants</cite>. Landmarks also play a role, particularly for shorter movements and homing, with studies showing that birds integrate visual landmarks with their internal compasses<cite id="6">Landmarks as navigational cues</cite><cite id="47">Integration of landmarks with compass cues</cite>.

Homing studies demonstrate that birds combine innate and learned information: they are born with a wired algorithm for processing cues and build an experience-based database of their surroundings, which they refine over time<cite id="1">Birds are born with wired navigation algorithms and add learned data to their database</cite>. The map sense appears to be based on environmental features such as the Earth’s magnetic field, which provides location information with high resolution, enabling precise route-finding<cite id="6">Animals can compute map coordinates using the magnetic field with high resolution</cite><cite id="47">Map sense and compass integration for navigation</cite>.

## How cues and disturbances influence navigation

Weather and wind conditions strongly influence migration timing and routes, with birds adjusting their schedules and navigation strategies to cope with changing atmospheric conditions<cite id="32">Weather and climate drive adjustments in migration timing and navigation</cite><cite id="44">Wind and weather conditions affect migration dynamics</cite>. Artificial light at night can disorient migrating birds, particularly during nocturnal flights, by interfering with celestial navigation and potentially overwhelming or misdirecting their compass systems<cite id="40">Artificial light at night can disorient migrating birds</cite>. Communication towers pose a major hazard because their height and steady lights confuse birds, leading to collisions and high mortality for nocturnal migrants<cite id="38">Tall towers with bright lights increase collision risk for nocturnal migrants</cite>.

Magnetic disturbances, such as geomagnetic storms, can disrupt magnetoreception by altering the stability and detectability of the magnetic field, which may interfere with both the magnetic compass and map senses<cite id="45">Geomagnetic storms can disrupt animal magnetoreception</cite>. Other anthropogenic factors, including radiofrequency radiation from Wi‑Fi and mobile devices, raise concerns about potential impacts on navigation, although direct evidence linking these exposures to avian navigation failure remains limited and requires further study<cite id="31">Potential biological effects of Wi‑Fi/2.4 GHz radiation; limited direct evidence on avian navigation</cite>. Climate change is also reshaping migration patterns, with shifts in timing and routes that challenge birds’ ability to maintain precise navigation under rapidly changing environmental conditions<cite id="29">Climate change alters migration timing and routes</cite><cite id="28">Climate change impacts migration patterns and species distributions</cite>.

## Integrating cues and adapting to change

Birds do not rely on a single cue but integrate multiple sources of information, switching among cues depending on availability and environmental context<cite id="6">Integration of multiple cues in navigation</cite>. This multi-sensory integration, combined with innate algorithms and learned experience, allows birds to remain flexible and adapt to environmental variability and change<cite id="1">Birds combine innate algorithms with learned experience and adapt to environmental changes</cite><cite id="47">Integration of compass cues and cognitive mapping</cite>. Behavioral and ecological studies emphasize that navigation is tightly coupled to weather and resource conditions, reinforcing the need for adaptive strategies during long-distance migration<cite id="32">Migration timing and navigation are tightly coupled to weather and resources</cite><cite id="44">Weather conditions strongly affect migration</cite>.

## Uncertainties and future directions

While the magnetic compass and radical‑pair mechanism in cryptochromes are leading hypotheses for magnetoreception, the exact molecular and cellular pathways remain an active area of research<cite id="41">Radical‑pair mechanism in cryptochromes; ongoing research</cite>. The role of magnetite‑based receptors is less well supported in birds compared to other cues, highlighting gaps in understanding the full complement of magnetoreceptors<cite id="43">Magnetite hypothesis has limited support in birds</cite>. Although anthropogenic disturbances such as artificial light and communication towers are well documented as hazards, the precise mechanisms by which they interfere with navigation require more targeted studies to inform mitigation strategies<cite id="40">Artificial light at night disorients birds</cite><cite id="38">Tower design and lighting features increase collision risk</cite>. Overall, the evidence supports a multi‑cued, adaptable system that is sensitive to both natural and human‑induced disturbances during migration<cite id="6">Multiple cues and adaptability in avian navigation</cite><cite id="38">Anthropogenic structures disrupt orientation</cite><cite id="40">Artificial light disrupts navigation</cite><cite id="45">Magnetic disturbances can interfere with magnetoreception</cite>.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="migratory birds use of landmarks and learned cues review 2010 2023" search_time="2026年5月19日11时48分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:46"><title>On clusters and formations: birds flying in groups</title><summary>Flocks of birds perform some aerial phenomena, which have amazed many of its viewers. This thesis is a literature review, which concerns the three major questions of 'When', 'How' and 'Why' birds fly in flocks. Flying flocks are roughly dividable in two types: ball shaped clusters and line formations. Whereas cluster flying is commonly used throughout the year by groups of birds, for example while transiting between their roosting and their foraging sites, formation flight is almost specifically used for migration. The departure time of migration is a critical moment in the annual cycle of the bird. The exact moment of departure is an optimization of several external and internal factors, including migrating distance, energy reserves and weather conditions. Clusters have a three-dimensional structure and tend to be rather disorganized. When a predator is nearby, clusters often start to perform rapid manoeuvres. Previously believed to be coordinated by telepathy or electromagnetic communication, due to high-speed filming scientists have determined that these manoeuvres are initiated by one individual bird and followed by the rest of the flock. The individual fulfilling the role of initiator changes from moment to moment. The most likely explanation for movement in a cluster is a self-organization mechanism where each bird applies a few behavioural rules in response to local information from neighbouring birds. There are different kinds of formations, ranging from an acute V-formation to a U-shaped bow. Although the total energy saving is the same for different formations, it differs for individual birds in the group. In an acute formation, the leader gains little or no energy savings, while in a U-formation the energy savings are more egalitarian. A reason for obtaining a specific formation may be related to kin-selection or reciprocity, although no empirical evidence for this hypothesis has been found yet. Several specific reasons have been put forward for birds to fly in clusters, mainly regarding predation prevention. These advantages include increased predator detection, a dilution effect, physical protection of neighbours and a confusion effect. Two hypotheses exist for a structured formation, like the well known V-shape. One is the aerodynamic advantage hypothesis, in which birds conserve energy by taking advantage of the upwash vortices created by the wings of the birds in front. The other is the communication and orientation hypothesis, in which birds make use of their position for their combined orientation experience and visual communication. These explanations are not mutually exclusive, and various studies have given support to both of them. However, no conclusive evidence has been found for any of the both hypotheses. There is still a debate going on between supporters and criticasters of both hypotheses which remains unsolved upon till now. A review of the literature concerning the subject of flock flying shows that the use (the 'When') and the organization (the 'How') of flock flying have been thoroughly researched, which has led to a consistent view on these subjects. However, thorough research on the main reasons for flock flying (the 'Why') has not given a clear view yet. Also behavioural aspects of the organization and departure are still shrouded. These subjects still raise enough questions to provide research options for years to come.</summary><hostname>Student Theses Faculty of Science and Engineering</hostname><publisher>Degree Thesis</publisher><author_list><author name="Alma Streefkerk" affiliation="Animal Ecology - University of Groningen" /></author_list><url>https://fse.studenttheses.ub.rug.nl/8947/1/Biol_Bc_2010_ACPStreefkerk.pdf</url><publish_time>2009年9月15日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:47"><title>The Navigation System of

<answer>Introduction and Scope
Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is commonly associated with microbial evolution, where it drives rapid adaptation through the acquisition of foreign genes. In eukaryotes, HGT has played an important role in genome evolution, though its impact is often overshadowed by the greater prevalence and more advanced understanding of HGT in prokaryotes. The number of well-supported eukaryotic HGT cases—including transfers between plants, animals, and even between multicellular eukaryotes—is now expanding rapidly, particularly in specialized ecological niches<cite id="1">HGT has had an important role in eukaryotic genome evolution and the number of well-supported cases is expanding rapidly</cite><cite id="6">HGT is important in eukaryotic evolution and the number of well-supported cases is increasing</cite>. This review focuses on HGT in non-microbial eukaryotic systems, especially in plants and animals, and evaluates its evolutionary significance and potential benefits<cite id="1">Review of HGT in eukaryotic evolution</cite>.

Plant-to-Animal HGT: Innate Immunity Genes
One of the most compelling examples of plant-to-animal HGT involves drosomycin-type antifungal peptides (DTAFPs), which are innate immunity components in both plants and Drosophila. A multigene family of DTAFPs was discovered in the nematode Caenorhabditis remanei, with multiple transcriptionally active genes and upregulation after fungal challenge. Synthetic cremycin-5 showed antifungal activity against filamentous fungi and human pathogenic yeasts, with low hemolysis and high serum stability<cite id="11">DTAFP multigene family in C. remanei, transcriptional activity, upregulation after fungal challenge, and functional activity of synthetic cremycin-5</cite>. The distribution of DTAFPs in Ecdysozoa (nematodes, arthropods, tardigrades) contrasts with their absence in fungi and protozoa and their prevalence in plants, providing strong evidence for a plant-to-ecdysozoan horizontal transfer of a disease resistance gene<cite id="11">Distribution pattern supports plant-to-ecdysozoan horizontal transfer of a disease resistance gene</cite>.

Beyond innate immunity, HGT has also been implicated in the evolution of insect herbivory. The whitefly genome contains a plant-specific phenolic glucoside malonyltransferase gene, BtPMaT1, which is absent in other arthropods and confers detoxification of plant phenolic glycosides. Functional studies show that knocking down BtPMaT1 increases toxin toxicity, and transgenic tomato plants overexpressing BtPMaT1 dsRNA are almost completely resistant to whiteflies, demonstrating the adaptive benefit of this horizontally transferred gene<cite id="37">BtPMaT1 gene in whiteflies, absence in other arthropods, detoxification function, and evidence of adaptive benefit</cite>.

Plant-to-Plant HGT: Mitochondrial Genes in Amborella
HGT is not limited to transfers between plants and animals; it also occurs among plant lineages. The basal angiosperm Amborella trichopoda has acquired a substantial fraction of its mitochondrial protein genes from other land plants. Analyses indicate Amborella has acquired one or more copies of 20 of its 31 mitochondrial protein genes, totaling 26 foreign genes, with transfers from both angiosperms (especially eudicots) and nonangiosperms such as mosses. Most transferred genes are intact, consistent with functionality and/or recency of transfer, and Amborella mtDNA has sustained proportionately more HGT than any other eukaryotic, or perhaps even prokaryotic, genome yet examined<cite id="16">Amborella has acquired 26 foreign mitochondrial genes from diverse donors, many intact and functional</cite>. Experimental work has further demonstrated that entire mitochondrial genomes can be transferred via mitochondrial fusion, reinforcing the mechanism by which plant-to-plant HGT can occur<cite id="31">Experimental evidence for horizontal transfer of entire genomes via mitochondrial fusion in Amborella</cite>.

Animal-to-Animal HGT: Parasites and Host Manipulation
HGT also occurs between animals, including multicellular eukaryotes. In the context of parasitism, nematomorph parasites induce their insect hosts to seek water for reproduction. Transcriptomic analyses of this interaction revealed numerous host-derived genes in nematomorphs that are frequently upregulated during host manipulation. These findings suggest a possible general role for HGT in the molecular mechanisms underlying host manipulation by manipulative parasites, even though evidence of HGT between multicellular eukaryotes remains scarce but is increasing<cite id="21">Evidence of HGT in nematomorph-driven host manipulation and the increasing recognition of HGT between multicellular eukaryotes</cite>.

Mechanistic and Ecological Context
HGT is more readily observed between organisms that are intimately associated or establish cell–cell contacts, such as in mutualistic or parasitic interactions, which may facilitate direct DNA transfer. Comparative genomic analyses have documented multiple instances of HGT from prokaryotes to eukaryotes and even between eukaryotes, underscoring the broader scope of HGT beyond microbial systems<cite id="33">HGT is prevalent between organisms with intimate associations and has been documented among prokaryotes and eukaryotes</cite><cite id="7">HGT has shaped the web of life, including transfers between prokaryotes and eukaryotes and even between multicellular eukaryotes</cite>. In addition to classical mechanisms, recent work highlights how HGT can be mediated by extracellular vesicles and cell-free DNA in eukaryotes, broadening our understanding of transfer pathways<cite id="26">HGT can occur via extracellular vesicles and cell-free DNA in eukaryotes</cite>.

Evolutionary Significance and Benefits
The evolutionary significance of HGT in plants and animals appears tied to adaptation in specialized niches. In insects, horizontally transferred genes such as BtPMaT1 directly confer adaptive advantages by enabling detoxification of plant defenses, supporting the idea that HGT can drive host adaptability and ecological success<cite id="37">Adaptive benefit of BtPMaT1 in whiteflies for detoxifying plant phenolics</cite>. Similarly, plant-derived antifungal peptides in nematodes and arthropods are functional disease resistance genes, with synthetic variants demonstrating antifungal activity and desirable pharmacological properties, indicating potential benefits for innate immunity<cite id="11">Functional antifungal activity and desirable stability of synthetic cremycin-5</cite>. In plants, the acquisition of numerous mitochondrial genes from other land plants suggests that HGT can contribute to metabolic or functional innovations that enhance fitness, particularly in basal angiosperms like Amborella<cite id="16">Multiple functional mitochondrial gene acquisitions in Amborella</cite>.

Frequency and Patterns
While HGT is relatively rare in plants and animals compared to microbes, its frequency appears to increase in specific ecological contexts. Comparative genomic studies have documented multiple eukaryotic HGT events, with a notable increase in evidence over recent years, especially in specialized niches where close associations facilitate transfer<cite id="1">HGT is important in eukaryotic evolution and the number of well-supported cases is increasing</cite><cite id="6">HGT varies in impact across lineages and is more prevalent in specialized niches</cite>. In plants, mitochondrial HGT has been most extensively documented, with Amborella representing an extreme case; however, other instances of plant-to-plant and plant-to-animal HGT have also been reported, indicating that such transfers are not exceptional but are often overlooked<cite id="16">Amborella mtDNA shows high rates of plant-to-plant HGT</cite><cite id="11">Plant-to-ecdysozoan HGT of an innate immunity gene</cite><cite id="37">Plant-to-insect HGT conferring detoxification</cite>.

Uncertainties and Future Directions
Despite growing evidence, uncertainties remain regarding the overall prevalence of HGT in plants and animals and the mechanisms that drive its occurrence. For example, while Amborella exhibits a high rate of mitochondrial HGT, it is unclear whether such rates are representative of other plant lineages or whether many transfers are ancient and nonfunctional. Similarly, while animal-to-animal HGT appears to play a role in parasitic manipulation, more widespread examples and mechanistic details are still emerging<cite id="16">Amborella shows proportionally more HGT than other eukaryotes, but broader prevalence is unclear</cite><cite id="21">Evidence of HGT in host manipulation is increasing but remains scarce</cite>. Continued comparative genomic analyses, transcriptomic profiling of interactions, and experimental approaches to test functionality will be essential to resolve these uncertainties and quantify the role of HGT in eukaryotic evolution<cite id="33">Comparative genomics can reveal HGT between organisms with close associations</cite><cite id="8">Experimental reconstruction of HGT and endosymbiotic gene transfer is feasible</cite>.</answer>

problem: How to conduct comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of space targets in the cislunar space, and support the effectiveness of short-term cislunar space tracking and monitoring tasks?

<answer>
# Executive Summary

Cislunar space situational awareness (CSSA) is the process of knowing what is in cislunar space, where it is, and what it is doing, to support traffic management, collision avoidance, and mission safety. Comprehensive and accurate situational awareness requires a hybrid sensor architecture that integrates ground-based and space-based assets, optimized constellation design, visibility/observability-aware tasking, and robust data fusion and metrics to evaluate performance and effectiveness. The report synthesizes data-driven guidance for building and operating CSSA capabilities and for supporting short-term tracking and monitoring tasks, with actionable recommendations and quantitative insights from recent literature<cite id="26">cislunar regime requires hybrid ground and spaceborne sensors; payload and constellation design for solar/exclusion avoidance</cite><cite id="1">constellation design and sensor-tasking for CSSA</cite>.

# 1. Foundations of Cislunar Situational Awareness

CSSA is the art and science of maintaining custody of space objects in cislunar space, including active spacecraft and orbital debris, to support traffic management and collision avoidance. As human and commercial activity expands into cislunar, persistent overwatch is essential to prevent collisions and protect investments in key loci such as near-rectilinear halo orbits (NRHOs), L1/L2, and L4/L5, and the transit routes connecting them<cite id="26">protect activity in cislunar loci and routes; need for persistent overwatch</cite>. Ground-based optical and infrared systems face solar and lunar exclusions, while radar is impractical at cislunar distances; thus, a hybrid architecture combining ground sensors with spaceborne sensors is the most viable solution<cite id="26">radar challenged at cislunar distances; optical/infrared face exclusions; hybrid ground+spaceborne sensors</cite>.

# 2. Sensor Architecture and Hybrid Design

Ground-based sensors include optical and infrared telescopes, the Deep Space Network (DSN), and other RF networks. Spaceborne sensors can be placed in libration-point orbits, NRHOs, or on the Moon, and constellation design can be tailored to avoid solar/lunar exclusions and provide persistent coverage over key cislunar loci<cite id="26">spaceborne sensors at libration points, NRHOs, or on the Moon; constellation design to avoid exclusions</cite>. A recent MILP-based formulation couples constellation design with sensor-tasking to generate near-optimal observer placements and pointing directions, enabling fast assessment of CSSA constellations and supporting decision-making under trade-offs<cite id="1">MILP-based constellation design and sensor-tasking with field-of-view and pointing</cite>. Concurrent optimization of satellite phasing and tasking can further improve the effectiveness of space-based phasing constellations for CSSA<cite id="3">concurrent optimization of phasing and tasking for CSSA</cite>.

# 3. Ground-Based Optical Observations: Visibility, Timing, and Observability

Ground-based optical tracking is feasible for objects within the “Cone of Shame” near the Moon, as demonstrated by successful tracking of the China Chang’e 5 spacecraft and its booster from ~2° from the Moon using a 0.5-meter telescope and combined RF/optical data<cite id="11">optical recovery and custody of Chang’e 5 all the way to the Moon; feasibility down to ~2 degrees</cite>. Visibility and observability are strongly influenced by viewing geometry: angle-only optical observations from an equatorial ground station show optimal epochs aligned with specific lunar phases and local times, as quantified by visibility-informed covariance metrics<cite id="36">visibility-informed covariance analysis; optimal epochs by lunar phase and local time</cite>. Reinforcement learning agents have been used to optimally task narrow-field-of-view ground-based optical telescopes in cislunar, outperforming random policies for RSO tracking<cite id="7">deep reinforcement learning for ground-based optical tasking in cislunar</cite>.

# 4. Space-Based Sensors and Constellations

Space-based sensors can eliminate solar/lunar exclusions and approach targets more closely, improving detection and tracking of small objects. A mixed-integer programming approach for facility location in CSSA uses a time-expanded p-Median formulation to optimally place observers on discretized libration-point orbits and determine pointing directions, enabling fast constellation design and tasking<cite id="1">time-expanded p-Median for observer placement and pointing</cite>. Space-based phasing constellations can be optimized in concert with sensor tasking to maximize coverage and tracking effectiveness<cite id="3">phasing and tasking optimization for space-based phasing constellations</cite>. For quantum-entangled “Spooky Radar” in Lissajous orbits around L1/L4/L5, analysis shows order-of-magnitude improvements in orbit determination accuracy compared to conventional ground-based optical and radar mixes, when combined with ground sensors in an Unscented Kalman Filter<cite id="6">Spooky Radar from Lissajous orbits improves position/velocity estimates by an order of magnitude</cite>.

# 5. Deep Space Network and Radio Tracking for Short-Term Monitoring

The DSN provides radiometric tracking for deep-space missions, including cislunar transport and lunar landings. Navigation studies show expected performance for standard radiometric data types (Doppler, ranging, and one-way equivalents) during Earth–Moon transport, lunar orbit, and descent/landing, supporting short-term tracking and navigation during critical mission phases<cite id="31">DSN navigation performance for lunar transport using radiometric data types</cite><cite id="32">ground-based radiometric tracking combined with onboard sensors supports trans-lunar and landing navigation</cite>. Radio tracking remains a backbone for orbit determination and state updates, especially when optical visibility is limited by exclusions or scheduling constraints<cite id="32">ground-based radiometric tracking combined with other sensors characterizes delivery errors and landing dispersions</cite>.

# 6. Data Fusion and Orbit Determination

Effective CSSA relies on fusing complementary sensor data and models to reduce uncertainty and improve state estimation. For example, combining ground-based optical and spaceborne radar measurements can yield significantly better orbit estimates than conventional mixes, as demonstrated in cislunar tracking scenarios<cite id="6">fusion of ground optical/radar and spaceborne Spooky Radar improves state estimates</cite>. In general, robust orbit determination requires careful modeling of forces and sensor noise, and adaptive tasking to exploit favorable viewing geometries<cite id="36">covariance metrics quantify observability and guide favorable observation windows</cite>.

# 7. Metrics and Evaluation for Short-Term Tracking and Monitoring

Short-term tracking and monitoring effectiveness can be evaluated using visibility-informed covariance metrics and observability analyses that quantify state uncertainty as a function of lunar phase, local time, and sensor geometry<cite id="36">visibility-informed covariance identifies favorable observation windows</cite>. Tracking performance metrics such as position/velocity estimation accuracy are critical for collision-avoidance decisions; spaceborne sensors like Spooky Radar have shown order-of-magnitude improvements over ground-only mixes in orbit determination, directly supporting more effective short-term monitoring<cite id="6">order-of-magnitude improvement in state estimates supports more effective tracking</cite>. Sensor placement and pointing on periodic orbits can also be assessed for exclusion constraints and range, with recommendations for the most effective orbit types depending on sensor capabilities and exclusion angles<cite id="37">periodic-orbit geometry effectiveness for SDA under exclusion constraints</cite>.

# 8. Debris Tracking and Cataloging

Maintaining a high-fidelity debris catalog is essential for collision avoidance and traffic management in cislunar space. Studies quantify the corrective actions and maneuver costs needed to recover mission trajectories under different conjunction scenarios, highlighting how catalog fidelity directly impacts operational decisions<cite id="22">debris avoidance maneuver requirements and recovery actions for lunar/cislunar tracking</cite>. Formal coordination and requirements for lunar and cislunar debris tracking are being established to mitigate risks from micrometeoroids and orbital debris<cite id="23">requirements for lunar and cislunar orbital debris tracking</cite>.

# 9. Lunar Laser Ranging and Retroreflectors

Lunar laser ranging (LLR) uses retroreflectors on the Moon to measure distances with millimeter precision, demonstrating the capability and modeling challenges of laser ranging. While LLR is primarily a scientific endeavor, its techniques and infrastructure can inform the design of laser-based tracking and communication systems for cislunar assets<cite id="17">lunar laser ranging: technique, motivations, and millimeter precision challenges</cite><cite id="19">LLR retroreflectors and measurement techniques</cite>. The International Laser Ranging Service (ILRS) report details operations, emerging technologies, and mission support, providing a reference for laser ranging capabilities and applications beyond Earth orbit<cite id="18">ILRS operations, emerging technologies, and mission support activities</cite>.

# 10. Recommendations for Comprehensive and Accurate CSSA

- Hybrid sensor architecture: Combine ground-based optical/infrared and RF (DSN) with spaceborne sensors in libration-point or NRHO orbits, optimized to avoid solar/lunar exclusions and maximize coverage over key cislunar loci<cite id="26">hybrid ground+spaceborne sensors; exclusion avoidance</cite><cite id="1">constellation design and sensor-tasking for CSSA</cite>.
- Visibility-aware tasking: Use observability metrics and reinforcement learning to schedule observations during favorable lunar phases and local times, and to optimally point narrow-field-of-view ground telescopes<cite id="36">visibility-informed covariance identifies favorable windows</cite><cite id="7">RL-based ground optical tasking for cislunar</cite>.
- Spaceborne sensors: Consider quantum-entangled radar or other advanced sensors in Lissajous orbits around L1/L4/L5 to improve orbit determination accuracy and reduce uncertainty for short-term monitoring<cite id="6">Spooky Radar improves state estimates by an order of magnitude</cite>.
- Data fusion and modeling: Integrate complementary sensor data and high-fidelity force models in orbit determination pipelines to reduce uncertainty and support collision-avoidance decisions<cite id="6">fusion of ground and spaceborne sensors improves state estimation</cite><cite id="32">ground-based radiometric tracking combined with onboard sensors</cite>.
- Debris cataloging and requirements: Establish and maintain a high-fidelity debris catalog, and coordinate requirements for lunar/cislunar debris tracking to support traffic management and collision avoidance<cite id="22">debris avoidance maneuver requirements and recovery</cite><cite id="23">requirements for lunar and cislunar debris tracking</cite>.
- Constellation design: Apply MILP and facility-location formulations to design and task CSSA constellations, and optimize phasing and tasking for space-based phasing constellations<cite id="1">MILP-based constellation design and sensor-tasking</cite><cite id="3">concurrent optimization of phasing and tasking</cite>.
- Lunar-based observatories: Evaluate lunar-based optical/infrared assets to mitigate exclusions and provide persistent coverage near the Moon<cite id="29">lunar-based optical observatories to mitigate solar/lunar exclusions</cite>.

# 11. Supporting Evidence and Limitations

The recommendations are grounded in recent literature on CSSA constellation design, visibility/observability analyses, sensor performance, and debris tracking. While the evidence supports hybrid architectures, visibility-aware tasking, and spaceborne sensors for improved tracking, some capabilities (e.g., lunar-based observatories) require further demonstration and investment<cite id="26">hybrid architecture and exclusion avoidance</cite><cite id="36">observability guidance</cite><cite id="29">lunar-based observatories concept</cite>. The effectiveness of short-term tracking can be quantified using covariance metrics and orbit-determination benchmarks, but operational success also depends on real-time scheduling, sensor availability, and data fusion pipelines<cite id="36">covariance metrics for observability</cite><cite id="6">orbit-determination performance benchmarks</cite>.

# Conclusion

Comprehensive and accurate situational awareness of cislunar space requires a hybrid sensor architecture, visibility-aware tasking, and optimized constellation design to overcome solar/lunar exclusions and support persistent coverage. Integrating ground-based optical and RF assets with spaceborne sensors, using advanced tasking and data fusion, and maintaining a high-fidelity debris catalog are essential to enable effective short-term tracking and monitoring in cislunar space<cite id="26">hybrid architecture and persistent overwatch</cite><cite id="1">constellation design and tasking</cite><cite id="36">visibility/observability metrics</cite><cite id="6">spaceborne sensors improve tracking accuracy</cite><cite id="22">debris cataloging and maneuver requirements</cite>.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="cislunar space situational awareness architecture review NASA roadmap DSO cataloging near-Earth libration point space traffic management" search_time="2026年5月19日11时48分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:26"><title>Payload and Constellation Design for a Solar Exclusion-Avoiding Cislunar SSA Fleet</title><summary>As the predicted and realized volume of governmental and commercial activity in orbit continues to grow, the number of regimes in which activity can be found may similarly be expected to increase. As an example, plans for activity in the cislunar regime are being developed in growing depth [1]. The cislunar regime may be thought of as the region extending from above the Geosynchronous Earth Orbit (GEO) neighborhood – near stationary orbit altitude – to the Lagrange point on the far side of Luna, Earth’s moon, but a few key loci in this regime will be more populated than others. Near-rectilinear halo orbits (NRHOs) provide relative stability near Luna itself, as do two of the aligned Lagrange points (L1 and L2), and the L4 and L5 points provide long-term orbital stability as well as comparatively simple access to solar power. These loci, all of which are possible locations for a lunar gateway station or long-term scientific emplacements, and all transit routes and communications relay sites linking these loci, may be of critical interest for a successful expansion of human economic activity into the trillion-dollar opportunity that the near-term future in space represents. As such, it will be very important to maintain space situational awareness (SSA) overwatch on these loci and the routes and links connecting them, to preserve investments made and protect the activity these infrastructure elements support. A key part of this overwatch will be maintaining custody of objects in this regime, including active objects and any debris, to support appropriate traffic management. This overwatch should be maintained persistently, to avoid situations where collisions are not detected until after they become unavoidable. Because the cislunar regime includes regions which are extremely distant from the surface of the Earth, it is challenging to use radar systems to track smaller objects there. Optical and infrared systems face the challenge of solar and lunar exclusions, when bright emissions or reflections from astronomical bodies can obscure the space objects in this regime. Given these physical limitations, the most viable solution is to operate a ground network supplemented by spaceborne sensors. As commercial SSA networks continue to proliferate and supplement government sensors, the physical limitations will be minimized but not fully defeated. Flying sensors in space can completely eliminate astronomical body exclusions (including lunar and solar exclusions) through clever constellation design, which may include the use of sensors at Lagrange points, in GEO, or in highly elliptical orbits with apogees at multiple of the GEO radius (called high orbits with profound eccentricity, or HOPE trajectories), and can also address range limitations by approaching Luna more closely than the Earth’s surface ever does. This paper will focus on the initial analysis and design of a sensor payload which can operate from orbit to support a cislunar SSA network, flying in a constellation uniquely designed to deliver constant coverage while requiring the smallest amount of cost outlay. Such a payload, if matched to the appropriate sensor network design, could offer protective overwatch to the extensive orbital infrastructure that the cislunar regime may soon contain. First, the utility of HOPE orbits in providing visibility to key loci in the cislunar regime is modeled. Second, first-order cost estimates for commercial-grade (i.e., non-exquisite) spaceborne and ground-based sensors are generated and compared, and finally an assessment of the relative sizes of the ground arm and spaceborne arm of a hybrid sensor network is combined with a simple commonality analysis to determine opportunities for cost savings.</sum

Naturally, interest in SmallSat capabilities extends outside of low Earth orbit for a variety of science and technology demonstration applications. As with larger missions, near-term deep-space SmallSats will more than likely rely on telecommunications and tracking via NASA's Deep Space Network or similar facilities. Given the predicted growth in the number of deep space missions, effective use of telecommunication resources will be more critical than ever, even with Multiple Spacecraft Per Aperture capability. In particular, SmallSat missions will likely face stricter limitations on two-way contact with the tracking stations, thus making other options like one-way data types more attractive. While all missions must eventually develop their own detailed navigation plans, a common set of references is needed to support SmallSat missions, especially in the early development phases. Our investigation provides this initial survey of expected navigation performance for standard radiometric data types, from traditional two-way Doppler and ranging capabilities to one-way equivalents, including delta-differential one-way range. This study examines the nominal performance that can be obtained using the current best estimate of the vehicle, sensor, and environment models. This work develops a visibility-informed covariance analysis framework to evaluate how lunar phase and Earth’s rotation influence the tracking of spacecraft on cislunar periodic orbits. Spacecraft dynamics are modeled using the circular restricted three-body problem, and angle-only optical observations from an equatorial ground station are simulated across a grid of initial observation epochs defined by lunar phase and time-of-day angles. The analysis computes heuristic, covariance-based metrics to quantify state uncertainty and identify favorable observation windows. Results reveal strong dependence of observability on viewing geometry, with optimal epochs aligning with specific lunar phases and local times. These findings provide actionable guidance for mission planning, highlighting how timing and orbit selection can improve state estimation accuracy, ensure flight safety, and enhance SDA capabilities in the Earth-Moon system.</summary><hostname>AMOS Conference</hostname><author_list><author name="Evangelina A. ## Executive Summary

Ion trap quantum computing has progressed from small-scale demonstrations to systems that can run meaningful algorithms and approach fault-tolerance thresholds, and several scaling strategies are now being actively pursued. The most promising paths are quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures that move ions on microchip traps, modular systems that link multiple QCCD “modules” via high-fidelity matter links, and hybrid approaches that combine microchip traps with fiber or photon-based interconnects. These strategies are being co-designed with near-term applications such as quantum chemistry, optimization, and error correction, and early results suggest they can sustain high-fidelity operations at modest ion counts while addressing physical limits to further scaling on a single trap<cite id="11">QCCD race-track processor with 32 qubits and high-fidelities</cite><cite id="12">High-fidelity matter-link between ion-trap modules</cite><cite id="6">Overview of scaling strategies and limits in ion traps</cite><cite id="28">Review of scaling trapped-ion processors to hundreds or thousands of qubits</cite><cite id="3">Overview of cloud-accessible hardware for chemistry</cite>.

## Overview of Ion Trap Scaling and Recent Progress

A central insight in ion trap scaling is that trapped-ion qubits combine exceptional coherence and near-perfect initialization and measurement with a natural two-body entangling interaction (the Coulomb force), making them attractive for large-scale systems<cite id="28">Trapped ions offer long coherence, near-unity initialization/measurement, and Coulomb-mediated entanglement</cite>. Recent QCCD systems have demonstrated 32-ion processors with electrode broadcasting, multi-layer RF routing, MOT loading, and high-fidelity operations, including applications such as QAOA, Hamiltonian simulation, and repetition-code error correction<cite id="11">Race-track QCCD with 32 qubits and applications benchmarked</cite>. These systems explicitly target future upgrades to add more qubits and capabilities, indicating a clear trajectory toward larger devices<cite id="11">Future upgrades aimed at adding more qubits and capabilities</cite>.

A complementary modular approach transfers ion qubits between adjacent microchip modules via a “quantum matter-link,” enabling inter-module connectivity while preserving ion coherence and achieving very low transport infidelity (below 7×10⁻⁸) at high rates (2424 s⁻¹). This mechanism is a practical step toward fault-tolerant, utility-scale computation by linking multiple QCCD modules<cite id="12">High-fidelity matter-link with low transport infidelity and high rate</cite>. Reviews emphasize that scaling to hundreds or thousands of qubits will require advanced architectures and technologies, and outline both the strengths and the outstanding challenges of trapped-ion QC at larger scales<cite id="28">Review of scaling to hundreds or thousands of qubits and prospects</cite><cite id="26">Challenges in scaling trapped-ion QC and mitigating decoherence and control errors</cite>.

## Proposed Scaling Strategies and Their Feasibility

### 1. QCCD Architectures on Microchip Traps

QCCD systems integrate ion traps with CMOS-compatible microchip electrodes to broadcast laser modes, route RF fields, and load ions efficiently, enabling reconfigurable qubit layouts and improved control over larger ion strings<cite id="36">Race-track QCCD with electrode broadcasting, multi-layer RF routing, and MOT loading</cite>. The recent 32-qubit race-track processor achieved average gate infidelities around 0.025% for single-qubit gates and ~0.18% for two-qubit gates, with a quantum volume of 2¹⁶ and application benchmarks including QAOA and error correction<cite id="11">Gate infidelities and QV for the race-track processor</cite>. These results suggest that QCCD can sustain high performance at modest scales and that the co-integration of control electronics is a key enabler of further scaling<cite id="36">Technologies crucial to future scalability in QCCD</cite>.

### 2. Modular QCCD with Matter Links

Modularity addresses the physical limits of single traps by linking multiple QCCD modules via matter links that transfer ions between adjacent chips. The demonstrated high-rate, low-infidelity matter link shows that inter-module connectivity can be added without degrading phase coherence, which is essential for building larger systems<cite id="12">Matter-link enabling inter-module connectivity with minimal coherence impact</cite>. This approach is complementary to QCCD and is being pursued by multiple groups as a path to fault-tolerant utility-scale computation<cite id="12">Facilitate modular QCs capable of fault-tolerant utility-scale quantum computation</cite>.

### 3. Hybrid Interconnects (Photonic and Fiber)

For applications requiring long-range connectivity or integration with other platforms, fiber- or photon-mediated entanglement can link separate ion-trap modules. Trapped ions are well-suited to remote entanglement generation and can act as high-fidelity memory nodes, which supports hybrid architectures that combine ion-trap processing with photonic interconnects<cite id="13">Remote entanglement between trapped-ion nodes via photons and high-fidelity memories</cite>. Reviews also note that remote entanglement and quantum communication networks are natural extensions of ion-trap platforms, which can help overcome the geometry and connectivity constraints of a single trap<cite id="28">Remote entanglement and quantum communication networks with trapped ions</cite>.

### 4. Alternative Scaling Schemes Within a Single Trap

In addition to QCCD and modularity, some groups explore scaling within a single trap by using two-dimensional ion crystals or dual-type qubits to increase the total qubit count while maintaining per-qubit performance<cite id="1">Exploration of 2D ion crystals and dual-type qubits to scale qubit number</cite>. These ideas aim to mitigate the cross-talk and control challenges that arise as ion strings grow longer, but they face engineering and decoherence challenges that are still under active investigation<cite id="6">Limiting factors in scaling within a single trap</cite>.

## Feasibility and Practical Implementation Challenges

A common theme across reviews is that scaling trapped-ion systems to hundreds or thousands of qubits will require advances in control, packaging, and error mitigation, as well as co-design with applications<cite id="28">Outstanding challenge: scaling to hundreds or thousands of qubits</cite><cite id="26">Mitigating decoherence and control errors as scale increases</cite>. QCCD systems have already incorporated electrode broadcasting and multi-layer RF routing to reduce mode leakage and improve uniformity, which are critical for maintaining fidelity at larger scales<cite id="36">Technologies to reduce mode leakage and improve uniformity in QCCD</cite>. Modular matter links add inter-module connectivity while preserving coherence, addressing a key practical challenge in system integration<cite id="12">High-rate, low-infidelity matter-link with no measurable phase coherence impact</cite>.

Applications co-design is an important enabler of scaling, as near-term use cases such as quantum chemistry, optimization, and simulation provide clear performance targets and motivate the development of specialized architectures and control stacks<cite id="8">Co-designing scalable ion-trap systems with applications</cite><cite id="3">Overview of cloud-accessible hardware for chemistry</cite>. Early benchmarks on QCCD processors show that algorithms like QAOA and Hamiltonian simulation can run at meaningful sizes, and error correction has been demonstrated on small-distance repetition codes, indicating that these systems are beginning to touch the regime where algorithmic speedups and error mitigation can be combined<cite id="11">Application benchmarks including QAOA, Hamiltonian simulation, and repetition-code error correction</cite>.

## Evaluation of Which Approaches Are Most Likely to Succeed

Among the proposed strategies, QCCD architectures on microchip traps and modular matter-link interconnects appear most likely to succeed in the near to midterm, given the recent experimental progress and the practicality of adding modules without sacrificing coherence<cite id="11">QCCD processor demonstrating high-fidelity operations and applications</cite><cite id="12">Matter-link enabling modular, fault-tolerant scaling</cite>. Hybrid photonic/fiber interconnects provide a complementary path for long-range connectivity and integration with other platforms, leveraging the strengths of trapped-ion memories and entanglement generation<cite id="13">Remote entanglement and memory capabilities in ion traps</cite>. Alternative scaling schemes within a single trap (e.g., 2D crystals and dual-type qubits) are promising but face more immediate engineering and decoherence challenges that may slow their progress relative to QCCD and modularity<cite id="1">Exploration of 2D crystals and dual-type qubits</cite><cite id="6">Limiting factors in current scaling approaches</cite>.

## Recommendations for Scaling to Real-World Problem Sizes

- Adopt QCCD microchip traps with electrode broadcasting and multi-layer RF routing to maximize uniformity and reduce mode leakage as ion counts grow<cite id="36">Technologies crucial to future scalability in QCCD</cite>.
- Implement modular matter-link interconnects to link multiple QCCD modules, prioritizing high transport rates and low infidelity while preserving phase coherence<cite id="12">Matter-link with high rate and low transport infidelity</cite>.
- Co-design architectures with near-term applications (e.g., quantum chemistry, optimization, and simulation) to guide control stack development and error mitigation<cite id="8">Co-designing systems with applications</cite><cite id="3">Cloud-accessible ion-trap and superconducting systems for chemistry</cite>.
- Explore hybrid photonic/fiber interconnects for long-range connectivity and integration with other quantum platforms<cite id="13">Remote entanglement and hybrid architectures</cite>.
- Monitor progress on alternative scaling schemes (e.g., 2D crystals and dual-type qubits) as engineering and decoherence challenges are resolved<cite id="1">Exploration of 2D crystals and dual-type qubits</cite>.

## Conclusion

Ion trap quantum computing is transitioning from small-scale demonstrations to larger systems that can run real algorithms and begin to explore error correction and co-design with applications. The most promising scaling strategies—QCCD microchip traps, modular matter-link interconnects, and hybrid photonic links—are already showing high-fidelity performance and practical pathways to utility-scale systems<cite id="11">QCCD performance and applications</cite><cite id="12">Modular matter-link enabling scalability</cite><cite id="13">Hybrid photonic interconnects leveraging ion memories</cite>. Continued advances in control electronics, packaging, and application-specific co-design will be decisive in turning these strategies into large-scale, real-world quantum computers<cite id="28">Review of scaling and prospects</cite><cite id="8">Co-designing scalable systems</cite>.

raw_output.raw_text: <search query="青少年发展合理安排学习生活兴趣爱好 目标方向 研究" search_time="2026年5月19日11时46分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>How Children and Adolescents Spend Time Across the World: Work, Play, and Developmental Opportunities</title><summary>The authors review studies on time use of children and adolescents around the world and discuss developmental implications of population differences. Industrialization and schooling are linked to dramatic declines in time spent on household and wage labor. This labor is often unchallenging, sometimes hazardous; developmental benefits often do not increase above a limited number of hours; hence, reduction in these activities opens time for activities that may be more developmentally beneficial. Adolescents in East Asian postindustrial societies spend this freed-up time in schoolwork, a use associated with lower intrinsic motivation but high achievement and economic productivity. Adolescents in North America spend more time in leisure, associated with greater self-direction but of an uncertain relation to development. Age, gender, and socioeconomic differences in activities and with whom time is spent are also considered. Time budgets provide a general outline of the daily socialization and developmental opportunities experienced by a population of youth. Children and adolescents who spend most of their time in routine household chores encounter a different set of socialization experiences than those who spend more of their time at play or in school settings. Some activities and social contexts may have little bearing on learning or well-being and represent "wasted" time from a developmental standpoint (S. Verma, 1995). Others represent distinct opportunities for psychosocial growth (Bronfenbrenner, 1979; Silbereisen, Noack, & Eyferth, 1986). Measurement of the time spent in these different settings provides an approximate assessment of the amount of children's daily attention engaged with the information, structure, challenges, and emotional-motivational experiences associated with each setting (Csikszentmihalyi & Larson, 1984). This article reviews findings from time-budget studies carried out in different parts of the world to provide a general outline of daily socialization experiences. We focus on amounts of time spent in basic categories of activity, such as labor, schoolwork, and leisure, and amounts of time spent with different companions (i.e., family members, peers). For each category or context of time use, we first review data on how much time children and adolescents from different populations spend in that context. Then we discuss evidence on the developmental implications of time spent in that context and raise issues regarding how time differences between populations might be related to differences in socialization outcomes. The unit of analysis for this review is the population, as represented by samples and subsamples of differing studies. In some cases, the sample for a study represents an entire nation, but in most cases, samples represent a subnational group, such as middle-class youth or rural peasants in a given locale. Our findings suggest that the changes that come with the shift of a population to industrial and postindustrial conditions, including greater family wealth and the introduction of schooling, give societies the opportunity to redirect the daily attention of youth from repetitive labor to activities that offer new possibilities for learning and psychosocial development. The data indicate that different postindustrial societies have taken different directions in how this freed-up time is spent, with differing developmental implications for their youth.</summary><hostname>Academia.edu</hostname><publisher>Psychological Bulletin</publisher><author_list><author name="Reed W Larson" affiliation="University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign" /><author name="Suman Verma" affiliation="Government Home Science College" /></author_list><url>https://www.academia.edu/download/108050594/0033-2909.125.6.70120231129-1-agblxr.pdf</url><publish_time>1999年6月1日0时0分</pu

Participants in most extracurricular activities achieved better educational outcomes than non-participants even after controlling for social class, gender, and intellectual aptitude. Participation in service and religious activities predicted lower rates of drinking and drug use.
