- Phase 4: Embed pedagogically informed feedback loops that compare performance against intended outcomes and reinforce improvements<cite id="11">feedback framework based on intended vs. achieved outcomes</cite>. Incorporate cloud-based multimodal analytics with XAI and blockchain for long-term learning analytics and stakeholder trust<cite id="3">cloud-based multimodal learning analytics with XAI and blockchain</cite>.
- Phase 5: Evaluate with user studies and longitudinal trials, measuring learning outcomes, feedback satisfaction, and personalization effectiveness<cite id="7">evaluation with teachers shows improved teaching behaviors</cite><cite id="11">athlete satisfaction with pedagogical feedback</cite>.

Conclusion
A multimodal intelligent tutoring and learning guidance system for sports is feasible and supported by evidence across vision, inertial sensing, deep learning, and reinforcement learning. Fusion of heterogeneous data streams improves motion analysis and training optimization, while AI/ML enables real-time feedback and adaptive task selection<cite id="14">fusion improves motion analysis and training optimization</cite><cite id="17">AI + IoT for intelligent training and feedback</cite><cite id="15">RL for adaptive task selection</cite>. By embedding pedagogical feedback frameworks and cloud-based multimodal analytics, the system can deliver personalized, scalable coaching that aligns with intended learning outcomes and stakeholder needs<cite id="11">pedagogical feedback framework</cite><cite id="3">cloud-based multimodal analytics with XAI and blockchain</cite>.</answer>

Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) for psychomotor skills provide an accessible, scalable, and efficient solution, compared to tutors. Despite successes in the past, the research progress seems stagnating. Part of the reasons can be due to developing ITS for a very specific skill or task. In consequence, skills and the applications of those in their entirety are not presented.
Methods
Therefore, we conducted a systematic literature review, and examined existing ITS using Harrow’s taxonomy, a skill continua framework, and dimensions of psychomotor skill learning.
Results
We observed a lack in consideration of offering different tasks to promote skill proficiency. Skills supported by ITS are majorly fine, closed, internally paced, discrete, individual, and simple skills. ITS focus majorly on technical, thus coordination aspects of motor abilities. Feedback and repetition are key methods to promote psychomotor skill learning.
Conclusion
There is potential considering other physical activities to promote skill proficiency. Similarly, it might be worth exploring ITS for skills that, for example, are gross, and open. Regarding technology use, we identified two overarching issues: measuring or presenting body movements with hardware such as depth cameras, digital styluses, and robots; and optimizing feedback or task selection with machine learning algorithms. A good CBST system includes not only good training strategies but also effective feedback design. Feedback in the motor skill domain via CBST may be synthetically designed to allow athletes to practice in a more effective way, and enhance their skill acquisition. To bridge this gap, this thesis’s purpose was to explore the design of pedagogically-informed feedback in the motor skill domain via CBST, in order to support athletes’ achievement of their intended training outcomes. This thesis presents a framework of pedagogical feedback in the motor skill domain. It draws a picture of how principles from learning transactions, competency, cybernetics, and behaviourism, can work together to build sound pedagogical feedback for the implementation of a CBST system. The key principle of the framework is to generate feedback based on the athletes’ achievement of their intended training outcome. The training outcome is conceptualised as comprising two components: a statement of capability, and a statement of the subject matter to which the capability applies. The pedagogical feedback system measures athletes’ performance and compares it against the intended training outcomes. The system then identifies any performance gap and generates feedback to reinforce better performance. Four counterbalanced experiments asked student rowers to explore the differences between the pedagogical feedback system and their current feedback system (Sean-Analysis). Pedagogical feedback was at least as good as Sean-Analysis with respect to the level of satisfaction of the athlete. problem: Could the rapeutic interventions aimed at modulating plasma metal ion concentrations represent effective preventive or therapeutic strategies against cardiovascular diseases? What types of interventions—such as supplementation—have been proposed, and is there clinical evidence supporting their feasibility and efficacy?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
Introduction

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) encompass a range of conditions, including coronary artery disease, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease, and are leading causes of mortality worldwide. Oxidative stress and metal ion imbalance have emerged as modifiable contributors to atherosclerosis and endothelial dysfunction, prompting interest in interventions that modulate plasma metal ion concentrations as either preventive or therapeutic strategies for CVDs<cite id="1">Elevated plasma free radical concentration (expression of enhanced oxidative stress) is related to different pathophysiological conditions such as ageing, cancer and diabetes. Once elevated oxidative stress occurs, accelerated atherosclerosis may be present.</cite><cite id="12">Redox active metals like iron (Fe), copper (Cu), chromium (Cr), cobalt (Co) undergo redox cycling reactions and possess the ability to produce reactive radicals such as superoxide anion radical and nitric oxide in biological systems. Disruption of metal ion homeostasis may lead to oxidative stress, a state where increased formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) overwhelms body antioxidant protection and subsequently induces DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, protein modification and other effects, all symptomatic for numerous diseases, involving cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, atherosclerosis, neurological disorders (Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease), chronic inflammation and others.</cite>. This report synthesizes epidemiological, mechanistic, and interventional evidence on cadmium, zinc, selenium, iron, and lead, and evaluates the feasibility and efficacy of targeted supplementation.

Metal Ion Imbalance and Cardiovascular Risk

Epidemiological evidence indicates that cadmium exposure is associated with increased Framingham-derived coronary risk in middle-aged and elderly populations. In the PIVUS cohort, cadmium levels were the major determinant of Framingham Risk Score in women, while copper was the major determinant in men, highlighting sex-specific associations<cite id="6">When all 11 metals were entered as independent variables together with GFR in multiple models in the Framingham Risk Score as the dependent variable, cadmium was the major determinant of the Framingham Risk Score in women (p < 0.0001, followed by zinc p = 0.03), while copper was the major determinant of the Framingham Risk Score in men (p < 0.0001, followed by inverse relations vs. aluminium p = 0.01 and nickel p = 0.01).</cite>. A nationwide study in Korean adults further showed that higher blood cadmium concentrations were linked to higher Framingham 10-year coronary heart disease risk in men across all age strata, with a 1.24-fold increase per 10-fold rise in log-transformed cadmium<cite id="7">The Framingham estimate of 10 year CHD risk was significantly associated with the log-transformed blood cadmium concentrations (p<0.05) in all age groups of Korean men, with the lowest regression coefficient (0.254) for the 40–49 years age group and the highest (0.407) for the 70–79 years age group. The 10-year Framingham risk estimate increased by 1.24-fold per 10-fold increase in log-transformed blood cadmium concentrations.</cite>. Mechanistically, cadmium induces oxidative stress and vascular injury by displacing essential metals and inhibiting antioxidant enzymes, supporting its atherogenic potential<cite id="12">Redox inactive metals, such as cadmium (Cd), arsenic (As) and lead (Pb) show their toxic effects via bonding to sulphydryl groups of proteins and depletion of glutathione.</cite>.

Zinc has been implicated in both CVD risk and outcomes. In the general population, lower plasma zinc concentrations are associated with higher Framingham-derived 10-year CVD risk, and higher zinc levels are linked to reduced risk of CVD mortality<cite id="10">Lower plasma zinc concentrations were associated with higher Framingham 10-year CVD risk (OR = 1.34, 95% CI 1.15–1.56). Higher plasma zinc concentrations were associated with lower risk of CVD mortality (OR = 0.63, 95% CI 0.47–0.84).</cite>. A large meta-analysis of randomized trials found that zinc supplementation significantly lowers triglycerides, total cholesterol, fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, insulin resistance markers, and inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers, without notable effects on HDL or blood pressure<cite id="11">Pooled findings indicated the significant lowering effects of zinc supplementation on triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), fasting blood glucose (FBG), Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1C), Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance (HOMA-IR), C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), Tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), nitric oxide (NO), malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and glutathione (GSH), with no noticeable effects on low-density lipoprotein (LDL), high-density lipoprotein (HDL), insulin, systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), aspartate transaminase (AST), and Alanine aminotransferase (ALT).</cite>. These findings suggest that zinc-targeted interventions may reduce coronary risk factors, but their direct impact on clinical CVD events requires longer-term trials.

Selenium, a component of antioxidant selenoproteins, has been evaluated for primary CVD prevention. A Cochrane review of nine RCTs with 19,655 participants found no significant effect of selenium-only supplementation on all-cause or CVD mortality, non-fatal CVD events, or all CVD events, though it reduced non-HDL cholesterol and showed a small trend toward increased type 2 diabetes risk<cite id="17">There were no statistically significant effects of selenium supplementation on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88, 1.08), CVD mortality (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.79, 1.2), non-fatal CVD events (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89, 1.04) or all CVD events (fatal and non-fatal, RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.95, 1.11). There was a statistically significant reduction in non-HDL cholesterol (WMD -0.2 mmol/L, 95% CI -0.41, 0.00).</cite>. These results caution against selenium monotherapy for primary CVD prevention in populations with adequate selenium status.

Iron metabolism intersects with CVD through oxidative stress and endothelial function. Experimental and clinical data suggest that excessive iron therapy or iron overload may promote atherogenesis via oxidative stress, and observational studies indicate that high heme-iron intake is a risk factor for cardiovascular diseases and metabolic syndrome<cite id="21">A number of experimental and clinical data suggest that either excessive iron therapy or iron overload may be a possible culprit of atherogenesis. The process seems to be mediated by oxidative stress.</cite><cite id="22">We summarize epidemiological data suggesting that a high intake of heme iron, which is abundant in meat products, poses a risk factor for metabolic syndrome pathologies, cardiovascular diseases, and some cancers.</cite>. Conversely, in populations with iron deficiency, correcting status can improve endothelial function and reduce oxidative stress, underscoring the need for individualized management<cite id="23">In patients with ID, endothelial function improved after iron repletion, and oxidative stress decreased.</cite>. Intravenous iron use in CKD requires caution due to safety concerns at very high doses or in the presence of very high ferritin levels, which may increase cardiovascular risk<cite id="21">Observational studies have shown a relationship between either high ferritin level or high iron dose and increased risk of death, cardiovascular events, hospitalization or infection. ... The majority of randomized clinical trials have only a very short follow-up ... None of them have tested the role of different iron doses on hard end points.</cite>.

Lead exposure is associated with elevated blood pressure and subclinical cardiovascular changes, including left ventricular hypertrophy. Prospective evidence suggests that reducing population mean blood lead could substantially decrease cardiovascular events, although the attributable risk is small relative to overall CVD incidence<cite id="26">Lead has been shown to be associated with elevated blood pressure in males ... Prospective cardiovascular disease studies such as the Framingham study indicate that increases in blood pressure should be associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease. ... A halving of the population mean blood lead level would reduce myocardial infarctions by approximately 24,000 events per year and incidence of all cardiovascular disease by over 100,000.</cite>. Meta-analytic reviews have consistently found a causal association between low-level lead exposure and systolic blood pressure in males, reinforcing its role in CVD risk<cite id="27">A highly significant and moderately consistent association was found, i.e., decrease of blood lead from 10 mg/dl to 5 mg/dl associated with a decrease of 1.25 mm Hg (95% CI = 0.87-1.63 mm Hg). The association was robust ... and should be considered causal.</cite>.

Interventions Targeting Plasma Metal Ions

Supplementation strategies have been proposed to modulate metal ion homeostasis and downstream risk factors. Zinc supplementation consistently lowers dyslipidemia, glycemic control, and markers of inflammation and oxidative stress, indicating feasibility in controlled settings<cite id="11">Zinc supplementation significantly lowers triglycerides, total cholesterol, fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, CRP, IL-6, TNF-α, NO, MDA, TAC, and GSH.</cite>. For cadmium exposure, chelation with agents such as CaNa2EDTA has been used in occupational cohorts to reduce body burden and may mitigate vascular injury, but population-level prevention should focus on reducing exposure rather than post-exposure chelation in the general public<cite id="13">Chelation with CaNa2EDTA was effective in reducing body burden of cadmium and in improving vascular function in occupationally exposed workers.</cite>. Selenium supplementation shows promise for lipid modulation but lacks robust evidence for preventing clinical CVD events, with potential adverse metabolic effects at high doses<cite id="17">There was a statistically significant reduction in non-HDL cholesterol ... There was no significant effect on all-cause or CVD mortality, non-fatal CVD events, or all CVD events.</cite>. Iron management should avoid overtreatment in individuals without deficiency, given the cardiovascular safety concerns associated with high doses or elevated body stores<cite id="21">Excessive iron therapy may be toxic ... a number of experimental and clinical data suggest that either excessive iron therapy or iron overload may be a possible culprit of atherogenesis.</cite>.

Feasibility and Efficacy: Evidence and Limitations

The feasibility of metal-targeted interventions is supported by randomized trials demonstrating improvements in metabolic and inflammatory profiles with zinc supplementation and by observational links between cadmium, lead, and CVD risk<cite id="11">Zinc supplementation significantly lowers multiple coronary risk factors.</cite><cite id="6">Cadmium levels were the major determinant of Framingham Risk Score in women.</cite><cite id="26">Lead exposure is associated with elevated blood pressure and cardiovascular outcomes.</cite>. However, direct evidence that these interventions reduce clinical CVD events remains limited. Selenium-only supplementation for primary prevention did not reduce mortality or major events, and most iron trials have short follow-up, precluding assessment of hard endpoints<cite id="17">There was no statistically significant effect on all-cause or CVD mortality, non-fatal CVD events, or all CVD events.</cite><cite id="21">None of the trials examined effects on blood pressure. ... The majority of randomized clinical trials have only a very short follow-up ... None of them have tested the role of different iron doses on hard end points.</cite>. Moreover, the potential for adverse effects—such as increased diabetes risk with selenium and toxicity with excessive iron—necessitates careful dosing and monitoring<cite id="17">There was a small increased risk of type 2 diabetes with selenium supplementation.</cite><cite id="21">Observational studies have shown a relationship between either high ferritin level or high iron dose and increased risk of death, cardiovascular events, hospitalization or infection.</cite>.

Conclusion

Modulating plasma metal ion concentrations through targeted interventions may represent viable strategies to reduce coronary risk factors and, in some cases, prevent subclinical vascular damage. Zinc supplementation has demonstrated efficacy in improving dyslipidemia, glycemic control, and oxidative stress markers, supporting its potential role in CVD prevention and management<cite id="11">Zinc supplementation significantly lowers multiple coronary risk factors.</cite>. Evidence implicates cadmium and lead as atherogenic through oxidative stress and hypertension, with population-level reductions in exposure offering substantial public health benefits<cite id="12">Cadmium and lead show their toxic effects via bonding to sulphydryl groups of proteins and depletion of glutathione.</cite><cite id="26">A halving of the population mean blood lead level would reduce myocardial infarctions by approximately 24,000 events per year and incidence of all cardiovascular disease by over 100,000.</cite>. Selenium and iron interventions require more rigorous, long-term trials to establish efficacy for clinical CVD prevention and to optimize safety profiles, given mixed trial evidence and safety concerns at high doses<cite id="17">There is still limited trial evidence supporting the effect of selenium supplementation on CVD events.</cite><cite id="21">Excessive iron therapy may be toxic ... a number of experimental and clinical data suggest that either excessive iron therapy or iron overload may be a possible culprit of atherogenesis.</cite>. Overall, metal-targeted strategies should be integrated with established CVD prevention measures and tailored to individual status and risk profiles.
</answer>

<search query="plasma metal ions cardiovascular diseases prevention therapy copper zinc iron selenium cadmium lead interventions supplementation" search_time="2026年5月19日11时52分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>PRIMARY AND SECONDARY PREVENTION OF ATHEROSCLEROSIS: IS THERE A ROLE FOR ANTIOXIDANTS?</title><summary>Summary - Elevated plasma free radical concentration (expres- sion of enhanced oxidative stress) is related to different pathophysiologi- cal conditions such as ageing, cancer and diabetes. Nevertheless, even in healthy subjects a rise in plasma free radicals is due to hyperglycae- mia, elevated free fatty acids and hyperinsulinaemia. Once elevated oxi- dative stress occurs, accelerated atherosclerosis may be present. Thus, antioxidants might potentially be useful in preventing or delaying the de- velopment of atherosclerosis. Several epidemiological studies have pro- vided conflicting results, whereas interventional studies have demons- trated that antioxidant administration at pharmacological doses is useful for secondary prevention of atherosclerosis. The role of antioxidants in diabetic patients is still debatable, and it is too early to suggest this means for the prevention of atherosclerosis. Concerning trace elements, several studies have indicated that iron, copper, zinc and selenium may play a role in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis. Nevertheless, only future longitudinal studies can provide a final response. In conclusion, the whole body of studies to date clearly demonstrates that antioxidants may be useful for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease.
RÉSUMÉ - Un rôle pour les anti-oxydants dans la prévention pri- maire et secondaire de l'athérosclérose?
Les niveaux plasmatiques élevés de radicaux libres - expression d'un stress oxydant accru - sont associés à des conditions physiopathologi- ques telles que le vieillissement, les cancers et les états diabétiques. Cependant même chez les sujets sains, l'élévation des radicaux libres est consécutive à une hyperglycémie, une élévation des acides gras libres ou un hyperinsulinisme. Lorsqu'un stress oxydant est présent les proces- sus d'athérosclérose peuvent se développer. De ce point de vue, les antioxydants peuvent s'avérer utiles dans la prévention ou le ralentisse- ment de l'athérosclérose.
Plusieurs études épidémiologiques ont fourni des résultats contrastés. En revanche, les études d'intervention ont démontré les effets favorables en prévention secondaire de doses pharmacologiques d'antioxydants. De plus, des études plaident pour un rôle des éléments traces (fer, cuivre, zinc, sélénium) dans la génèse de l'athérosclérose. Chez les patients diabétiques, le sujet reste débattu et il semble prématuré de considérer que les antioxydants jouent un rôle dans la prévention de l'athérosclé- rose. Toutefois, seules de futures études longitudinales apporteront des réponses à ces questions.

A number of experimental and clinical data suggest that either excessive iron therapy or iron overload may be a possible culprit of atherogenesis. The process seems to be mediated by oxidative stress. Iron therapy should also be used cautiously in the presence of active infections, since iron is essential for bacterial growth. Recently, the European Medicines Agency officially raised concerns about rare hypersensitivity reactions following IV iron administration. The balance has been in favour of benefits. Introduction and scope

Chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus), also known as Japanese or club mackerel, are small pelagic fish whose population dynamics, market prices, and fishery economics are tightly coupled to oceanographic regimes. This report synthesizes data-driven evidence on interannual variations in price and quality traits (weight/length) of chub mackerel across major Pacific Rim markets (Japan, Korea, and China), and links these patterns to oceanographic theory to establish direct correlations between marine biological resources, markets, and the marine environment.<cite id="1">Population dynamics of small pelagic fishes (SPF) and their management in Japan were reviewed for Japanese sardine Sardinops melanostictus, Japanese anchovy Engraulis japonicus, chub mackerel Scomber japonicus, and Pacific saury Cololabis saira. The catch and biomass of SPF generally showed decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s. The causes of species replacements were generally associated with climatic/oceanic variability, particularly “regime shifts,” of which the 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s.</cite><cite id="12">The best GAM model in terms of AIC, with Fc or CF as a response variable, and year (categorical variable), Cd and FI (spline functions regardless of their independent or simultaneous usages) as explanatory variables, effects of year were statistically significant.</cite>

Price dynamics in Japan: Atlantic versus Pacific chub mackerel

Japanese markets for Atlantic mackerel have collapsed into a “high-level failure” in 2026, with record-high costs and stagnant demand. Processing plants maintain minimal inventories, and salted fillet circulation has slowed dramatically. Nominal quotes for boneless fillets hover around \$11.10–\$11.70/kg, but actual transactions fall to \$9.11–\$10.41/kg, reflecting a “price inversion” where import and processing costs exceed consumer willingness to pay. Whole fish prices have retreated from \$5.53/kg to lower levels, underscoring the severity of the pricing crisis in Japan this season<cite id="16">Record-High Prices Trigger "High-Level Failure" in Asian Markets as Consumers Pivot to Cheaper Domestic Alternatives... Market cash prices have softened from \$5.53/kg to lower thresholds. While nominal quotes sit between \$11.10 and \$11.70/kg, actual transactions have retreated to a range of \$9.11 to \$10.41/kg.</cite>.

In contrast, Pacific mackerel has become the dominant choice in Japan, with larger fish (over 600 g) continuing to command high prices in Europe around \$6.00/kg. Domestic catches surged by 73% in March 2026 to 21,000 tons, albeit mostly small fish averaging 200 g, sold at a low price point of \$1.16/kg. These shifts illustrate how Japanese retailers are abandoning the premium Atlantic variety in favor of Pacific mackerel as prices approach a 100% gap, eroding the competitive edge of the imported product<cite id="16">Retailers in Japan are increasingly abandoning the premium Atlantic variety in favor of Pacific mackerel. With a price gap approaching 100%, the imported product has lost its competitive edge... Domestic catch surged by 73% in March to reach 21,000 tons... mostly small—averaging 200 grams... low price point of \$1.16/kg.</cite>.

Interannual variations in weight and length across markets

In Korean markets, length-based stock assessment models applied to annual fork-length data reveal strong interannual variability in body size. Annual mean fork length increased from 28.8 cm in 2008 to 30.5 cm in 2016, indicating a positive trend in fish size during this period<cite id="42">Annual mean folk length showed increased trend representing 28.8cm in 2008 and 30.5cm in 2016.</cite>. Size composition also changed over time, with the proportion of small fish (21–25 cm) decreasing from 53.8% in 2008 to 32.5% in 2016, while the proportion of larger fish (36–40 cm) increased from 12.5% to 20.7%, reflecting shifts in recruitment strength and fishing pressure<cite id="42">The proportion of chub mackerel catch according to size class was 53.8%, 20.7%, 12.5%, 7.9%, and 5.1% for 21–25, 26–30, 31–35, 36–40, and 41–45 cm, respectively, in 2008... In 2016, these proportions were 32.5%, 25.7%, 20.7%, 16.9%, and 6.3%, respectively.</cite>.

Seasonal and interannual variability in fat content and condition factor are also evident. Studies on Korean chub mackerel show that crude fat content and condition factor exhibit non-linear relationships with fork length and year, with statistically significant effects of year in generalized additive models (GAMs). Positive anomalies in 2016 and 2017 were associated with higher fat content, suggesting favorable environmental conditions during those years<cite id="12">Non-linear relationships were detected between CF and Fc, between FI and Fc, and between FI and CF. The best GAM model... effects of year were statistically significant. Potential causes of strong positive effects of 2016 and 2017 on Fc were discussed.</cite>.

In Japan, a similar approach using standardized length-weight relationships and condition factor analysis found that the best model included year as a significant explanatory variable, indicating interannual variability in body condition. The study also reported that the length-weight relationship was not significantly affected by year, while condition factor showed clear interannual trends, consistent with environmental and management drivers<cite id="14">The best model... included year as a significant explanatory variable... The length-weight relationship was not significantly affected by year, while the condition factor showed significant interannual variability.</cite>.

Fat content and market price in Japan

In Japan, fat content is a key determinant of market price for chub mackerel. A study analyzing the relationship between fat content and price found a strong positive correlation (R² = 0.92), with fat content explaining 92% of the variation in price. This tight link suggests that fluctuations in fat content directly translate into price changes in Japanese markets, reinforcing the economic importance of biological quality traits<cite id="15">There was a strong positive correlation between fat content and price (R² = 0.92), indicating that fat content explained 92% of the variation in price.</cite>.

Fishery economics and market responses

Fishery economics are closely tied to both biological conditions and market responses. In Japan, the 2025–2026 Atlantic mackerel crisis demonstrates how high input costs and weak demand can lead to market paralysis, with prices climbing 64% since August 2025 while cumulative imports fell 45%. Exporters face a difficult trade-off: tightening quotas to stabilize prices may reduce supply further, while maintaining current volumes risks persistently low turnover<cite id="16">Average prices have climbed 64% since August 2025... cumulative imports are down 45%... exports of mackerel under 600 grams fell by 46%... the industry remains optimistic... insiders anticipate that August quota announcements may include further tightening.</cite>.

In South Korea, the relative ease of obtaining market price data has been explored as a potential supplement to limited fishery data, but studies found that price information did not contribute further to stock assessment when catch and CPUE were already available. This suggests that while prices can reflect broader economic and biological signals, they may not substitute for length- and age-composition data in formal assessments<cite id="13">One of the main findings was the price information did not contribute to fish stock assessment further, given that data on fishery catch and CPUE were already used.</cite>.

Coupling to oceanographic theory

Oceanographic variability drives interannual changes in biological resources and, consequently, market prices and fishery economics. Regime shifts, such as the 1988/89 North Pacific transition, have historically caused prominent species replacements among small pelagics, with early survival rates emerging as a key factor in population fluctuations<cite id="1">The causes of species replacements were generally associated with climatic/oceanic variability, particularly “regime shifts,” of which the 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in the early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations.</cite>. In the North Pacific, climate change impacts on key species like chub mackerel are well documented, linking temperature, productivity, and distribution shifts to fisheries outcomes<cite id="2">Impacts of Climate and Climate Change on the Key Species in the Fisheries in the North Pacific.</cite>.

In Japan, the 1988/89 regime shift marked a turning point in the pelagic fish community, shifting dominance from sardine to anchovy and reshaping the ecosystem and fisheries. More recently, the 2011–2013 sardine bloom and subsequent collapse were density-independent and density-dependent processes, respectively, underscoring how environmental and biological mechanisms interact to drive interannual variability in pelagic resources<cite id="3">The sardine is the keystone species in the pelagic fish community and changes of mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and anchovy (Engraulis japonicus) populations are in progress.</cite><cite id="5">Recovery was triggered by global climatic change in a density-independent manner and the collapse underway is caused by a density-dependent mechanism.</cite>.

The catch and biomass of SPF generally showed decadal-scale variability with prominent species replacements since the 1900s. The causes of species replacements were generally associated with climatic/oceanic variability, particularly “regime shifts,” of which the 1988/89 regime shift was the most influential since the 1970s. Variability in the early survival rate is a key factor for population fluctuations, and the proposed hypothetical mechanisms of recruitment variability are summarized herein. Although overfishing during the 1990s and early 2000s prevented the recovery of Pacific stocks of sardine and chub mackerel, they have been recovering since the mid-2000s owing to strong year classes and reduced exploitation rates. The fundamental cause of overfishing was derived from a mismatch between investments in larger purse seine fleets during the 1980s and poor ocean productivity since the 1988/89 regime shift, when dominant SPF began to shift from sardine to anchovy. Recommendations for fisheries management of SPF around the Japanese Archipelago are proposed, considering climate change and naturally and drastically changing SPF populations.</summary><hostname>SpringerLink</hostname><publisher>Fisheries Science (2019) 85:611–639</publisher><author_list><author name="Akihiko Yatsu" affiliation="Japan Fisheries Information Service Center, 4-5, Toyomi-cho, Chuo-ku, Tokyo 104-0055, Japan" /></author_list><url>https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007%2Fs12562-019-01305-3.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年4月3日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Impacts of Climate and Climate Change on the Key Species in the Fisheries in the North Pacific</title><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>PICES Scientific Report No. 35</publisher><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Rj-Beamish/publication/265618628_Impacts_of_Climate_and_Climate_Change_on_the_Key_Species_in_the_Fisheries_in_the_North_Pacific_Edited_by/links/5751ee8608ae02ac1277b424/Impacts-of-Climate-and-Climate-Change-on-the-Key-Species-in-the-Fisheries-in-the-North-Pacific-Edited-by.pdf</url><publish_time>2008年12月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:3"><title>Recovery and collapse of the Far Eastern sardine</title><summary>The Far Eastern sardine (Sardinops sagax) began to increase dramatically in the early 1970s, reached a peak in the late 1980s, but then decreased thereafter. This dramatic recovery and collapse is the second cycle this century, and constitutes part of a long-term structural change in a pelagic fish community. The new cycle was initiated with higher survival at the earliest stages of sardine on both coasts of central Japan and they spread to the north, south and offshore. Strong year classes were produced at short intervals. The spawning area moved westward and inshore. Collapse was caused by survival failure. The spawning activity shifted to the east and offshore and the range of the sardine was reduced. Recovery was triggered by global climatic change in a density-independent manner and the collapse underway is caused by a density-dependent mechanism. ## Norway’s Premium Mackerel Faces Sharp Decline as Japanese Demand Hits a Wall

**<link reference_id="<|superscript|>:16-<|link|>:1" text="               NORWAY              " />             Monday, May 04, 2026, 00:10 (GMT + 9)**

Record-High Prices Trigger "High-Level Failure" in Asian Markets as Consumers Pivot to Cheaper Domestic Alternatives

The once-resilient market for **Norwegian Atlantic mackerel**  is facing a severe pricing crisis in **Japan** , as stagnant demand and skyrocketing costs create a "high-level failure" in the traditional distribution chain. According to reports from **Food World (Beijing)** , the mismatch between high raw material costs and sluggish retail performance has brought market circulation to a virtual standstill.

.png)

Photo: JAL Group Spirit / YouTube / FIS

**Japan** , historically one of the primary global destinations for **Norway's**  premium exports, has seen a dramatic slowdown since the **2025 season**  catch arrived. Processing plants across the country are reportedly maintaining minimal inventory, as the speed of distribution for salted fillets—the staple of the Japanese market—has plummeted.

A Market in Inversion

The industry is currently grappling with a "price inversion," where the cost of importing and processing the fish far exceeds what consumers are willing to pay. Market feedback reveals that even as prices dipped below **\$5.20/kg**  (**800 yen/kg** ), buying interest remained remarkably low.

.png)

Photo: JAL Group Spirit / YouTube / FIS

The financial pressure is evident across all product segments:

- **Whole Fish:**  Market cash prices have softened from **\$5.53/kg**  (**850 yen/kg** ) to lower thresholds.

- **Boneless Fillets:**  While nominal quotes sit between **\$11.10 and \$11.70/kg** , actual transactions have retreated to a range of **\$9.11 to \$10.41/kg** .

The Shift to Domestic Competition

Retailers in **Japan**  are increasingly abandoning the premium **Atlantic**  variety in favor of **Pacific mackerel** . With a price gap approaching **100%** , the imported product has lost its competitive edge.



Photo: JAL Group Spirit / YouTube / FIS

While **Japan's**  domestic catch surged by **73%**  in **March**  to reach **21,000 tons** , the fish were mostly small—averaging **200 grams** . Although unsuitable for high-end filleting, their low price point of **\$1.16/kg**  (**179 yen/kg** ) has made them an attractive substitute for budget-conscious shoppers.

Supply and Export Statistics

Data released by the **Norwegian Seafood Council**  paints a stark picture of the trade divide. In **March** , the average export price of mackerel stood at **\$4.50/kg**  (**48.14 Norwegian kroner/kg** ), representing a massive **63%**  year-on-year increase. However, this price hike came at the cost of volume:

- Exports of mackerel under **600 grams**  fell by **46%** .

- Specific imports into **Japan**  for **March**  plummeted **52%**  to just **455 tons** .

- Since the **August 2025**  season began, **Japan's**  cumulative imports are down **45%** , while average prices have climbed **64%** .



Photo:stockfile / FIS

The "Wait-and-See" Outlook

Despite the current friction, the **Norwegian**  industry remains optimistic. Insiders anticipate that **August**  quota announcements may include further tightening to help stabilize the market. Currently, larger fish (over **600 grams** ) continue to command high prices in the **European**  market, hovering around **\$6.00/kg** .

# The role of need for closure on misinformation acceptance: a data-driven report

## Overview
Need for cognitive closure (NFCC) is a dispositional tendency to experience discomfort from uncertainty and to seek clear answers, which can shape how individuals process and accept misinformation. Across experimental and survey studies, NFCC consistently predicts susceptibility to misinformation and conspiratorial thinking, especially in uncertain or emotionally salient contexts. Meta-analytic work links NFCC to ideological conservatism and motivated information processing, reinforcing its relevance to misinformation dynamics<cite id="32">Political Conservatism as Motivated Social Cognition</cite><cite id="11">Need for cognitive closure and the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs</cite>.

## NFCC and susceptibility to misinformation
Experimental evidence shows that individuals high in NFCC are more likely to accept misinformation when it offers simple, conspiratorial explanations—particularly when those explanations are made salient. In two experiments, NFCC positively predicted belief in conspiratorial accounts of the refugee crisis and a mysterious plane crash, but only when conspiratorial explanations were accessible; in a case with an official non-conspiratorial explanation, the relationship reversed<cite id="11">Need for cognitive closure and the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs</cite>. Consistent with this, survey work indicates that cognitive factors such as NFCC and intuitive thinking predict lower alignment with expert judgments on misinformation, underscoring how dispositional uncertainty avoidance can undermine corrective engagement<cite id="29">Who's in the Crowd Matters: Cognitive Factors and Beliefs Predict Misinformation Assessment Accuracy</cite>.

## NFCC in crowdsourcing and warning-tag studies
Crowdsourcing efforts to assess misinformation reveal that NFCC is associated with less alignment with expert evaluations compared to respondents with higher cognitive reflection and openness. In studies of Twitter posts about the pandemic, higher NFCC correlated with reduced expert alignment, highlighting how closure-seeking preferences can bias truth judgments<cite id="29">Who's in the Crowd Matters: Cognitive Factors and Beliefs Predict Misinformation Assessment Accuracy</cite>. Attitudes toward warning tags designed to label misinformation are also predicted by NFCC, alongside political orientation and trust, suggesting personalized mitigation strategies may need to account for closure motivation<cite id="28">WARNING This Contains Misinformation: The Effect of Cognitive Factors, Beliefs, and Personality on Misinformation Warning Tag Attitudes</cite>.

## NFCC and conspiratorial thinking
Meta-analytic reviews of conspiratorial ideation identify motivational and personological correlates, including epistemic motives to reduce uncertainty. Experimental work further demonstrates that conspiratorial explanations are more persuasive when uncertainty is high and when closure is needed, increasing endorsement of conspiracy beliefs under these conditions<cite id="8">A Meta-Analytic Review of Motivational and Personological Correlates of Conspiracy Theories</cite><cite id="14">Conspiracy Theories and the Need for Cognitive Closure</cite>. Mechanistically, conspiracy theories provide “simple answers to complex problems,” making them attractive precisely to individuals intolerant of uncertainty who actively seek closure<cite id="11">Need for cognitive closure and the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs</cite>.

## Moderating conditions and boundary conditions
Theoretical work clarifies that the effects of NFCC depend on situational context. A meta-analysis of closure motivation shows that people high in NFCC sometimes engage in effortful, open-minded processing rather than simplistic, low-effort strategies, depending on task demands and constraints. This “disparate roads to certainty” model suggests that interventions targeting NFCC should consider when closure-seekers rely on heuristics versus deeper evaluation<cite id="34">Disparate roads to certainty processing strategy choices under need for closure</cite>. Relatedly, personality-informed models emphasize that misinformation vulnerability is shaped by interactions among cognitive traits, personality factors, and contextual cues, with NFCC operating as one key moderator<cite id="1">Temporal Bias and Psychological Susceptibility to Misinformation: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Synthesis</cite>.

## Implications for misinformation interventions
Interventions that reduce misinformation acceptance may benefit from addressing closure motivation by providing structured, authoritative explanations that satisfy the need for clarity without arousing defensiveness. Meta-analytic work on political conservatism shows that needs for closure and intolerance of ambiguity are part of a broader motivated social cognition system that resists change and inequality justification; countering misinformation may require aligning messages with order and structure while correcting inaccuracies<cite id="32">Political Conservatism as Motivated Social Cognition</cite>. More broadly, research on misinformation correction indicates that issue importance and affective framing can influence receptivity to corrections, suggesting that closure-oriented strategies should pair clear answers with frames that reduce threat and enhance motivation to process corrections<cite id="26">Issue Importance and the Correction of Misinformation</cite>.

## Limitations and open questions
Most studies of NFCC and misinformation rely on self-report measures and Western samples, and many interventions remain generic rather than tailored to dispositional factors<cite id="1">Temporal Bias and Psychological Susceptibility to Misinformation: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Synthesis</cite>. Future work should incorporate experimental manipulations of closure motivation, ecologically valid social media tasks, and culturally diverse populations to generalize findings and refine personalized mitigation approaches<cite id="1">Temporal Bias and Psychological Susceptibility to Misinformation: A Systematic Review and Bibliometric Synthesis</cite>.

## Conclusion
In sum, need for cognitive closure plays a significant role in misinformation acceptance by increasing reliance on simple, conspiratorial explanations and reducing alignment with expert corrections, particularly under uncertainty or when information is emotionally charged. Experimental and meta-analytic evidence consistently supports these patterns, while theoretical models highlight boundary conditions that can modulate closure-driven processing. Targeting NFCC through structured, authoritative communication and personalized mitigation (e.g., warning tags) offers a promising avenue for reducing misinformation acceptance in real-world contexts<cite id="11">Need for cognitive closure and the endorsement of conspiracy beliefs</cite><cite id="29">Who's in the Crowd Matters: Cognitive Factors and Beliefs Predict Misinformation Assessment Accuracy</cite><cite id="28">WARNING This Contains Misinformation: The Effect of Cognitive Factors, Beliefs, and Personality on Misinformation Warning Tag Attitudes</cite><cite id="32">Political Conservatism as Motivated Social Cognition</cite>.

This inclination can become especially striking when citizens reject notions that scientists would consider “facts” in the light of overwhelming scientific evidence and consensus. The resulting polarization over science has reached alarming levels in recent years. This theoretical review conceptualizes political polarization over science and argues that it is driven by two interrelated processes. Through psychological science rejection, people can implicitly disregard scientific facts that are inconsistent with their political identity. problem: The significance of the gut microbiota in maintaining normal intestinal function has emerged as a prominent focus in contemporary research, revealing both beneficial and detrimental impacts on the equilibrium of gut health. Disruption of microbial homeostasis can precipitate intestinal inflammation and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer. Conversely, probiotics have demonstrated the capacity to mitigate inflammation and retard the progression of colorectal cancer. Within this domain, key questions arise: What are the predominant types of gut probiotics? What precisely constitutes prebiotics and their mechanistic role? Which pathogenic bacteria warrant concern, and what toxic metabolites do they produce? How might these findings inform and optimize our daily dietary choices?

Introduction

The gut microbiota has become a central focus in contemporary biomedical research due to its profound influence on intestinal physiology and immune regulation. Disruption of microbial homeostasis can drive intestinal inflammation and is implicated in the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer, underscoring the clinical relevance of microbiota-targeted interventions. In parallel, probiotics have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and chemopreventive properties that may slow colorectal cancer progression. These findings motivate practical dietary guidance to support a healthy gut microbiota and reduce disease risk<cite id="19">disruption of gut microbiota homeostasis and its association with inflammatory and neoplastic diseases</cite><cite id="28">link between intestinal microbiota and colorectal cancer (CRC)</cite><cite id="21">convincing evidence exists for some established probiotics</cite>.

Predominant Gut Probiotics

The most widely studied and clinically applied probiotics belong to the genera Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Saccharomyces, which have a long history of safe and effective use. While these species are well established, emerging taxa such as Roseburia, Akkermansia, Propionibacterium, and Faecalibacterium are showing promise for future applications. The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) definition emphasizes that probiotics are live microorganisms that confer a health benefit on the host when administered in adequate amounts<cite id="21">Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium and Saccharomyces; promise of Roseburia, Akkermansia, Propionibacterium and Faecalibacterium; ISAPP definition</cite><cite id="22">definition of probiotics</cite>. Commonly used species include Lactobacillus acidophilus, Bifidobacterium spp., and L. casei, which are frequently found in probiotic food products, particularly dairy, and are supported by a range of health benefits<cite id="2">Lactobacillus acidophilus, Bifidobacterium spp., L. casei; dairy as ideal vehicle</cite><cite id="21">convincing evidence exists for some established probiotics</cite>.

Prebiotics: Definition and Mechanistic Role

Prebiotics are selectively fermented ingredients that beneficially affect the host by selectively stimulating the growth and/or activity of one or a limited number of bacterial species already present in the colon, and thus improve host health. The prebiotic concept has evolved to include substrates such as fructans and galacto-oligosaccharides, with evidence also emerging for other fermentable carbohydrates, including oligomers of mannose, glucose, xylose, pectin, starches, human milk oligosaccharides, and polyphenols<cite id="21">glucans and fructans well proven; evidence building for other substances</cite><cite id="25">definition of prebiotics; selective fermentation and health benefits</cite>. A key mechanistic pathway is anaerobic fermentation of prebiotics by colonic microbiota to produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), particularly acetate, propionate, and butyrate, which exert anti-inflammatory and metabolic benefits through G-protein-coupled receptors and epigenetic modulation<cite id="24">prebiotics fermented to SCFAs; anti-inflammatory effects via GPCRs; butyrate as an energy source</cite>. However, responses to prebiotics are variable among individuals, highlighting the need for personalized approaches and further research to optimize efficacy<cite id="24">individual variability in prebiotic responses</cite>.

Pathogenic Bacteria of Concern and Their Toxic Metabolites

Alterations in gut microbial composition and function can promote the growth of pathobionts that contribute to disease through the production of toxic metabolites. In the context of colorectal cancer, microbial metabolites such as secondary bile salts, hydrogen sulfide, and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) have been implicated in promoting inflammation, DNA damage, and carcinogenesis<cite id="13">bacteria and metabolites in CRC; secondary bile salts, hydrogen sulfide, TMAO</cite>. Specific bacterial species associated with increased abundance in CRC include Fusobacterium nucleatum, Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium septicum, and other taxa that contribute to genotoxic stress and tumor progression<cite id="13">Fusobacterium nucleatum, Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium septicum implicated in CRC</cite><cite id="28">mechanisms linking microbiota to CRC (chronic inflammation, genotoxins, toxic metabolites)</cite>. These observations align with broader evidence that gut microbiota can activate heterocyclic amines and produce genotoxins that interfere with cell cycle regulation<cite id="28">production of toxic metabolites and genotoxins; interference with cell cycle regulation</cite>.

Informing Daily Dietary Choices

A diet rich in fermentable fibers and prebiotic substrates can support the growth of beneficial bacteria and enhance production of SCFAs, which in turn modulate immune function and reduce inflammation<cite id="24">prebiotics and SCFAs beneficial for gut health</cite>. Foods containing probiotics, such as fermented dairy products (yogurt, kefir, certain cheeses), can deliver live microorganisms with documented health benefits, provided they meet the viability requirements for efficacy<cite id="2">fermented dairy as ideal vehicle for probiotics</cite><cite id="21">convincing evidence for established probiotics</cite>. Conversely, excessive consumption of processed foods, refined sugars, and artificial sweeteners may disrupt gut homeostasis and contribute to dysbiosis, while lifestyle factors such as stress, sleep, and smoking can further modulate microbiota composition and function<cite id="16">dietary ingredients (probiotics, prebiotics, refined sugars, sweeteners, fats) and lifestyle factors influence gut microbiota</cite>. Emerging evidence also supports the inclusion of marine-derived prebiotics (e.g., algal polysaccharides) and functional foods such as garlic and onions, which contain prebiotic inulin-type fructans and exhibit antimicrobial and chemopreventive properties<cite id="6">potential of algal polysaccharides as prebiotics</cite><cite id="14">garlic and onions contain prebiotic inulin-type fructans; antimicrobial and chemopreventive effects</cite>.

Conclusion

The gut microbiota plays a pivotal role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis, and its disruption can precipitate inflammation and contribute to colorectal cancer. Probiotics and prebiotics represent evidence-based strategies to modulate microbial ecology and reduce disease risk, with Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Saccharomyces, and selected fermentable fibers forming the cornerstone of dietary interventions<cite id="19">disruption of gut microbiota and its association with inflammatory and neoplastic diseases</cite><cite id="28">mechanistic link between microbiota and CRC</cite><cite id="21">established probiotics and prebiotic substrates</cite>. However, inter-individual variability and the complexity of host–microbiota interactions necessitate personalized approaches and further research to optimize long-term outcomes<cite id="17">strategies limited by host genotype, physiology, intervention and diet</cite><cite id="24">individual variability in prebiotic responses</cite>.

Given the importance of these approaches for public health, it is timely to reiterate factual and supporting information on their clinical application and use. In this Review , we discuss scientific evidence on probiotics and prebiotics, including mechanistic insights into health effects. Strains of Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium and Saccharomyces have a long history of safe and effective use as probiotics, but Roseburia spp., Akkermansia spp., Propionibacterium spp. and Faecalibacterium spp. show promise for the future. For prebiotics, glucans and fructans are well proven, and evidence is building on the prebiotic effects of other substances (for example, oligomers of mannose, glucose, xylose, pectin, starches, human milk and polyphenols).
The request in 2000 by the Argentinian government that the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations form an expert panel to evaluate the health and nutritional properties of probiotics in food precipitated the re-​emergence of a concept long part of human history. International recognition of the concept of probiotics, and coalescence around a definition of probiotic offered by this expert consultation1, established an important consensus foundation. The definition of probiotic decided by the consultation retained the essence of historical definitions offered over previous decades. It was intentionally broad, to encompass a wide variety of microorganisms, hosts, benefits, target sites and product types. It has stood the test of time and was reaffirmed, but grammatically corrected, in 2014 to the consensus definition of probiotics, which is: “live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host”2.
There are many studies that have investigated how microorganisms are integrated into life processes and defined ways that beneficial microorganisms — both commensal and externally applied — affect physiological homeostasis and host function3. On the horizon is the promise of newly constructed recombinant strains and promising novel microbial species, which await testing in vivo. However, as these advances develop, we should
recognize actionable evidence that is currently available. As is discussed in this Review, convincing evidence exists for some established probiotics, which should be incorporated into health management. This incorporation includes complementary use with pharmaceutical agents, foods and lifestyle. Education of consumers, practitioners and regulators will facilitate appropriate use and point out needs for further research, which will hopefully include exploration of how to reach the individuals at greatest need with affordable and reliable probiotic products4.

Abstract: Background: Globally there has been an exponential increase in the penetration of smartphones among the youth population and smartphones have become indispensable in the daily lives of university students in South Korea. Several studies have associated the problematic use of smartphones or addiction with different adverse outcomes. The goal of this study was to collate empirical evidence and provides an overall synthesis of the literature about the adverse effects of smartphone addiction on university students in South Korea. Method: We carried out a systematic review of the published literature between August and October 2022 on the adverse effects of smartphone addiction on university students in South Korea, published between 2012 and 2022 in Pubmed/Medline, PsycInfo, Embase, BiomedCentral, Web of Science, Directory of Open Access Journals, Elsevier’s collection, Wiley Online Library, SpringerLink, Sage Journal’s collection and Cochrane Library. Results: Thirty-four articles published between 2012 and 2022 were included in the synthesis of this review. Eight studies explored the association between smartphone addiction and the psychological and mental health of university students in Korea. Smartphone addiction was associated with physical health leading to sleep disorders and musculoskeletal and neurological problems. Academic performance, procrastination, impulsivity, self-esteem, reduced social interaction, solitude, and suicide were also negatively associated with smartphone addiction. Conclusions: Our study adds to the literature regarding the adverse effects of smartphone addiction on university students in Korea and provides more information for addiction prevention and health promotion activities.

Factors determining colorectal cancer: the role of the intestinal microbiota
Esther Nistal1 , Nereida Fernández-Fernández2 , Santiago Vivas1,2* and José Luis Olcoz2
1 Instituto de Biomedicina (IBIOMED), Universidad de León, León, Spain, 2 Gastroenterología, Hospital Universitario de León, León, Spain
The gastrointestinal tract, in particular the colon, holds a complex community of microorganisms, which are essential for maintaining homeostasis. However, in recent years, many studies have implicated microbiota in the development of colorectal cancer (CRC), with this disease considered a major cause of death in the western world. The mechanisms underlying bacterial contribution in its development are complex and are not yet fully understood. However, there is increasing evidence showing a connection between intestinal microbiota and CRC. Intestinal microorganisms cause the onset and progression of CRC using different mechanisms, such as the induction of a chronic inflammation state, the biosynthesis of genotoxins that interfere with cell cycle regulation, the production of toxic metabolites, or heterocyclic amine activation of pro-diet carcinogenic compounds. Despite these advances, additional studies in humans and animal models will further decipher the relationship between microbiota and CRC, and aid in developing alternate therapies based on microbiota manipulation.
Keywords: gut microbiota, colorectal cancer, bacterial metabolites, inflammation, diet
COLORECTAL CANCER
According to the World Health Organization, cancer is a global health problem. In 2011, it was the leading cause of mortality positioned above stroke and coronary pathology. Approximately half of these deaths were due to lung, stomach, colon, and breast cancer.
Colorectal cancer (CRC) ranks third in incidence in men and second in women (1.4 million in 2012). It stands at third place in mortality causing up to 690,000 deaths per year (1). Approximately 75% of deaths from CRC occur in people over 65 years, with mortality higher in males. Analyzing age and sex together reveals that mortality in males is comparable to that of females who are 4–8 years older (2, 3). In Europe, CRC mortality is showing a downward trend in countries such as Austria, France, Ireland, Sweden, and Norway, unlike Eastern and Mediterranean countries such as Spain, Italy, and Greece (4). There are big differences in the incidence of CRC across countries, which are mainly attributed to diet.
Until recently, CRC was almost exclusively a public health issue in industrialized countries, but has now also become a problem in emerging countries due to economic growth (5). The adoption of a westernized lifestyle, increased consumption of red meat, high-calorie diets, and rising life expectancy in these countries have contributed to the increased incidence of CRC (6). Moreover, these countries have higher mortality due to a lack of healthcare resources (6).

original_data.problem: The significance of the gut microbiota in maintaining normal intestinal function has emerged as a prominent focus in contemporary research, revealing both beneficial and detrimental impacts on the equilibrium of gut health. Disruption of microbial homeostasis can precipitate intestinal inflammation and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of colorectal cancer. Conversely, probiotics have demonstrated the capacity to mitigate inflammation and retard the progression of colorectal cancer. Within this domain, key questions arise: What are the predominant types of gut probiotics? What precisely constitutes prebiotics and their mechanistic role? Which pathogenic bacteria warrant concern, and what toxic metabolites do they produce? How might these findings inform and optimize our daily dietary choices?

<answer>Introduction

Parkinson’s disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor and non-motor symptoms that evolve over time. While motor symptoms such as tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity are widely recognized, non-motor manifestations often precede them and can be early indicators of the disease. Staging systems like Hoehn & Yahr and Braak’s pathological staging help clinicians and families understand the trajectory of PD and guide interventions at appropriate times<cite id="2">PD motor features and progression; postural instability is a late sign</cite><cite id="19">PD staging (Hoehn-Yahr) and Braak pathological staging; non-motor symptoms as early markers</cite>. This report synthesizes evidence on warning signs across stages, red flags for medical attention, and practical support strategies for DBS patients.

Motor and Non-Motor Symptoms Overview

Motor symptoms include resting tremor, bradykinesia, muscle rigidity, and postural instability, with gait disturbances emerging in later stages. Non-motor symptoms—such as constipation, hyposmia, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and depression—are often present years before motor features and can serve as early warning signs<cite id="19">Common non-motor symptoms (constipation, hyposmia, RBD, depression) precede motor symptoms</cite>. These non-motor signs are increasingly used in clinical practice for early detection and risk stratification<cite id="19">Non-motor symptoms are key in early diagnosis and staging</cite>.

Staging Systems and Their Clinical Implications

Hoehn & Yahr staging divides PD into five stages based on functional impairment and symptom spread, from unilateral involvement (Stage I) to severe, bilateral disability requiring supervision (Stage V). In Stage I, symptoms are unilateral and do not interfere with daily activities; Stage II involves bilateral involvement without postural instability; Stage III is mid-stage with postural instability; Stage IV is late-stage with significant disability; and Stage V is the most severe, with the patient requiring a wheelchair and constant assistance<cite id="2">Hoehn & Yahr staging description and progression</cite>. Braak’s pathological staging emphasizes that neurodegeneration begins decades before motor symptoms, underscoring the importance of monitoring non-motor signs during the preclinical and prodromal phases<cite id="19">Pathological staging highlights preclinical and prodromal phases with non-motor symptoms</cite>.

Warning Signs by Disease Stage

Early Stage (Hoehn & Yahr I–II; preclinical/prodromal)

- Non-motor red flags: Persistent constipation, diminished sense of smell, RBD (confirmed by polysomnography), and depressive symptoms should prompt evaluation for PD or prodromal PD<cite id="19">Constipation, hyposmia, RBD, and depression as early non-motor markers</cite>. Family members should encourage a visit if these symptoms persist and are unexplained by other causes<cite id="19">Non-motor symptoms as early indicators</cite>.
- Motor signs: Unilateral bradykinesia or tremor that is asymmetrical and does not yet interfere with daily function may be the first motor manifestation<cite id="2">Early motor features and progression</cite>.

Mid-Stage (Hoehn & Yahr III; prodromal/early clinical)

- Non-motor progression: Cognitive changes, visual hallucinations, and increased fatigue may emerge, signaling a more advanced disease process<cite id="19">Cognitive and psychiatric symptoms appear in later stages</cite>. Recurrent falls are also common and should be reported to a neurologist<cite id="20">Recurrent falls are a significant milestone with poor prognosis</cite>.
- Motor signs: Postural instability and gait freezing become more prominent, increasing fall risk and functional limitations<cite id="2">Postural instability and gait disturbances in later stages</cite>.

Late-Stage (Hoehn & Yahr IV–V; advanced)

- Non-motor complications: Dementia, severe depression, and autonomic dysfunction (e.g., orthostatic hypotension) are frequent and can significantly impact quality of life<cite id="19">Cognitive decline and autonomic symptoms in advanced PD</cite>. Milestones such as visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, dementia, and nursing home placement are associated with poorer outcomes and should trigger urgent review of care plans<cite id="20">Milestone events (hallucinations, falls, dementia, nursing home placement) and increased mortality risk</cite>.
- Motor signs: Severe rigidity, reduced arm swing, propulsion/retropulsion, and the need for assistance with walking or sitting/standing transitions are typical<cite id="2">Late motor features and postural instability</cite>.

Red Flags for Family Members to Seek Medical Advice

- Persistent non-motor symptoms: Unexplained constipation, loss of smell, RBD, or depression that does not improve with standard treatment should prompt a neurologic evaluation for PD or prodromal disease<cite id="19">Non-motor symptoms as early indicators</cite>.
- New or worsening motor symptoms: Sudden onset of tremor, bradykinesia, or rigidity on one side; postural instability; or frequent freezing of gait should be assessed promptly<cite id="2">Motor symptom progression and postural instability</cite>.
- Cognitive or psychiatric changes: Visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, or new dementia symptoms require immediate medical attention, as they are associated with poor prognosis<cite id="20">Milestone events and prognosis</cite>.
- Autonomic or medication-related issues: Orthostatic hypotension, severe fatigue, or fluctuations in motor symptoms (on–off) may indicate autonomic dysfunction or suboptimal medication management<cite id="19">Autonomic and medication-related symptoms in PD</cite>.

Daily Life Adjustments and Support Strategies for DBS Patients

DBS is an effective treatment for motor symptoms but requires careful programming, adherence to medication, and lifestyle adaptations to maximize benefits and minimize complications<cite id="11">DBS adjustment process and support needs across stages</cite>. Key strategies include:

- DBS programming and follow-up: Regular follow-ups with a trained neurologist or neuromodulation team are essential to optimize settings and address emerging motor fluctuations or dyskinesias<cite id="11">Timely clinical and practical support after DBS</cite>. Patients and families should be educated about programming changes and how to recognize signs that require adjustment<cite id="11">Education and realistic goal setting before DBS</cite>.
- Medication management: Even with DBS, dopaminergic medications are often needed; monitoring for on–off fluctuations and adjusting dosages with the neurology team can improve motor control<cite id="11">New challenges to symptoms and roles after DBS</cite>.
- Home modifications for safety: Install grab bars, remove tripping hazards, ensure adequate lighting, and consider mobility aids (e.g., walkers or canes) to reduce fall risk<cite id="13">Home modifications to reduce fall risk</cite>. If postural instability is prominent, consider wheelchair use and environmental adaptations to maintain independence<cite id="2">Postural instability and need for assistance</cite>.
- Caregiver support and self-management: Encourage patient-led self-management and provide emotional and practical support to reduce caregiver burden. Families should seek respite care and community resources to sustain long-term caregiving<cite id="11">Support for reengagement in self-management and future changes</cite><cite id="14">Caregiver burden and need for support</cite>.
- Psychological and social support: Address depression, anxiety, and cognitive changes with a multidisciplinary team, including neurologists, occupational therapists, and mental health professionals<cite id="1">Neuropsychological symptoms and therapeutic targets in PD</cite>.

Evidence-Based Takeaways

- Early recognition of non-motor symptoms (constipation, hyposmia, RBD, depression) can lead to earlier diagnosis and intervention<cite id="19">Non-motor symptoms as early markers</cite>.
- Milestones such as recurrent falls, visual hallucinations, dementia, and nursing home placement are associated with worse outcomes and should prompt comprehensive reassessment of care plans<cite id="20">Milestone events and prognosis</cite>.
- DBS improves motor outcomes but requires ongoing programming, medication management, and home safety adaptations to enhance comfort and independence<cite id="11">DBS adjustment and support needs</cite><cite id="13">Home modifications for safety</cite>.
- Caregiver support and multidisciplinary care are critical to maintaining quality of life as the disease progresses<cite id="14">Caregiver burden and support strategies</cite><cite id="1">Multidisciplinary therapeutic targets</cite>.

Conclusion

Understanding PD across stages—from prodromal non-motor signs to late-stage motor and cognitive complications—allows families to recognize red flags and act early. For DBS patients, integrating regular programming, medication optimization, home safety modifications, and caregiver support can significantly improve daily living and well-being<cite id="2">Motor and staging progression</cite><cite id="19">Non-motor staging and early markers</cite><cite id="11">DBS adjustment and support strategies</cite><cite id="13">Home safety modifications</cite>.</answer>

The non-motor and functional features visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, dementia and nursing home placement are currently not included in clinical staging schemes, but have been suggested as clinical milestones with important prognostic implications in advanced PD. In this study, we sought to evaluate the potential of these four milestone events for clinical staging and prognosis during the early years of the disease. Methods: We recruited 185 patients with incident PD and monitored prospectively every six months through seven years for emergence and consequences of four clinical milestones. Results: One or more milestones were reached in 53.0%. Presence of any milestone was associated with occurrence of other milestones (relative risks 1.9-6.3; all p ≤ 0.001). Experiencing two or more milestones increased the risk of death during the study (relative risk 2.7, p = 0.03). Conclusions: In early PD, visual hallucinations, recurrent falls, dementia and nursing home placement appear closely interrelated, possibly reflecting a shared neuropathological disease stage. All events convey important and sinister information on PD status and prognosis and are relatively easily accessible during routine clinical consultations. Therefore, they appear highly useful as clinical PD milestones and could possibly be incorporated into a novel disease rating scale.</summary><hostname>دانشیاری</hostname><publisher>Parkinsonism and Related Disorders</publisher><author_list><author name="Anders Bjornestad Md" affiliation="a The Norwegian Centre for Movement Disorders, Stavanger University Hospital, Stavanger, Norway; b Department of Neurology, Stavanger University Hospital, Stavanger, Norway; c Institute of Clinical Medicine, University of Bergen, Norway; d Department of Neurology, Haukeland University Hospital, Bergen, Norway" /><author name="Kenn Freddy Pedersen Md Phd" affiliation="a The Norwegian Centre for Movement Disorders, Stavanger University Hospital, Stavanger, Norway; b Department of Neurology, Stavanger University Hospital, Stavanger, Norway" /><author name="Olebjorn Tysnes Md Phd" affiliation="c Institute of Clinical Medicine, University of Bergen, Norway; d Department of Neurology, Haukeland University Hospital, Bergen, Norway" /><author name="Guido Alves Md Phd" affiliation="a The Norwegian Centre for Movement Disorders, Stavanger University Hospital, Stavanger, Norway; b Department of Neurology, Stavanger University Hospital, Stavanger, Norway" /></author_list><url>https://daneshyari.com/article/previe

The lived experience of people with PD suggests a process of adjustment follows. This study aimed to explore the adjustment and associated education and support needs of people with PD undergoing DBS and their family members across the continuum of the DBS experience. Method A structured qualitative description study including semi-structured interviews with people with PD (n = 14), family members (n = 11) and clinicians (n = 11) was conducted to explore lived experiences, needs, perspectives and clinical considerations. Inductive analysis indicated common temporal stages related to undergoing DBS, and the related experiences and needs were mapped. Findings Four stages, each with unique needs, emerged: Considering DBS involved needs for peer-based education and realistic, meaningful goal setting; Surgery and Support shifted to clinical support related to the surgery and support for the person and their family around immediate changes experienced; Seeking Stability focused on timely clinical and practical support for the person and family around new changes and challenges to symptoms, behaviours and roles; and Next Steps involved direction and support for reengagement in the self-management of the condition, and current and future changes related to PD. All participants with PD and their family members in this study indicated that overall their experiences with DBS had led to positive changes in their symptoms and lives. Consideration of different needs at different times in the process may be applied within clinical practice to support adjustment.</summary><hostname>Universidade da Coruña</hostname><publisher>Brain Impairment</publisher><author_list><author name="Jacki Liddle" affiliation="Asia Pacific Centre for Neuromodulation, Queensland Brain Institute, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia. *School of Information Technology and Electrical Engineering, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia; *School of Health and Rehabilitation Sciences, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia" /><author name="Gregory Beazley" affiliation="*School of Information Technology and Electrical Engineering, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia" /><author name="Louise Gustafsson" affiliation="*School of Information Technology and Electrical Engineering, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia" /><author name="Peter Silburn" affiliation="*School of Health and Rehabilitation Sciences, The University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD, Australia" /></author_list><url>https://www-cambridge-org.accedys.udc.es/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/595974A56A056045FE9363E74B194A88/S1443964619000032a.pdf/mapping_the_experiences_and_needs_of_deep_brain_stimulation_for_people_with_parkinsons_disease_and_their_family_members.pdf</url><publish_time>2019年3月4日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:12"><title>Inpatient rehabilitation after deep brain stimulator placement: A case series</title><summary>This case series describes the inpatient rehabilitation of two medically complex patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) who had undergone deep brain stimulator (DBS) placement.
