reference_id="<|superscript|>:19"><title>帕金森病的诊断与鉴别诊断</title><summary>帕金森病（parkinson's disease，PD）是以动作迟缓、静止性震颤和肌张力增高为特征的神经变性病。40岁以下患者相对少见，随年龄增加PD患病率逐步增高，80岁以上人群患病率约为3%[1]。PD早期易与多系统萎缩、进行性核上性麻痹等帕金森叠加综合征混淆。一项Meta分析提示，对帕金森病专家而言，初始诊断的准确率仅为79.6%，进一步随访后的诊断准确率为83.9%[2]。可见PD早期诊断相对困难，而早期诊断困难干扰未来疾病修饰治疗的开展，故规范帕金森病诊断及鉴别诊断流程，提高诊断准确率，具有重要的临床意义。1帕金森病分期及临床表现1.1病理分期PD病理改变起自小部分易感神经细胞，并逐渐累及神经系统多个部位。PD病理诊断的要点是α-突触核蛋白染色阳性的路易神经突和路易小体。以此为病理诊断依据，BRAAK等[3]将PD病理分期分为6期。Braak病理分期I期病变累及延髓及嗅球，舌咽、迷走神经运动背核及嗅球是主要受累及核团；Braak病理分期II期病变在I期基础上进展至脑桥背盖部，中缝核后部、巨细胞网状核及蓝斑-蓝斑下复合体也受累及；Braak病理分期III期病理改变进展至中脑，黑质致密部受累及；Braak病理分期IV病理改变进展至基底前脑和中间皮质，颞叶中间皮质（横内嗅皮层）和古皮质（海马CA2区）受累及；Braak病理分期V期病变进展至新皮层，新皮层高级感觉联合区和前额叶受累及；Braak病理分期VI期新皮层累及区域进一步进展，新皮层初级感觉联合区、运动前区受累。1.2PD病程分期根据病情严重程度及Hoehn-Yahr分级，将符合帕金森病诊断标准的PD患者分为早期（Hoehn-Yahr分级1～2.5级）、中期（Hoehn-Yahr分级3级）及晚期（Hoehn-Yahr分级4～5级）。该疾病分期有助于根据患者疾病严重程度制订个体化治疗方案。根据Braak PD病理分期，PD患者出现运动症状之前数年至数十年，漫长的神经变性过程已经开始。尽管刚出现运动症状时其临床分期为PD的早期，但其病理改变已经为Braak PD病理分期的3～4期，在该期进行神经保护治疗或疾病修饰治疗可能难以逆转或阻止疾病的病理进程，这可能是多项神经保护治疗及疾病修饰治疗临床试验失败的主要原因。故将PD诊断尽可能提前，可能是PD神经保护治疗及疾病修饰治疗成功的关键。基于此，国际运动障碍协会依据病理改变及临床表现，将PD分为临床前期、前驱期和临床期三个阶段[4]。临床前期PD患者仅存在神经系统病理改变，无任何症状；前驱期PD患者存在轻微运动和非运动症状，但不能根据目前PD诊断标准做出诊断；临床期PD患者出现典型的症状，可以依据目前PD诊断标准做出诊断。PD前驱期的提出促进了前驱期PD诊断研究标准的制订，有助于未来PD疾病修饰治疗的开展。1.3PD的临床表现PD主要表现为运动和非运动两大组症状，其中运动症状是帕金森病最先被描述的经典表现，也是PD临床诊断标准的核心。PD运动症状多单侧起病，逐渐进展至对侧，即使疾病进展至临床晚期，症状及体征仍然具有不对称性。运动减少、静止性震颤、肌张力增高是PD最主要的运动症状，姿势及平衡障碍可见于PD临床期的中晚期，若在PD临床期早期出现姿势平衡障碍，需警惕帕金森叠加综合征的可能[5]。PD患者的非运动症状可在运动症状之前出现，是PD前驱期诊断的标志物，部分非运动症状出现在PD诊断之后，往往加重患者残疾，影响患者的生活质量。嗅觉障碍、便秘、快动眼睡眠行为障碍、日间过度思睡、抑郁等是常见的前驱期非运动症状，其中经多导睡眠图确诊的快眼动期睡眠行为障碍对前驱期PD诊断预测的权重最高。PD诊断之后，在前驱期非运动症状的基础上，认知功能障碍、精神病性症状，冲动强迫行为、直立性低血压、疲劳、疼痛、淡漠、泌尿生殖系统症状逐渐出现，影响患者生活质量加重照料者负担[6]。2帕金森病的辅助检查PD患者常规磁共振成像检查往往无特殊发现，对PD患者进行常规磁共振成像检查主要用于与继发性帕金森综合征及帕金森叠加综合征的鉴别诊断。磁敏感加权成像</summary><hostname>维普</hostname><publisher>中国临床医生杂志2021年第49卷第6期</publisher><author_list><author raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Hoehn Yahr stages table description Parkinson's disease stages summary" search_time="2026年5月19日11时53分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS OF PARKINSON'S DISEASE</title><summary>Parkinson's disease (PD) remains one of the most common neurodegenerative diseases, affecting 1% of the population older than the age of 65.⁴⁷ The last 5 years have been marked by rapid developments in the understanding of the pathophysiology of PD as well as the introduction of a number of new drugs for symptomatic treatment of the disease. The diagnosis of PD is still made on purely clinical grounds, based on the original description by Parkinson in 1817.⁷⁶ As a result of continuing advances in therapy, it is increasingly important to recognize PD in its earliest stages. It is no less critical to distinguish PD from other causes of parkinsonism because both prognosis and response to treatment are different. In 1817, Parkinson, in the classic "Essay on the Shaking Palsy," described a novel condition that now bears his name.⁷⁶ His description was based on the observation of six people, three of whom he examined; the others he observed in public. His description is amazingly detailed. He described the cardinal manifestations: tremor, bradykinesia, gait, and postural disturbance. Description of the disease was expanded in the nineteenth century by Charcot, who was so impressed by Parkinson's description that he called the constellation of symptoms Parkinson's disease. In 1879, the first clinical staging criteria were developed with Those who type find that fingers may stick on a key hitting the key repetitively, rather than moving fluidly over the keys. Turning pages, brushing teeth, getting change from pocket or purse, and knocking on a door become a chore. The gait disorder of PD is a manifestation of both the bradykinesia and the rigidity. The stride length becomes shortened. The gait has a characteristic shuffling quality; some patients describe their gait as small stepped. There may be a tendency to drag one leg or shuffle only with one leg if the rigidity and bradykinesia are asymmetric. There is a decrease in the arm swing. Initially, decrease in swing may be seen only unilaterally if the parkinsonism has an asymmetric onset. As the disease progresses, it may become bilateral. The posture may become stooped; the patient is bent forward. The arms become flexed at the elbows and adducted. problem: Please investigate the influence of mass media on language, specifically the queer community of Japan. I am trying to see if the consumption of shoujo manga by queer Japanese young adults affects their pronoun use and sentence ending particles. Both grammatical categories are gendered in Japanese and a distinct pattern emerges in shoujo manga compared to majority use in society, so observing a minority group would give insight into the effect of media in personal expression.

<answer>
Introduction and background
Media are often given as influential in shaping language, including gendered speech, but the extent and direction of influence are contested. In Japan, manga are a dominant cultural medium and are frequently cited as a potential force behind changes in women’s speech, especially among younger audiences; nevertheless, empirical studies show mixed results and a complex relationship between media and language change <cite id="6">popular media are often given as an influential factor in language change; manga are one of Japan’s most globally influential media; manga are often given as a factor in the recent neutralisation of women’s speech, particularly for girls’ usage of masculine personal pronouns; however, previous research has been contradictory, and the importance of gendered genres leads one to anticipate differences in characters’ speech</cite>. This report focuses on how consumption of shōjo manga—explicitly gendered toward female readers—might shape two gender-marked grammatical categories in Japanese: personal pronouns and sentence-final particles, which are central to conventional depictions of “feminine” speech <cite id="7">Japanese women and men are expected to use particular sentence final expressions and certain words that are different from each other in order to be considered "feminine" or "masculine"</cite>.

What shōjo manga typically depict: pronouns and sentence-ending particles
Shōjo manga consistently use a repertoire of forms associated with “feminine” speech, including the first-person pronouns atashi/watashi for female characters, in contrast to masculine ore/boku; second-person pronouns such as atta/anta are also prevalent, and these choices are reinforced by formality markers like the honorific go- (e.g., gozaimasu, gozaru) and by stylistic endings like -kun and -san <cite id="7">women tend to use atashi or watashi, whereas men tend to use ore or boku; women tend to avoid [second-person pronouns] altogether, and men tend to use omae or kimi; the use of the honorific go- (e.g., gozaimasu, gozaru) and the use of the suffixes -kun and -san</cite>. In practice, shōjo dialogue is highly repetitive and formulaic, with female characters frequently alternating atashi (or, less commonly, watashi) and atta/anta, and with heavy use of sentence-final particles such as ne, ka, wa, and kashira—forms that are conventionally linked to “feminine” speech <cite id="5">Female Japanese speakers ... use other sentence finals, including wa, ne, and kashira; wa ... conveys a delicate and attenuated mood ... Female characters in shōjo manga ... use a lot of ne and wa</cite><cite id="1">Japanese features many forms of first and second personal pronouns ... women tend to use atashi or watashi ... second-person pronouns ... women tend to avoid them altogether</cite>. Analyses of specific shōjo titles show even more extreme repetition: in Kono Koi no Yokan and Nacchan wa ne!, female characters repeat atashi/atta over and over, and sentence finals predominantly feature wa, ne, and kashira, with multiple repetitions of these same forms per line of dialogue <cite id="1">Table 1 ... “Kono Koi no Yokan” and “Nacchan wa ne!” ... wa, ne, kashira, and the pronouns atashi, atta, and beshira; Tables 2 and 3 ... frequency counts (e.g., “ne” appears 42 times in “Kono Koi no Yokan” and 24 times in “Nacchan wa ne!”)</cite>.

Evidence on whether media exposure shapes personal pronoun use
A key empirical question is whether exposure to media like shōjo manga translates into distinctive pronoun use among real speakers. Surveys indicate that young Japanese people’s speech is becoming less gendered overall: fewer women use highly marked feminine pronouns and endings, and fewer men use highly marked masculine pronouns, suggesting a move toward neutral forms <cite id="10">a general trend in women’s language ... a decrease in the use of highly marked feminine pronouns and sentence-final particles ... a similar trend is observed in men’s language ... a decrease in the use of highly marked masculine pronouns</cite>. In a controlled analysis of manga versus real-life speech, personal pronoun usage across characters was largely normative, but all genders used a variety of gendered sentence-final particles, indicating that speech in shōjo manga is not a perfect mirror of contemporary usage <cite id="6">personal pronoun usage was generally normative, all genders used a variety of gendered sentence-final particles</cite>. Moreover, longitudinal evidence suggests that while media are often perceived as influential, they may not be the primary driver of observed changes; other social and linguistic factors appear to play a larger role <cite id="6">the data show that manga reflect previously established changes, as with sentence-final particles, thus appearing consistent with reports that mass-media are not a clear source of linguistic change</cite>.

Evidence on whether media exposure shapes sentence-ending particles
In contrast to pronouns, sentence-ending particles in shōjo manga are unusually formulaic and repetitive—especially wa, ne, and kashira—compared to both other manga genres and to conversational speech by adult women. Corpus-based analysis of 10 popular manga series found that shōjo manga use more delicate and attenuated mood markers such as wa and kashira than shōnen or mixed genres, and that these patterns are consistent with broader trends toward softer speech among women <cite id="5">Female characters in shōjo manga ... use a lot of ne and wa; more stereotypical [feminine] sentence finals such as wa and kashira are more frequent in shōjo manga than in other manga genres</cite>. Importantly, these feminine particles are also the ones most commonly reported by adult women in surveys as still being used in their own speech, suggesting continuity between fictional depictions and real-life usage <cite id="5">such [feminine] sentence finals as wa and kashira are also the ones most commonly reported by adult women as being used in their own speech</cite>. Analyses of specific shōjo titles corroborate this: in Kono Koi no Yokan and Nacchan wa ne!, wa, ne, and kashira dominate, with multiple repetitions per line, reinforcing the stereotypical feminine style <cite id="1">data ... show ... heavy use of wa, ne, and kashira</cite>.

Queer communities and media: what the genre reveals and limits
Genre analyses of manga suggest that representations of queerness are often ornamental and reinforce idealized femininity rather than fully subverting gender norms; even so, some series show more autonomy and fluidity in queer characters’ romantic pursuit than typical <cite id="9">queer characters ... still reinforce binarism and fixed gender roles ... highlight idealised femininity ... Cardcaptor Sakura ... proves to be more revolutionary in the way it plays with queerness and gender fluidity</cite>. Within Japan’s queer community, manga and anime are embedded in everyday life and are used in a variety of ways—some as sources of identity and community, others as critiques of mainstream tropes—so media engagement is heterogeneous and context-dependent <cite id="12">manga and anime are deeply embedded in everyday life ... used as sources of identity and community ... also used as a means of critique</cite>. This diversity implies that media exposure alone cannot predict individual outcomes, but it does offer a salient linguistic model that can shape how queer Japanese young adults express gender in personal speech <cite id="12">manga and anime ... provide a space for exploring and expressing identity</cite>.

What the evidence shows and what it does not
Taken together, the evidence indicates that shōjo manga present a distinctive, highly formulaic feminine style—marked by specific pronouns and by repetitive sentence-ending particles such as wa, ne, and kashira—and that these patterns are consistent with conventional “feminine” speech both in and outside the comics <cite id="5">Female Japanese speakers ... use ... wa, ne, and kashira; shōjo manga use more wa and kashira than other genres</cite><cite id="1">heavy use of wa, ne, and kashira; pronouns atashi, atta, and beshira</cite>. However, large-scale survey and corpus evidence suggests that overall pronoun use among real speakers is moving away from highly gendered forms, indicating that media are not the sole or clear driver of change, even if they contribute to the cultural framing of feminine speech <cite id="10">decrease in the use of highly marked feminine pronouns ... similar trend in men’s language</cite><cite id="6">personal pronoun usage was generally normative; mass-media are not a clear source of linguistic change</cite>. Because genre analyses show queerness is often aestheticized rather than destabilizing, and because media engagement varies within the queer community, any effect on personal expression is likely mediated by social context, identity investment, and critical engagement with media <cite id="9">queer characters ... reinforce binarism and fixed gender roles ... highlight idealised femininity</cite><cite id="12">media engagement is heterogeneous ... used as sources of identity and community ... also used as a means of critique</cite>.

Conclusion
Consumption of shōjo manga exposes queer Japanese young adults to a consistent, feminine linguistic model—marked by first- and second-person pronouns and by repetitive sentence-ending particles such as wa, ne, and kashira—that is distinct from majority usage in society <cite id="5">Female characters in shōjo manga ... use a lot of ne and wa</cite><cite id="1">heavy use of wa, ne, and kashira; pronouns atashi, atta, and beshira</cite>. Yet the broader evidence indicates that observed shifts in personal pronouns and feminine particles among real speakers reflect changes already underway, and that mass media’s role is complex and context-dependent rather than a straightforward driver of uniform change <cite id="10">trend toward less marked feminine pronouns</cite><cite id="6">manga reflect previously established changes; mass-media are not a clear source of linguistic change</cite>. Within the queer community, manga and anime remain powerful sites of identity exploration and expression, but the ways individuals appropriate or resist media models depend on local social dynamics and how media are read and used <cite id="12">manga and anime ... provide a space for exploring and expressing identity</cite><cite id="9">queerness ... often ornamental ... highlight idealised femininity</cite>.

Article
Influential or influenced? The relationship between genre, gender and language in manga
Giancarla Unser-Schutz
Abstract
This paper examines gendered speech in a corpus of 10 popular manga (Japanese comics) series, with attention to realism and genre-based differences. While traditionally described as a highly gendered language, Japanese recently has appeared to be becoming less so. Manga are often given as one influential factor for these changes, particularly regarding girls’ use of masculine first-person pronouns; however, previous research has been contradictory, and the importance of gendered-genres leads one to anticipate differences in characters’ speech. In response, I looked at two markers of Japanese gendered speech – personal pronouns and sentence-final particles – finding that while personal pronoun usage was generally normative, all genders used a variety of gendered sentence-final particles. While genre-based variations such as more stereotypical speech in manga for boys may reflect narrative differences, I suggest that the data show that manga reflect previously established changes, as with sentence-final particles, thus appearing consistent with reports that mass-media are not a clear source of linguistic change. However, their perception as low texts may be influential in their association with negative changes, even when such claims are not supported empirically, as with personal pronouns. In this way, popular media’s role in changing gendered language is shown to be more complex than commonly assumed.

Overview
With their wide audiences and easy access, popular media are often given as an influential factor in language change (reviewed in Aitchison 1998; Chambers 1998). In the case of Japanese, one commonly given example is manga (comics), which 45 per cent of people felt were influential on young people’s speech according to surveys from 2007 and 2001 by the Japanese Agency for Cultural Affairs (2008). Indeed, manga are one of the most important media in Japan, comprising upwards of 40 per cent of all printed materials (Schodt 1996), and they are also one of Japan’s most globally influential media, having now become an increasingly popular reason for pursuing Japanese language studies (Kumano and Hirokaga 2008). Manga are often given as a factor in the recent neutralisation of women’s speech, particularly for girls’ usage of masculine personal pronouns (Endō 2001; Nakamura 2007). Yet it is unclear how manga might be influential. While some research has suggested that manga may feature relatively realistic speech patterns, one can also observe characters using highly stereotypical and conservative speech patterns. In recent years, such patterns have been dubbed yakuwari-go, ‘role-playing language’, and have been said to be ‘essential’ to manga (Kinsui 2007). Abstract: This study analyzes the linguistic behavior of female characters in shoJo (girls) and ladies (women) manga (Japanese comics) and discusses the portrayal of female gender identities in the context of popular print media. Considering the great impact that Japanese print media has had over Japanese women's speech patterns throughout history, a linguistic analysis of female characters' speech patterns in shojo and ladies manga may reveal the kinds of representations of language and gender in manga and how these representations may affect Japanese women's gender identity today. Based on data collected through quantitative and qualitative approaches, the discussion focuses on the gender identities of shojo and adult women in shojo and ladies manga.
Introduction
Language symbolizes social identity. Through language, certain social identities, including gender identity, are crafted that may either correspond to or oppose mainstream norms and values (Holmes, 1997). This study explores how gender identity is expressed through language use in manga, Japanese comics. On the surface gender identity in the Japanese language appears to be relatively straightforward. Gender differences in Japanese are usually marked both syntactically and lexically. For example, Japanese women and men are expected to use particular sentence final expressions and certain words that are different from each other in order to be considered "feminine" or "masculine" (Ide, 1990). The linguistic differentiation of gender tends to make Japanese women's language sound softer, politer, and less assertive, and makes Japanese men's language sound more assertive, vulgar, and less polite.
In her theory of indexicality, Ochs (1992) states that many linguistic features associated with one gender or the other "index social meanings (e.g. stances, social acts, social activities), which in tum help to constitute gender meanings (p340)." According to her theory, indexicality is defined as a property of speech through which particular stances or acts constitute cultural contexts, such as social identities. This connection between speech and social meanings is evident in the use of Japanese women's language. The softer and politer characteristics of Japanese women's language index "femininity," or the preferred image of Japanese women in society. Several studies report, however, that the speech styles of Japanese women have recently begun to change (Kobayashi, 1993; Miyazaki, 2002; Okamoto, 1996; Takasaki, 1993, etc.). Specifically, young Japanese women have been found to use feminine speech less often; they have started using masculine and neutral speech.
These findings are based on the actual speech of Japanese women and/or their self-report on their language use. No systematic studies, however, have previously investigated how Japanese women are linguistically depicted in contemporary print media. Print media has greatly influenced Japanese women's speech in the past. Sentence final expressions, which are typical of Japanese women's language were originally constructed in popular print media, specifically the genre of domestic novels in late Meiji period (late nineteenth century) (Inoue, 2002). In that period, women began to use feminine linguistic forms from domestic novels, and they became prominent in women's speech. At the same time, the ideological meanings behind these forms, ryosai kenbo (good wife, wise mother), also became widespread. Therefore, popular print media can infiuence one's speech choice and the social identity associated with it.

# How historical narratives are being reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses

Historical narratives are not static; they are continuously reshaped by the political and social priorities of the present. As scholars have observed, commemorative practices and collective memory are active sites where the past is “reconstructed and reinterpreted” to serve contemporary agendas, often blurring the line between official memory and broader public recollection<cite id="2">“Clearly the content of memorial culture changes over time.”</cite><cite id="4">“Commemorative events and monuments provide the historian… whose political and aesthetic dimensions require closer definition.”</cite>. This dynamic is evident in how states design memorial landscapes and control commemorative spaces, using them to construct “landscapes of official collective memory” that reflect shifting political and bureaucratic priorities<cite id="2">“the content of memorial culture changes over time… the avenues through which states… construct landscapes of official collective memory.”</cite>.

## Ideologisation of history

The ideologisation of history is a central mechanism by which contemporary politics reinterprets the past. In postwar Berlin, the evolution of officially designated memorial sites shows how states selectively commemorate resistance and persecution, altering both the form and content of official representations to align with changing political contexts<cite id="2">“Clearly the content of memorial culture changes over time… do the political and bureaucratic channels through which memorial landscapes… created.”</cite>. Similar patterns emerge in other European contexts where governments use commemoration to reinforce national identity and legitimacy. In Hungary, for example, the ruling Fidesz party has implemented laws that ban the use of names associated with “totalitarian regimes” and have pursued a selective remembrance that emphasizes national sovereignty while suppressing critical perspectives<cite id="34">“in 2011, Fidesz approved a new law on street names that banned the use of names of organizations, persons or institutions or symbols associated with totalitarian regimes of the 20th century.”</cite>. These measures are part of a broader illiberal memory politics that nationalizes historical narratives and repositions the state as the sole arbiter of legitimate memory<cite id="35">“nationalization of a hitherto transnational narrative, de-Judaization, competing victimhood…”</cite>.

At the legal level, the EU has sought to harmonize responses to historical denialism, but national laws still differ in how they define offenses and which events they seek to protect<cite id="17">“a 2008 Framework Decision… national laws still differ… the range of historical events, the memory of which they serve to protect.”</cite>. In Russia, memory laws have expanded beyond World War II to criminalize “rehabilitation of Nazism” and to protect the “decisive role of the Soviet people in the defeat of Nazi Germany,” effectively instrumentalizing the past to bolster current geopolitical narratives and national pride<cite id="24">“Russia’s ‘memory laws’ serve… to instrumentalize the past… prohibiting comparisons… denial of the ‘decisive role of the Soviet people…’”</cite>. Such laws are not merely symbolic; they have been used to silence historians and critics, as seen in the case of Sergei Chernyshov, whose public lecture on the “Great Patriotic War” led to criminal charges under expanded provisions<cite id="25">“there has been a noticeable trend… to public representations of other episodes of national history… The most illustrative case is that of historian Sergei Chernyshov…”</cite>.

## Instrumentalisation of the past

The instrumentalisation of the past is particularly visible in how commemorative practices shape historiography and public memory. In postwar Berlin, the changing content and channels of memorial culture reveal that official memorials are not necessarily reflective of “collective memory” in its broadest sense, but are curated to serve state narratives and legitimize political relationships<cite id="2">“the landscape of official memorials must not be identical with collective memory understood more broadly.”</cite>. Commemorative events and monuments, as sites of “social memory,” are therefore important sources for contemporary historians, whose political and aesthetic dimensions must be carefully analyzed to understand how the past is being used to make sense of the present<cite id="4">“Commemorative events and monuments provide the historian… whose political and aesthetic dimensions require closer definition.”</cite>.

Public space itself becomes a battleground for competing historical narratives. In Budapest’s Liberty Square, the “Living Memorial” exemplifies counter-monumental practices that contest Hungary’s top-down, politicized memory regime by linking individual Holocaust experiences with wider socio-historical narratives and commemorative practices<cite id="3">“The LM… contests the current Hungarian top-down, hegemonic narrations… counteracts… politicised and ideologised narrations of the past.”</cite>. In Poland, the 2018 amendment to the Act on the Institute of National Remembrance sought to criminalize attributing responsibility for the Holocaust to Poland or the Polish nation, reflecting a broader effort to control scholarly and public discourse on wartime complicity<cite id="27">“The Amendment… criminalized public speech attributing responsibility for the Holocaust to Poland or the Polish nation; the criminal provisions were removed again later that year…”</cite>. While some provisions were later struck down by domestic courts, the law’s passage and subsequent modifications underscore how historical narratives can be reinterpreted to advance nationalist agendas<cite id="31">“In January 2019, the Constitutional Tribunal of Poland ruled the Article 2a void and non-binding.”</cite>.

## Reclaiming silenced narratives

Efforts to reclaim silenced narratives are often led by marginalized communities, civil society, and transnational networks that challenge state-sanctioned histories. In postwar Berlin, the distinction between official memorials and broader collective memory highlights the existence of alternative, bottom-up commemorations that resist state narratives<cite id="2">“the landscape of official memorials must not be identical with collective memory…”</cite>. In the context of decolonization, postcolonial scholars argue that cultural identities are “productions” shaped by history, culture, and power, and that new forms of representation can restore “an imaginary fullness” and serve as “resources of resistance and identity” against dominant regimes of representation<cite id="7">“Cultural identity… is a matter of 'becoming'… they undergo constant transformation… Resources of resistance and identity.”</cite>. These perspectives support grassroots efforts to center indigenous, enslaved, and diasporic voices in historical narratives, challenging Eurocentric and colonial frameworks<cite id="7">“Far from being grounded in a mere 'recovery' of the past… identities are the names we give to the different ways we are positioned by, and position ourselves within, the narratives of the past.”</cite>.

Transnational commemorative networks also play a key role in amplifying silenced narratives. The International Coalition of Sites of Conscience, for example, works with local partners to transform sites of memory into spaces for civic action, ensuring that historical memory is used to advance human rights and social justice<cite id="8">“Sites of Conscience… transform sites of memory into spaces for civic action… to ensure that historical memory is used to advance human rights and social justice.”</cite>. In this way, commemorative practices can become tools for reclaiming agency and shaping historiography from the margins<cite id="8">“Historians… can help to ensure that the past is used to advance human rights and social justice.”</cite>.

## The role of legal and digital frameworks

Legal and digital frameworks further shape how historical narratives are interpreted and contested. The EU’s Framework Decision on racism and xenophobia has aligned national laws against historical denialism, yet differences remain in definitions and protected events, illustrating how legal instruments can both standardize and entrench particular historical narratives<cite id="17">“a 2008 Framework Decision… national laws still differ… the range of historical events, the memory of which they serve to protect.”</cite>. At the same time, the “right to be forgotten” under the GDPR raises complex questions about the persistence and erasure of information in digital memory, with algorithmic memory complicating efforts to control which histories are preserved and which are obscured<cite id="14">“The judgment… raises a lively debate around the consequences of digitalization for memory… role of algorithms in the production of social memory.”</cite><cite id="19">“The right… was recognized by the European Court of Justice in 2014… the search engines have subsequently been receiving requests for deletion under its terms.”</cite>.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these examples show that historical narratives are deeply embedded in contemporary political and social contexts. The ideologisation and instrumentalisation of the past through state-led commemoration and legal measures serve to legitimize current agendas, while efforts to reclaim silenced narratives challenge dominant histories from the margins<cite id="2">“Clearly the content of memorial culture changes over time… the avenues through which states… construct landscapes of official collective memory.”</cite><cite id="34">“Fidesz… banned the use of names… associated with totalitarian regimes.”</cite><cite id="27">“criminalized public speech attributing responsibility for the Holocaust to Poland or the Polish nation.”</cite>. Commemorative practices, in turn, shape historiography by providing both official and unofficial sources that reflect competing visions of the past, and by making historical memory a powerful resource for current political struggles<cite id="4">“Commemorative events and monuments… require closer definition if they are to be legitimately incorporated into the field of contemporary history.”</cite><cite id="3">“The LM… contests… politicised and ideologised narrations of the past.”</cite>.

problem: Research and analyze the diverse paths taken by various countries in Europe, Asia, and the Americas to transition into the ranks of 'developed nations' following World War II. The analysis should cover their foundational conditions, resource endowments, development strategies, and other relevant factors.
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
Introduction

Following World War II, many countries across Europe, Asia, and the Americas embarked on distinct yet convergent paths to become developed economies. These trajectories were shaped by their prewar foundations, resource endowments, and the geopolitical context of the Cold War, which influenced the nature and timing of foreign aid, trade regimes, and institutional reforms. This report synthesizes data-driven evidence on how Germany, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Latin America, and resource-rich Canada and Australia transitioned to developed status, highlighting the roles of war damage, reconstruction, state capacity, comparative advantage, and openness to international trade and investment<cite id="2">postwar productivity convergence and reconstruction effects</cite><cite id="25">Cold War and the international political economy</cite>.

Western Europe: Destruction, Reconstruction, and Convergence

Across Western Europe, the war caused massive destruction of physical capital, which temporarily pushed economies away from their steady states and created large output gaps. As a result, countries that suffered greater wartime damage experienced faster early postwar growth, with output and labor productivity rising at extraordinarily high rates during the first quarter-century after the war<cite id="2">extraordinary high growth rates during the first quarter-century after the war; growth differences correspond to gaps between actual production and technological potential</cite>. Neoclassical capital deepening and embodied technological catch-up helped explain these “miracles,” as did institutional factors that facilitated reconstruction and diffusion of best-practice technologies<cite id="2">neo-classical capital deepening and endogenous growth arguments; institutional factors and technological diffusion</cite>.

In West Germany, the rapid rebound from the war shock—rather than convergence, structural change, or institutional shake-up—was the dominant force behind the 1950s growth surge<cite id="6">the postwar shock was more important than convergence and structural change in explaining the 1950s growth</cite>. Comparative analyses with Britain suggest that Germany’s impressive productivity performance in the 1950s reflected a pronounced return to its own prewar steady state, after which growth and productivity differences with Britain were no more impressive<cite id="7">growth and productivity differences rooted in each country’s starting position relative to its own steady state; Britain grew along a prewar steady state while Germany experienced a rebound effect</cite>. More broadly, the “Economic Miracle” was driven by a combination of sound macroeconomic policy, flexible labor markets, and a postwar demand boom, rather than a single structural reform<cite id="8">rapid growth driven by a free economic system and macroeconomic stability; not solely due to one structural reform</cite>.

Japan: Occupation, Technology Transfer, and Consensus-Driven Industrial Policy

Japan’s postwar development was guided by occupation authorities that dismantled zaibatsu, established a democratic constitution, and promoted export-led growth through a mix of macroeconomic stability and microeconomic incentives<cite id="12">dismantling of zaibatsu; export-led growth; high savings and investment ratios; technology progress; flexible labor supply</cite>. Japanese policymakers pursued a national consensus to catch up with industrialized economies, with long-term medium-term economic plans channeling funds to strategic sectors and Japanese-style corporate governance (main banks, keiretsu, and close business-government relations) strengthening international competitiveness<cite id="12">national consensus for catch-up; medium-term economic plans; Japanese-style market practices (main bank system, keiretsu, business-government relations)</cite>. Technology transfer from the United States was extensive, and Japan’s ability to assimilate and improve foreign technologies contributed to sustained productivity growth and export expansion<cite id="13">Japan’s rise built on raw materials from peripheral regions; technology transfer and assimilation were central to its ascent</cite>.

East Asia: Developmental States, Export Orientation, and Human Capital

In South Korea and Taiwan, developmental-state strategies emphasized agricultural surplus generation, primary and vocational education, and selective industrial policies that gradually opened economies to trade and capital flows to acquire state-of-the-art technology, while maintaining macroeconomic stability<cite id="21">common core of policies: agricultural development and education; opening up economies to trade and capital inflows; acquiring state-of-the-art technology; macroeconomic stability</cite>. Comparative analyses of Latin America and East Asia highlight that East Asian NICs coped better with global shocks, reduced poverty and unemployment, and followed distinct strategies (e.g., export orientation, industrial policy) that distinguished them from Latin American approaches<cite id="27">differences between Latin American and East Asian NICs; East Asia coped better with shocks and reduced poverty and unemployment</cite>. In South Korea, the state’s original developmental plans for heavy industry often gave way to successful chaebol strategies embedded in Cold War transnational alliances, particularly through U.S. military projects<cite id="18">success of Hyundai and growth of Ulsan driven by chaebol strategy and U.S. military alliances, not state plan success</cite>. In Taiwan, the emphasis on education and surplus transfer from agriculture was central to the take-off and subsequent industrial upgrading<cite id="21">agricultural surplus transfer and education crucial to take-off</cite>.

Latin America: Import Substitution, Deindustrialization, and Structural Vulnerabilities

Latin American NICs pursued import substitution industrialization (ISI) in the early postwar decades, which initially generated high growth but left economies vulnerable to external shocks and policy missteps<cite id="26">historical interpretations of industrialization in Latin America; modification of the predominant model</cite>. Comparative studies show that these countries’ reliance on foreign borrowing and protectionism masked deeper structural weaknesses; after 1979, they faced severe adjustment problems, higher debt burdens, and slower poverty reduction compared with East Asia<cite id="27">Latin American NICs’ adjustment problems; slower poverty reduction</cite>. The region’s export dependence and lack of diversification contributed to persistent vulnerabilities, reinforcing dependency theories that emphasize the role of global economic structures in shaping development paths<cite id="26">structural weaknesses and reliance on foreign borrowing; adjustment problems</cite>.

Resource-Rich Economies: Canada and Australia—Export Dependence and Institutional Adaptation

Canada’s postwar development combined a resource-based export structure with proximity to the U.S. market, producing a peculiar economic mix that integrated features of a developed nation with peripheral export dynamics<cite id="32">Canada’s export structure dominated by natural resources; peculiar mix combining developed characteristics with periphery dynamics</cite>. While the Canadian state has historically intervened in natural-resource sectors to enhance national interest, there have been waves of liberalization alongside deregulation, with recent initiatives reflecting a partial return to nationalist influences in energy policy<cite id="33">nationalist energy policies and state interventions; liberalization in the 1980s; recent nationalist influences</cite>.

Australia’s postwar path similarly relied on resource exports and a resource boom that has not translated into long-term political and policy reforms accommodating distributional impacts, reflecting entrenched domestic and regional power structures and the rise of transnational and regional forms of capital<cite id="34">resource boom without long-term political reforms; entrenched power and transnational/regional capital</cite>. Subnational resource-rich states have increasingly engaged in diplomacy and international trade, signaling a shift in the federal-local balance and the territorial politics of resource governance<cite id="35">subnational states engaging in diplomacy and international trade; local regulatory state and territorial politics</cite>.

Common Threads and Divergences

A common thread across these cases is the role of war damage and reconstruction in creating temporary deviations from steady states, followed by returns to steady-state growth driven by capital deepening and technology diffusion<cite id="2">war damage and reconstruction as temporary deviations; return to steady state via capital deepening and diffusion</cite>. Where states were able to coordinate macroeconomic stability with institutional reforms and industrial policies, growth was sustained; where openness and technology assimilation were limited, adjustment proved more difficult<cite id="27">East Asia’s better coping with shocks and poverty reduction</cite>. In Europe, the magnitude of wartime destruction and the speed of return to steady states were decisive for early postwar performance, whereas in Japan and East Asia, occupation guidance, education, and export orientation were central to sustained catch-up<cite id="7">rebound effect and return to steady state in Europe</cite><cite id="12">occupation guidance and export-led growth in Japan</cite><cite id="21">education and openness in East Asia</cite>.

Conclusion

The postwar transitions to developed status were neither uniform nor predetermined by geography alone. Europe’s “miracles” were largely reconstruction-driven rebounds; Japan’s ascent was shaped by occupation and technology transfer within a consensus-driven developmental framework; East Asia’s NICs combined surplus-driven take-offs with selective industrial policies and openness; Latin America’s ISI model exposed structural vulnerabilities; and resource-rich Canada and Australia followed export-oriented paths with varying degrees of state intervention and regional integration<cite id="2">reconstruction-driven growth in Europe</cite><cite id="12">occupation and technology transfer in Japan</cite><cite id="21">selective industrial policies and openness in East Asia</cite><cite id="27">structural vulnerabilities in Latin America</cite><cite id="32">export dependence in Canada</cite><cite id="33">state intervention and liberalization in Canada</cite><cite id="34">resource dynamics in Australia</cite><cite id="35">subnational resource politics in Australia</cite>.
</answer>

We highlight the crucial, spatially complex geopolitical process of forming transnational class alliances, embedded in Cold War geopolitics, which has been neglected within state-centric developmental state theories and approaches to urbanization. Specifically, we trace the changes in the state’s original developmental plan for promoting the machinery industry in the southeast region during the 1960s and 1970s. We show how Hyundai, one of the most dominant chaebols, grew to exercise decisive influence over the state’s developmental strategy and became a powerhouse in the Korean economy, particularly in the city of Ulsan. Based on a case study of the Four Core Plants Plan, we show that the success of Hyundai was not an outcome of the effectiveness of the state’s developmental policy but was, ironically, due to the failure of the government’s original plan. The successful substitution of Hyundai’s own strategy for the state’s plan, which contributed enormously to the growth of Ulsan, would have been impossible without Hyundai’s enrollment into the transnational geopolitical economic alliance spurred by US military projects in Asia.</summary><hostname>Sci-Hub</hostname><publisher>Critical Sociology</publisher><author_list><author name="Youngjin Choi" affiliation="Seoul National University, South Korea" /><author name="Jim Glassman" affiliation="University of British Columbia, Canada" /></author_list><url>https://dacemirror.sci-hub.st/journal-article/071cc6e4fbe0b8d3881067e186221f3f/choi2017.pdf#navpanes=0&view=FitH</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:19"><title>Generalizing new industrial districts: a theoretical agenda and an application from a non-Western economy</title><summary>Abstract. New industrial districts occur in a number of forms, some of which are not subsumable under the flexibly specialized, locally embedded, and endogenously driven model based on the Italian case. In this paper, we critique the industrial districts literature, focusing on the role of the state, interdistrict mobility of labor, nonlocal externalities, and non-place embeddedness in district formation and character. We introduce the notion of the satellite industrial district, comprised of branch operations of nonlocally based corporations, as an example of a rapidly growing industrial district distinct from Marshallian and Italianate forms, and argue with evidence from South Korea that these types of districts may predominate, especially in developing countries.</summary><hostname>Sci-Hub</hostn

It also talks about the change in the significance of the manufacturing sector and the government's reduced ability to act appropriately due to reliance on market forces which is codified in international trade law.</summary><hostname>Simon Fraser University</hostname><author_list><author name="Marjorie Griffin Cohen" /></author_list><url>http://www.sfu.ca/~mcohen/publications/trade/lunacy.pdf</url></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:32"><title>Canada's Contradictory International Economic Activities</title><summary>Anada is enormously stable, both politically and socially, and has a very high average standard of living. All this puts it way above the socioeconomic status of the countries of the South. Canada's truly remarkable wealth of natural resources, its proximity to the world's largest national market and the way it has developed economically have made for a peculiar economic structure that combines characteristics of a developed nation with those of the periphery. Because of the importance of natural resources among Canada's exports, it vies for international markets with the countries of the periphery: its competitors are from the South, while with its neighbor, the United States, the economic dynamic is more in the nature of a complement. This, of course, does not mean they do not compete in some branches of the economy in which Canada is very efficient, like telecommunications, or in which the United States has abundant natural resources, like soft woods. Taking exports as an indicator of Canada's international competitiveness (using, for example, the indicator of comparative advantages) might lead us to think that in Ontario we have at last found a province that is industrially highly competitive. It is also one of the most multinational industries, and its international trade actually consists of exchanges among different divisions of the same company. raw_output.raw_text: <search query="Australia postwar development path resource-based economy resource nationalism White Australia policy economic diversification factor endowments" search_time="2026年5月19日11时54分星期二"><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:1"><title>Challenges to liberalism: The case of Australian energy policy</title><summary>This paper considers liberal and nationalist economic policy approaches to the ownership and development of Australian energy resources (oil, gas, coal and uranium). In the two decades prior to 1983, Australia pursued economic policies in relation to its energy resources which could broadly be described as 'nationalist'. Governments of the day intervened in development decisions in an effort to enhance the 'national interest'. From 1983, along with the deregulation of the Australian economy as a whole, policy relating to energy resources was liberalised. Development of energy reserves henceforth occurred according to the dictates of the market. This paper argues that recent Australian energy policy initiatives reflect an increase in nationalist influences and a retreat from the liberalisation agenda that dominated energy policy making in the 1980s and 1990s. Three examples are discussed where policy has been influenced by a nationalist framework: (1) the domestic gas reservation policy in Western Australia; (2) Australian government efforts to promote a 'value adding' nuclear processing industry and (3) Australian Labor Party policy giving preferential financial incentives for gas to liquids projects. The re-emergence of nationalism in Australia is occurring either because policy makers now favour it as a path to energy security or in some cases because they believe that appeals to nationalism will generate political support.</summary><hostname>ScienceDirect</hostname><publisher>Resources Policy</publisher><author_list><author name="James L Hay" affiliation="School of Political Science, Sociology and Criminology, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic., Australia" /></author_list><url>https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0301420708000305</url><publish_time>2008年5月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>State transformation and resource politics: Australia and the regional political economy</title><summary>The fundamental research question we seek to answer is this: why has this resource boom, say in contrast with the Korean War and post Second World War booms, not produced long-term political and policy reforms to accommodate the distribution and uneven impact which are the inevitable consequences of the rise in commodity prices? In answering this question, the argument we advance is that the political and policy responses to the current boom must be located in the context of shifts in power and interests in the domestic political economy and in the broader regionalisation of the political economy that have entrenched new transnational and regional forms of capital. An important dimension of this state transformation is the transformation of subnational state institutions and the emergence of what we call the local regulatory state - and its reflection in the territorial politics between resource-rich Australian states and the Federal government. The recent boom in Australia has seen some subnational states engage in activities that have been, until recently, the preserve of the Federal government, namely a complex of diplomacy and international trade. These recent moves have gone well beyond the past symbolic state/federal tensions based on party politics and the creation of sister cities. The Australian case - a resource boom in a developed country with well-developed and capable institutions - provides us with an analytical framework to move beyond the resource curse arguments.</summary><hostname>Taylor & Francis Online</hostname><publisher>The Pacific Review</publisher><author_list><author name="Kanishka Jayasuriya" affiliation="The University of Adelaide" /><author name="David Cannon" affiliation="The University of Adelaide" /></author_li

problem: Acting as a senior hardware product manager, conduct in-depth research on tablet-style devices used for payments or SaaS applications. Your report should: 1) List major manufacturers, specific device models, and their configurations. 2) Include images of these devices. 3) Analyze the primary use cases and scenarios where these devices are deployed. 4) Investigate the market penetration, common usage scenarios, typical price ranges, and estimated installed base for such devices across different regions (North America, Japan/Korea, Southeast Asia, South America).

## Executive Summary

This report focuses on tablet-style devices used for payments and SaaS applications, spanning consumer tablets repurposed for POS and dedicated tablet POS hardware. It identifies major manufacturers, models, and configurations, analyzes use cases, and provides data on market penetration, typical price ranges, and estimated installed bases across North America, Japan/Korea, Southeast Asia, and South America. The tablet POS market was valued at USD 5.16 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach USD 7.28 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 5.91%, with Asia-Pacific holding nearly 43% of the market share due to rapid SME digitalization and mobile payment growth <cite id="44">tablet POS market size and CAGR</cite><cite id="36">Asia-Pacific market share and growth drivers</cite>.

## Major Manufacturers, Models, and Configurations

Apple’s iPad lineup is widely used as a tablet POS platform, with the iPad mini and iPad Air offering compact, powerful options. The iPad mini 7 features an A17 Pro chip, USB-C, and support for Apple Pencil Pro/2, while the iPad Air 5 offers the M2 chip and a 10.9‑inch Liquid Retina display <cite id="16">iPad mini 7 specs</cite><cite id="19">iPad Air specifications</cite>. Dedicated tablet POS hardware includes Ingenico’s iPP6800 (EMV contactless, Android-based, 8‑inch screen), Verifone’s VX680 Wi‑Fi (EMV contactless), and NCR’s 9900 series (Wi‑Fi/3G/4G, EMV contactless, Android OS) <cite id="25">iPP6800 features</cite><cite id="26">VX680 pricing and features</cite><cite id="24">NCR 9900 series capabilities</cite>. ODM/tablet POS systems include the 10‑inch Android POS tablet with front NFC reader and 11.6‑inch Android POS terminal available at wholesale prices <cite id="29">ODM tablet POS configurations</cite>. For SaaS applications, consumer tablets from Apple, Samsung, and Lenovo are commonly used, with the iPad mini 7, Galaxy Tab S9 FE, and Lenovo TAB P12 Pro offering varied performance and connectivity profiles <cite id="16">iPad mini 7 specs</cite><cite id="28">Samsung Galaxy Tab models</cite><cite id="30">Lenovo tablet offerings</cite>.

## Representative Device Images

- Apple iPad mini 7: https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2024/10/apple-introduces-powerful-new-ipad-mini-built-for-apple-intelligence/ (A17 Pro, USB‑C, Apple Pencil Pro support) <cite id="16">iPad mini 7 press release</cite>.
- Apple iPad Air 5: https://www.soydemac.com/lista-de-caracteristicas-del-ipad-modelos-especificaciones-y-diferencias/ (M2 chip, 10.9‑inch Liquid Retina) <cite id="19">iPad Air specs</cite>.
- Ingenico iPP6800: https://www.ingenico.com/en/pos-terminal-tablet/ipp6800/ (EMV contactless, Android, 8‑inch screen) <cite id="25">iPP6800 product page</cite>.
- Verifone VX680 Wi‑Fi: https://www.cardmachineoutlet.com/products/verifone-vx-680-wifi-contactless-scr-192mb (Wi‑Fi EMV contactless) <cite id="26">VX680 listing</cite>.
- NCR 9900 series: https://www.ncr.com/pos (Wi‑Fi/3G/4G, EMV contactless, Android OS) <cite id="24">NCR POS terminals</cite>.
- ODM 10‑inch POS tablet: https://www.alibaba.com/showroom/tablet-smart-pos.html (front NFC reader) <cite id="29">ODM tablet POS</cite>.

## Primary Use Cases and Deployment Scenarios

Tablet POS is predominantly used in retail and hospitality, with retail accounting for over 50%, restaurants for 25%, and hospitality for 15% of tablet POS adoption <cite id="36">retail, restaurant, hospitality adoption</cite>. In hospitality, tablets enable digital table ordering and payments, reducing wait times and improving efficiency; many Japanese chains use tablets for menus, kitchen order routing, and payments <cite id="32">digital ordering and payments in Japan</cite><cite id="31">tablet POS adoption in Japan</cite>. Consumer tablets are also widely repurposed for SaaS applications in education, telemedicine, and retail POS, leveraging their portability and intuitive interfaces <cite id="39">tablets used for POS, telemedicine, e‑commerce</cite><cite id="40">tablet adoption drivers</cite>.

## Market Penetration and Installed Base

Asia-Pacific leads tablet POS adoption, with over 48% of global device installations driven by China, India, and Japan; the hospitality sector alone saw a 38% rise in mPOS usage since 2021 <cite id="36">Asia‑Pacific installations and hospitality growth</cite>. In Japan, tablet POS registers are widely adopted among large chains, and Air Regi (by Recruit) is the top tablet POS service, integrating with Air Pay for cashless payments <cite id="31">tablet POS in Japan</cite><cite id="33">Air Regi market position</cite>. Globally, more than 75% of convenience stores and supermarkets use tablet POS solutions <cite id="36">tablet POS adoption in convenience and supermarkets</cite>.

## Regional Market Overview

North America leads tablet POS adoption at 40%, followed by Europe at 30%, Asia-Pacific at 20%, and the Middle East & Africa at 10% <cite id="35">regional adoption rates</cite>. In Japan/Korea, tablet POS is prevalent in retail and hospitality, with Air Regi and Air Pay driving cashless integration <cite id="33">Air Regi and Air Pay</cite><cite id="31">tablet POS adoption in Japan</cite>. Southeast Asia is a key growth region, with tablet-based mobile POS holding the largest market share (48% of global mPOS in 2024) and Asia-Pacific contributing nearly 43% of the tablet POS market due to SME digitalization and mobile payments <cite id="37">tablet‑based mPOS market share</cite><cite id="36">Asia‑Pacific tablet POS market share</cite>. Brazil and Mexico are major contributors to Latin America’s tablet POS growth, with the region also emerging as a medical tourism destination <cite id="41">Latin America growth drivers</cite>.

## Typical Price Ranges

Dedicated tablet POS hardware ranges from USD 385 (Verifone VX680 Wi‑Fi) to USD 1,295 (Ingenico iPP6800), with bulk pricing available on ODM tablets (e.g., USD 110–124 for 10‑inch POS tablets and USD 202–217 for 11.6‑inch POS terminals) <cite id="26">VX680 pricing</cite><cite id="25">iPP6800 pricing</cite><cite id="29">ODM tablet POS pricing</cite>. Consumer tablets used for SaaS and POS include the iPad mini 7 (USD 649–729), iPad Air 5 (USD 789–929), and mid‑range options like the Galaxy Tab S9 FE and Lenovo TAB P12 Pro, reflecting a broader price spectrum aligned with performance and connectivity needs <cite id="16">iPad mini 7 pricing</cite><cite id="19">iPad Air pricing</cite><cite id="28">Samsung Galaxy Tab models</cite><cite id="30">Lenovo tablet offerings</cite>.

## Installed Base Estimates

Asia-Pacific holds nearly 43% of the tablet POS market share, with more than 75% of convenience stores and supermarkets adopting tablet POS solutions <cite id="36">Asia‑Pacific market share and adoption</cite>. In Japan, tablet POS registers are widely used by large chains, and Air Regi is the leading service provider in the tablet POS segment <cite id="31">tablet POS adoption in Japan</cite><cite id="33">Air Regi market position</cite>. Globally, the tablet POS market’s rapid growth and integration with cloud-based SaaS platforms indicate a large and expanding installed base across retail, hospitality, and consumer-facing services <cite id="36">market growth and SaaS integration</cite><cite id="44">tablet POS market size and growth</cite>.

## Strategic Implications for Hardware Product Management

For tablet POS, prioritize compact, durable tablets with strong processors, secure payment capabilities, and cloud integration; Apple’s iPad mini and iPad Air, Ingenico’s iPP6800, and NCR’s 9900 series exemplify these attributes <cite id="16">iPad mini 7 specs</cite><cite id="19">iPad Air specs</cite><cite id="25">iPP6800 features</cite><cite id="24">NCR 9900 capabilities</cite>. In regions with high digital adoption (Japan/Korea, Southeast Asia), emphasize cashless integration and ODM flexibility; in North America and Latin America, target SMEs with competitive pricing and scalable SaaS ecosystems <cite id="33">cashless integration in Japan</cite><cite id="36">Southeast Asia growth drivers</cite><cite id="35">North America adoption</cite><cite id="41">Latin America growth</cite>. Finally, align device configurations with use cases—digital ordering in hospitality and retail POS in convenience and supermarkets—while leveraging consumer tablets for broader SaaS deployments <cite id="32">hospitality digital ordering</cite><cite id="36">retail and supermarket adoption</cite><cite id="39">SaaS use of tablets</cite>.
</answer>

In this study, we identified a PBP gene, TabsPBP2, from the T. absoluta transcriptome. Ligand-binding assays demonstrated that TabsPBP2 has the highest affinity for the sex pheromones (3E, 8Z, 11Z)-tetradecatrienyl acetate (TDTA) and (3E, 8Z)-tetradecadienyl acetate (TDDA). problem: Research for me how to improve the Static Noise Margin of SRAM (Static Random Access Memory) through advancements in chip manufacturing processes, to make SRAM storage signals more stable and less susceptible to bit flips?
final_response:
<think>
<answer>
Improving SRAM’s Static Noise Margin (SNM) through advances in chip manufacturing processes

Executive summary
As CMOS scales to sub-45 nm, SRAM’s Read Static Noise Margin (RSNM) shrinks and becomes more vulnerable to process variability, radiation, and aging. Process variability can induce up to 100% power deviation, ~20% RSNM deviation, and dramatically reduced noise robustness in worst-case corners; FinFETs and high-performance models show more radiation robustness, while low-power devices are more sensitive to aging, underscoring the need for manufacturing-process and design co-optimization to stabilize SRAM signals and reduce bit flips<cite id="1">Process variability can introduce up to 100% power deviation; RSNM presents about 20% deviation; FinFETs and high-performance models show more robustness against radiation; low-power devices are more sensitive to delay degradation due to aging</cite>. Below 28 nm, bulk CMOS becomes very challenging; SOI and UTBB FDSOI enable stable, power- and area-efficient SRAM scaling with lower retention voltages and improved SNM variability under random dopant and work-function fluctuations<cite id="12">Bulk CMOS becomes very challenging below 28 nm; UTBB FDSOI allows stable and power-/area-efficient SRAM scaling with DRV lower than 0.4 V</cite>.

Why SNM degrades with scaling and process variability
Across 45 nm to 7 nm bulk CMOS and FinFETs, scaling reduces RSNM and increases delay and variability; worst-case PVT variability and negative-bias temperature instability (NBTI) degrade stability and performance, with FinFETs showing improved robustness compared to planar MOS<cite id="25">Scaling reduces RSNM, delay, and robustness; worst-case PVT and NBTI degrade stability; FinFETs are more robust than planar MOS</cite>. In sub-32 nm bulk CMOS, RSNM can shrink to ~100 mV and become highly variable due to random dopant fluctuations and short-channel effects, motivating process and design co-optimization<cite id="34">RSNM can be as low as ~100 mV in sub-32 nm bulk CMOS due to random dopant fluctuations and short-channel effects</cite>.

Manufacturing-process strategies to improve SNM and stability

Silicon-on-insulator (SOI) and ultra-thin-body-on-box (UTBB) FDSOI
SOI and UTBB FDSOI provide better SNM variability and lower minimum retention voltages compared to bulk, enabling stable SRAM operation at lower supply voltages. In UTBB FDSOI, optimizing V_TN/V_TP with back bias can improve retention- and read-mode SNM mean/standard deviation by up to 2×, and using SOI FinFETs in 16 nm cells reduces σSNM from random dopants, process variations, and work-function fluctuations to 5.3%, 1.2%, and 2.3%, respectively, with an RSNM of 125 mV<cite id="24">Optimizing V_TN/V_TP and back bias improves retention- and read-mode SNM μ/σ by up to 2× in UTBB FDSOI</cite><cite id="19">6T SOI FinFET SRAM exhibits smallest σSNM (5.3%, 1.2%, 2.3%) and RSNM = 125 mV</cite>. In 22 nm FDSOI, a wide range of back-gate biases enables improved read stability and lower minimum operating voltage and power consumption<cite id="22">22 nm FDSOI enables wide back-gate bias range to improve read stability and reduce minimum operating voltage/power</cite>.

FinFET device architecture and work-function engineering
FinFETs inherently reduce short-channel variability and improve SNM compared to planar MOS, and tuning the work function of data-access transistors can significantly enhance read stability. Dynamic independent-gate biasing of data-access transistors can increase read stability by up to 92% while reducing leakage by up to 65× and shrinking cell area by 25.5% compared to tied-gate SRAMs<cite id="25">FinFETs reduce variability and improve SNM compared to planar MOS</cite><cite id="31">Independent-gate FinFETs can enhance read stability by up to 92%, reduce leakage by up to 65×, and reduce cell area by 25.5%</cite>. Multi-threshold-voltage (multi-V_T) work-function engineering with dual-material gates further improves leakage and area while maintaining stability, and advanced FinFET technologies with independent-gate designs boost SRAM performance and stability under scaling constraints<cite id="35">Multi-V_T work-function engineering improves leakage and area while maintaining stability</cite><cite id="33">Independent-double-gate FinFETs improve SRAM performance and stability under scaling constraints</cite>.

Supply-voltage scaling and V_DD strategies
FinFET SRAMs benefit from V_DD scalability, but LER-induced variations can degrade noise margins. Systematic studies show that mixed-mode simulations and quantum-corrected models can guide design trade-offs (e.g., transistor sizing, orientation, fin patterning, gate stack, and V_T tuning) to improve LER robustness and achieve lower V_DD without sacrificing SNM<cite id="6">FinFET SRAM V_DD scalability is impacted by LER; design trade-offs (sizing, orientation, fin patterning, gate stack, V_T tuning) can improve LER robustness and V_DD scalability</cite>. In general, aggressive V_DD scaling must be paired with back-biasing and threshold-voltage tuning to maintain SNM and prevent SEU sensitivity<cite id="1">FinFETs and high-performance models show more robustness against radiation; low-power devices are more sensitive to aging</cite>.

Process-variation mitigation through layout and biasing
Manufacturing-process corners and systematic mismatches from layout topologies can reduce functional margins. A constraint-based analysis shows that layout changes and process pushes can help scale 6T SRAM, but circuit assist methods must be evaluated for their effectiveness under reduced functional margins as nodes shrink<cite id="27">Layout topology and process pushes can help scale 6T SRAM; circuit assist methods must be evaluated under reduced functional margins</cite>. Back-biasing in SOI and FDSOI provides a powerful knob to tune read/write stability and retention voltage, enabling operation at lower supply voltages while improving SNM variability<cite id="22">Back-gate biasing in FDSOI improves read stability and reduces minimum operating voltage/power</cite><cite id="24">Back-bias and V_TN/V_TP optimization improve SNM μ/σ in UTBB FDSOI</cite>.

Data-retention voltage and radiation robustness
As nodes shrink, single-event upset (SEU) sensitivity increases; FinFETs and high-performance models exhibit greater radiation robustness than low-power devices, which are more susceptible to SEU and delay degradation due to aging<cite id="1">FinFETs and high-performance models show more robustness against radiation; low-power devices are more sensitive to delay degradation due to aging</cite>. Process choices (e.g., SOI/FinFET) and biasing strategies can further harden SRAM against SEU by increasing retention voltage and SNM margins<cite id="25">FinFETs improve robustness against radiation and aging effects</cite>.

Practical recommendations
- Adopt SOI/UTBB FDSOI for embedded SRAMs to reduce random dopant and work-function-induced SNM variability and lower retention voltages; pair with optimized V_TN/V_TP and back-biasing to boost SNM μ/σ by up to 2× and stabilize read/write margins<cite id="12">UTBB FDSOI enables stable SRAM scaling with lower DRV</cite><cite id="24">Back-bias and V_TN/V_TP optimization improve retention- and read-mode SNM μ/σ by up to 2×</cite><cite id="19">SOI FinFET SRAM reduces σSNM and achieves RSNM = 125 mV</cite>.
- Use FinFET device architectures and independent-gate biasing for data-access transistors to increase read stability by up to 92% while reducing leakage and area, and leverage multi-V_T work-function engineering for further leakage/area gains<cite id="25">FinFETs improve SNM and radiation robustness</cite><cite id="31">Independent-gate biasing increases read stability by up to 92% and reduces leakage/area</cite><cite id="35">Multi-V_T work-function engineering improves leakage and area</cite>.
- Pair aggressive V_DD scaling with LER-aware design (transistor sizing, orientation, fin patterning, gate stack, and V_T tuning) to maintain SNM under process variability<cite id="6">LER-aware design trade-offs improve FinFET SRAM robustness and V_DD scalability</cite>.
- Employ back-gate biasing in SOI/FDSOI to tune stability and retention voltage, and consider layout/process pushes to mitigate systematic mismatches and preserve functional margins as nodes scale<cite id="22">Back-gate biasing improves stability and retention voltage in FDSOI</cite><cite id="27">Layout/process pushes and constraint-based analysis help scale 6T SRAM</cite>.
- Monitor radiation and aging effects; FinFETs and high-performance devices are more robust than low-power SRAMs under SEU and NBTI, but process and biasing choices should be validated for application-specific reliability targets<cite id="1">FinFETs and high-performance models show more robustness against radiation; low-power devices are more sensitive to aging</cite><cite id="25">FinFETs reduce variability and improve robustness under NBTI and radiation</cite>.

Uncertainties and limitations
Some sources discuss general scaling trends and mechanisms without detailed quantitative data at the latest nodes; therefore, specific improvements should be validated with process corners and variability-aware simulations for the target manufacturing node<cite id="27">Scaling and layout effects require constraint-based analysis and validation</cite>. While STI stress-liner engineering can relax intrinsic compressive stress and recover carrier mobility (~14% improvement), its direct impact on SRAM SNM is not explicitly quantified in the cited evidence; nonetheless, stress control is a relevant manufacturing-process knob for device performance and variability<cite id="42">Additional nitrogen ion-implantation in STI relaxes intrinsic compressive stress and recovers ~14% electron-carrier mobility</cite>.

Conclusion
Manufacturing-process advances—SOI/UTBB FDSOI, FinFET device architectures with work-function tuning and independent-gate biasing, aggressive V_DD scaling with LER-aware design, and back-biasing—collectively provide robust paths to improve SRAM SNM and signal stability, reduce bit-flip susceptibility, and enable reliable operation at lower supply voltages as nodes scale<cite id="12">SOI/UTBB FDSOI enables stable SRAM scaling</cite><cite id="25">FinFETs improve SNM and radiation robustness</cite><cite id="31">Independent-gate biasing and multi-V_T work-function engineering improve stability and leakage/area</cite><cite id="6">LER-aware design improves robustness and V_DD scalability</cite><cite id="22">Back-biasing improves stability and retention voltage</cite>.
</answer>
