<answer>Light-Based Therapies in Aesthetic Medicine: Applications and Recent Advancements for Photoaging, Skin Whitening/Brightening, and Hyperpigmentation

Overview
Light-based therapies—laser, intense pulsed light (IPL), and light-emitting diode (LED)—are widely used in aesthetic dermatology to address photoaging, skin tone modulation, and hyperpigmentation. Recent systematic reviews and clinical trials provide robust evidence on efficacy and safety profiles across these modalities, guiding clinical decision-making and patient selection. For example, network meta-analyses comparing laser-based treatments for melasma have identified combinations that outperform single-agent lasers, while IPL and LED-based photodynamic therapy (PDT) have demonstrated measurable improvements in photoaging and dyspigmentation with distinct mechanisms of action<cite id="1">Network meta-analysis comparing laser-related therapies for melasma</cite><cite id="12">Systematic review of LED-based PDT for photoaging, scars, and dyspigmentation</cite>.

Photoaging: Clinical and Histological Evidence
IPL has been established as a nonablative option for photo-rejuvenation, with clinical and histological evidence supporting collagen remodeling and wrinkle reduction. A randomized, split-face trial in Asian skin showed significant global improvement in photoaging signs after four IPL sessions, with 87.5% of patients rating their improvement as excellent or good. Histology revealed increased collagen types I and III, more organized elastin fibers, and increased fibroblast activity, consistent with collagen synthesis and extracellular matrix remodeling<cite id="7">Split-face IPL trial in photoaging with global improvement and histologic changes</cite><cite id="6">IPL clinical and histologic effects on collagen and elastin</cite>. Additional clinical trials report high patient satisfaction rates for IPL in photoaging, with improvements in texture, pigmentation, and telangiectasias, reinforcing its role in non-ablative skin rejuvenation<cite id="33">IPL efficacy and safety in photoaging</cite><cite id="34">IPL clinical outcomes and patient satisfaction in photoaging</cite>.

Fractional lasers remain a cornerstone for more aggressive photoaging treatment, with ablative and non-ablative fractional CO2/Er:YAG devices demonstrating significant wrinkle reduction, laxity improvement, and pigment modulation. Systematic reviews and clinical series consistently report durable outcomes, though they emphasize the need for careful patient selection and sun protection to mitigate complications such as hypopigmentation and thermal injury<cite id="19">Systematic review of fractional lasers for photoaging</cite><cite id="20">Fractional lasers for photoaging: outcomes and safety</cite><cite id="23">Fractional CO2 laser for photoaging: efficacy and safety</cite><cite id="24">Fractional Er:YAG laser for photoaging: efficacy and safety</cite>.

Skin Whitening and Brightening: Mechanisms and Evidence
LED-based PDT has shown beneficial effects for dyspigmentation, with systematic reviews reporting global skin improvements such as smoother texture and reduced rhytides, alongside histologic evidence of increased collagen and decreased elastin. These findings support the use of LED-mediated PDT for skin quality and tone modulation, although the authors note a paucity of high-quality trials and call for better-designed randomized studies<cite id="12">LED-based PDT efficacy and safety for photoaged skin and dyspigmentation</cite>. Mechanistically, visible light from LEDs can modulate inflammatory pathways and oxidative stress, which are implicated in melanogenesis, thereby contributing to skin brightening effects<cite id="13">Visible light therapy mechanisms relevant to skin brightening</cite>.

Hyperpigmentation: Melasma and Age Spots
For melasma, network meta-analyses of laser-related therapies indicate that combinations such as Q-switched Nd:YAG plus topical agents are superior to monotherapy with Q-switched Nd:YAG or picosecond lasers, with higher surface under the cumulative ranking (SUCRA) values. Microneedling plus topical agents also ranked highly, underscoring the importance of combining modalities and tailoring treatment to patient skin type and disease duration<cite id="1">NMA of laser-related therapies for melasma</cite>. A separate systematic review and meta-analysis of picosecond laser for melasma found limited evidence of superiority over Q-switched lasers, highlighting the need for more rigorous trials to clarify its role<cite id="2">Meta-analysis of picosecond laser for melasma</cite>.

For epidermal hyperpigmentation such as solar lentigines, Q-switched (QS) lasers are effective but carry a higher risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), particularly in darker skin types. Reviews emphasize that longer-pulsed Nd:YAG and IPL pose a lower PIH risk but require more sessions, and that combination approaches with cooling and multiple lasers can target diverse chromophores while optimizing safety<cite id="32">PIH risk with QS lasers and safer alternatives (Nd:YAG, IPL) for lentigines</cite><cite id="31">IPL safety and efficacy for lentigines in Asian skin</cite>. Clinical series report high clearance rates for lentigines with QS ruby/alexandrite lasers, reinforcing their utility for epidermal pigmentation while noting the need for strict parameters to prevent PIH<cite id="35">QS ruby/alexandrite lasers for lentigines</cite>.

Safety Considerations in Asian Skin
Asian skin types II–IV are prone to PIH and scarring after light-based therapies, necessitating careful IPL settings and adjunctive sun protection. Reviews highlight that QS lasers are effective for epidermal pigmentation but require cautious use due to PIH risk, whereas longer-pulsed Nd:YAG and IPL are safer but less aggressive. Non-ablative combination approaches with cooling and fractional resurfacing can achieve optimal results while minimizing adverse events, provided patients are well-informed and protected from sun exposure<cite id="32">Safety and management of PIH in Asian skin with lasers and IPL</cite><cite id="31">IPL safety in Asian skin and PIH risk</cite><cite id="33">IPL safety profile and PIH considerations</cite>.

Future Directions and Integration with Topical Agents
Recent melasma NMA and clinical trials emphasize that laser monotherapy is often insufficient; combining lasers with topical agents (e.g., tranexamic acid, hydroquinone, retinoids) improves outcomes and reduces recurrence. Emerging combination protocols integrate low-level light therapy (LLLT/LED) with chemical peels and oral agents, with multi-month regimens showing gradual pigmentation reduction and safety, underscoring the value of multimodal, personalized treatment plans<cite id="1">Combination laser + topical agents superior for melasma</cite><cite id="11">Multimodal melasma management with visible light, peels, and topical/oral agents</cite>. Continued research on LED wavelengths, photosensitizer delivery, and patient-specific parameters will further refine safety and efficacy for photoaging and dyspigmentation<cite id="12">Need for better-designed LED-based PDT trials</cite>.

Conclusion
Light-based therapies—laser, IPL, and LED—offer evidence-based solutions for photoaging, skin brightening, and hyperpigmentation, with distinct mechanisms and safety profiles. IPL and fractional lasers provide non-ablative to ablative skin rejuvenation with measurable collagen and elastin changes, while LED-based PDT and combination laser/topical regimens support tone modulation and melasma management. In darker skin types, prioritizing lower-PIH lasers (long-pulsed Nd:YAG, IPL) and combination approaches, alongside strict sun protection, is critical to achieving safe, durable results<cite id="7">IPL photoaging improvements</cite><cite id="12">LED-based PDT benefits and safety</cite><cite id="1">Combination laser + topical agents for melasma</cite><cite id="32">PIH risk and safer modalities in Asian skin</cite>.</answer>

<answer>## Crafting Techniques for Non-Alcoholic Cocktails: A Data-Driven Report

### Introduction
Non-alcoholic cocktails (mocktails) are increasingly sophisticated, leveraging ingredient pairing, texture, and presentation to rival traditional spirits-based drinks. Contemporary crafting emphasizes balancing sweetness, acidity, and carbonation, while extending shelf life through advanced preservation techniques. This report synthesizes current methods and formulations supported by recent studies and industry practices.

### Formulation Strategies
Sweetness is often achieved with simple syrup, honey, or agave nectar, which can be adjusted for intensity and mouthfeel. A practical guideline is to start with 1:1 simple syrup and modify based on taste, noting that honey can be thinned with water to match syrup’s viscosity and offers a distinct flavor profile<cite id="19">simple syrup, honey, and agave nectar; start with 1:1 syrup; adjust; thin honey with water</cite>. To reduce sugar content in fruit juices while preserving nutrients, emerging techniques such as mixing, membrane processes, and enzymatic treatments are reviewed, highlighting their limitations and future potential<cite id="6">mixing, membrane, enzymatic processes for sugar reduction in juices</cite>.

Fruit and vegetable blends are optimized using statistical design methods. For example, a study on pineapple–guava–passion fruit blends found that 70% pineapple, 20% guava, and 10% passion fruit produced the best sensory profile, with optimal pH and TSS/TAA ratios supporting consumer acceptability<cite id="19">70% pineapple, 20% guava, 10% passion fruit; pH 3.45; TSS/TAA 13.4</cite>. For vegetable cocktails, a D-optimal mixture design yielded an optimal formulation of 62.511% water, 37.138% sugar, and 0.352% citric acid, achieving desirable organoleptic and chemical qualities<cite id="3">62.511% water, 37.138% sugar, 0.352% citric acid; organoleptic and chemical quality</cite>.

### Flavor Enhancement
Odor-induced taste enhancement (OITE) is a powerful tool to increase perceived sweetness without added calories. Fruit volatiles can amplify sweetness, though optimal combinations and consumer awareness remain areas for further research<cite id="22">fruit aromas/volatiles enhance sweetness; research gaps on saturation and awareness</cite>. Supercritical CO₂ extracts from Lamiaceae plants (e.g., lemon balm, savory) have been used to produce soft drinks with harmonious flavor profiles, demonstrating the viability of green extraction technologies in non-alcoholic beverages<cite id="21">CO₂ extracts from Satureja hortensis, Melissa officinalis, Dracocephalum moldavica; harmonious taste; lemon balm best</cite>.

Citrus zest and microdistillation of citrus peels can intensify aromatic compounds, improving the sensory profile of beverages. A study on lemon zest showed that microdistillation increased aromatic compounds, enhancing the drink’s flavor<cite id="25">microdistillation of lemon zest increases aromatic compounds</cite>. In mojito analogs, a commercial formulation includes sugar, water, benzoic acid, potassium sorbate, gum arabic, flavoring, colorants, and citric acid, mixed homogeneously and adjusted with additional water and citric acid to achieve stability and taste<cite id="1">sugar, water, benzoic acid, potassium sorbate, gum arabic, flavoring, colorants, citric acid; homogenized; additional water and citric acid</cite>.

### Carbonation and Texture
Carbonation is crucial for effervescence and mouthfeel. For carbonated non-alcoholic malt beverages, fermentation at low temperatures (38–45°F) with a thick yeast slurry followed by carbonation yields a stable product with minimal alcohol content<cite id="17">fermentation at 38–45°F with yeast slurry; carbonation; <0.5% alcohol</cite>. In sparkling water production, gas purging, mechanical shaking, and gas-permeable membranes are superior to ultrasonic baths for decarbonation while preserving alcohol and extract, with residual CO₂ affecting real extract by about 0.11% per volume<cite id="16">gas purging, mechanical shakers, membrane decarbonation; 0.11% real extract per CO₂ volume</cite>. Solid chemical agents can also be used to carbonate water quickly and safely without preservatives, offering a simple method for home or small-scale use<cite id="18">solid chemical agents for carbonation without preservatives</cite>.

### Layering and Presentation
Layering techniques create visual appeal by exploiting density differences. A three-layer approach—fizzy/creamy base, syrup/puree middle, and garnish top—can be achieved with a bar spoon to avoid mixing layers, and contrasting flavors (e.g., sweet pineapple with spicy ginger or bitter grapefruit with sweet basil) elevate the drinking experience<cite id="10">three-layer method; fizzy/creamy base; syrups/purees; contrasting flavors</cite>. Creative garnishes and presentation, such as serving in vintage teacups or using fresh herbs and citrus zest, further enhance the mocktail’s sensory impact<cite id="9">break mocktail rules; specialty teas, homemade syrups; presentation in teacups</cite>.

### Equipment and Dilution
Proper dilution and chilling are essential for balanced flavor. Oversteeping tea to a stronger brew and cooling it to room temperature before use mimics tannic qualities of barrel-aged spirits, while chilling ingredients in a shaker ensures a refreshing final product<cite id="6">oversteep tea; cool to room temperature</cite><cite id="8">chill ingredients in a shaker for a refreshing drink</cite>. Classic alcohol-free cocktails demonstrate muddling, shaking, and dilution with ice and soda water to achieve the right mouthfeel and balance<cite id="7">muddle, add ice, non-alcoholic rum, soda; dilution and balance</cite>.

### Shelf-Life Extension
Non-alcoholic beverages require preservatives to maintain quality and safety. Sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate are commonly used to inhibit microbial growth, with formulations including these acids in specified ranges to ensure stability and taste<cite id="1">benzoic acid and potassium sorbate in a mojito analog</cite>. Emerging trends include nanoencapsulation of bioactive preservatives (e.g., bacteriocins, natamycin, polylysine) to improve antimicrobial activity, stability, and controlled release, extending shelf life while protecting nutrients<cite id="26">nanoencapsulation of biopreservatives; improved antimicrobial activity and stability</cite>. Metallic nanoparticles are also being explored for antimicrobial and antioxidant functions in alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages, offering potential for shelf-life extension and quality preservation<cite id="27">metallic nanoparticles for antimicrobial/antioxidant functions in beverages</cite>.

### Case Studies
Several mocktail recipes illustrate innovative crafting. A kiwi margarita combines ginger, mint, lemon juice, simple syrup, and grapefruit juice, shaken and strained into a glass with sparkling water, demonstrating fruit-forward, effervescent profiles<cite id="8">kiwi margarita with ginger, mint, lemon juice, simple syrup, grapefruit juice, sparkling water</cite>. A basil-infused gin fizz uses fresh basil, lime juice, simple syrup, non-alcoholic gin, and sparkling water, highlighting herbaceous notes and effervescence<cite id="11">basil-infused non-alcoholic gin fizz with lime, syrup, sparkling water</cite>. A lavender-lemonade cocktail blends lavender syrup, lemon juice, and sparkling water, showcasing floral and citrus contrasts<cite id="12">lavender-lemonade with lavender syrup, lemon juice, sparkling water</cite>.

Mojito analogs provide a template for aromatized, stabilized non-alcoholic bases. A commercial formulation balances sugar, water, acids, preservatives, and flavoring to achieve a stable, appealing drink, with adjustments to acidity and sweetness for optimal mouthfeel<cite id="1">molecular composition and preservation in a mojito analog</cite>.

### Emerging Trends
Green extraction technologies, such as supercritical CO₂, are increasingly used to produce natural flavorings for non-alcoholic beverages, improving flavor profiles and sustainability<cite id="21">CO₂ extracts from Lamiaceae; harmonious taste; sustainable extraction</cite>. Nanoencapsulation and metallic nanoparticles are promising avenues for extending shelf life and enhancing antimicrobial/antioxidant properties in non-alcoholic drinks<cite id="26">nanoencapsulation for biopreservatives</cite><cite id="27">metallic nanoparticles in beverages</cite>. Consumer-driven trends emphasize contrasting flavors (sweet–spicy, bitter–sweet) and creative presentation, encouraging experimentation beyond traditional mocktail norms<cite id="9">pair bitter herbs with fruit; creative presentation</cite><cite id="10">contrasting flavor pairings in layered mocktails</cite>.

### Conclusion
Crafting non-alcoholic cocktails benefits from precise formulation, flavor enhancement, controlled carbonation, and thoughtful presentation. Data-driven approaches—ranging from statistical design of fruit/vegetable blends to nanoencapsulation for preservation—offer robust methods to innovate and stabilize these beverages. By integrating these techniques, bartenders and beverage scientists can create complex, appealing mocktails that rival their alcoholic counterparts in taste, texture, and shelf life<cite id="19">fruit blend optimization</cite><cite id="3">vegetable cocktail formulation</cite><cite id="21">green extraction for flavor</cite><cite id="26">nanoencapsulation for preservation</cite><cite id="10">layering and contrasting flavors</cite>.</answer>

# AI Interaction and Interpersonal Relations: A Data-Driven Overview

## Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in how people relate to each other, from chatbots and voice assistants to social robots and algorithmic matchmaking. These systems can provide companionship and support, reshape relationship formation, and even blur boundaries between real and synthetic interactions, with implications for trust and social cohesion. Understanding these effects requires synthesizing evidence on both benefits and risks to interpersonal relations, grounded in empirical studies and theoretical frameworks of human–computer interaction.<cite id="1">Companion chatbots can offer everyday social support, reducing loneliness and providing emotional and informational support</cite><cite id="2">AI chatbots can offer virtual social support, helping to alleviate loneliness and anxiety</cite><cite id="6">Cues in emerging media technologies shape how users interpret interactions and evoke social presence</cite>

## The Dual Role of AI in Social Support and Loneliness
AI-driven companions can fulfill social roles when human relationships are limited, offering emotional and informational support. A thematic analysis of Replika users found that chatbots can curb loneliness, provide a “safe space” for discussion, increase positive affect, and offer helpful advice when normal sources of support are unavailable.<cite id="1">Replika provides companionship, a safe space, increased positive affect, and helpful information/advice</cite> Randomized experiments with AI chatbots similarly show that voice-based interactions can initially reduce loneliness, but these benefits can diminish at high usage levels, with heavier use correlating with greater loneliness and reduced socialization with real people across text and voice modalities.<cite id="11">Voice-based chatbots initially reduce loneliness but advantages fade at high usage; higher daily usage correlates with higher loneliness and lower socialization</cite>

Voice assistants, especially in personal voice assistant (PVA) form, have shown promise in reducing loneliness among older adults, with video PVAs outperforming text PVAs and control groups on several measures, including perceived social support and emotional well-being. However, the effects were not consistently significant across all outcomes, underscoring the importance of modality and user context.<cite id="12">Video PVAs reduced loneliness and improved perceived social support and emotional well-being compared to text PVAs and controls</cite> Theoretical work on “computational theories” emphasizes how AI can be engineered to support human interaction by modeling and responding to social cues, reinforcing the potential for AI to complement rather than replace human relationships.<cite id="5">Computational theories of human–computer interaction highlight modeling and responding to social cues</cite>

## Design and Interaction Modalities Matter
The design of AI interaction—voice expressiveness, conversation type, and cue richness—shapes outcomes. In a large longitudinal experiment, engaging voice modes did not show clear advantages over neutral voice, and personal conversation topics slightly increased loneliness among users, whereas open-ended and non-personal topics were associated with different dependence patterns. These findings highlight the need to align interaction design with intended relational outcomes.<cite id="11">Voice expressiveness and conversation type shape loneliness and dependence; personal topics can increase loneliness</cite> Social presence theory and cue typologies further explain how multimodal cues and concurrent communication can foster a sense of presence and intimacy in digital interactions, guiding the development of AI systems that support meaningful connections.<cite id="6">Cues shape social presence in emerging media technologies</cite><cite id="7">Concurrent communication increases social presence, emotional arousal, and intimacy</cite>

## AI in Relationship Formation and Family Dynamics
Algorithmic matchmaking has become central to modern dating, with users relying on AI-driven platforms to find partners. Survey data indicate that perceptions of fairness, social presence, and threat associated with AI influence how users judge the effectiveness of matchmaking algorithms, and prior relationship success moderates these perceptions. This suggests that algorithmic curation can shape relational opportunities but also raises questions about agency, fairness, and the role of human unpredictability in attraction.<cite id="22">User perceptions of AI fairness, social presence, and threat affect perceived effectiveness of matchmaking algorithms</cite><cite id="21">Machine learning predicts only a fraction of attraction variance, indicating that compatibility elements are challenging to predict before meeting</cite> In family contexts, social robots can become part of daily life, with studies showing that robots can be accepted over time and even strengthen family bonds when they support caregiving routines and communication.<cite id="16">Social robots can be designed to support older adults and integrate into family life</cite><cite id="19">Robots can strengthen family bonds by supporting caregiving routines and communication</cite>

## Risks: Deepfakes, Misinformation, and Trust Erosion
AI-generated content, particularly deepfakes, poses significant risks to interpersonal trust and social cohesion. Experimental evidence shows that deepfakes increase uncertainty and reduce trust in news, without necessarily misleading viewers, which can erode civic discourse and social bonds.<cite id="26">Deepfakes increase uncertainty and reduce trust in news, without necessarily misleading viewers</cite> Media discourse frames deepfakes as threats to truth, political processes, and consent, amplifying societal anxieties about synthetic media’s impact on relationships and power dynamics.<cite id="28">News media characterizes deepfakes as easily produced/distributed, creating false beliefs, undermining the political process, and non-consensual sexual content</cite> Broader concerns about AI’s potential to exacerbate socioeconomic inequalities and deepen divides further complicate its role in shaping equitable interpersonal relations.<cite id="29">Generative AI can exacerbate and ameliorate socioeconomic inequalities, with implications for policy and equity</cite>

## Global Trends in Loneliness and Social Isolation
Loneliness is a widespread public health issue, with systematic reviews across 109 countries indicating that problematic loneliness is common and varies considerably by region. These findings underscore the potential role of AI in addressing loneliness, but also the need for context-sensitive interventions that consider cultural, economic, and demographic differences.<cite id="31">Problematic loneliness is common across 109 countries, with considerable regional variation</cite><cite id="32">Loneliness is widespread but data are insufficient in low- and middle-income countries</cite> Social media use is often linked to loneliness and social anxiety, with vulnerable groups—such as those with pre-existing social difficulties—using platforms more problematically, which can reinforce isolation rather than alleviate it.<cite id="36">Socially anxious and lonely individuals engage with social media more problematically</cite><cite id="38">Social comparison orientation and fear of missing out mediate links between social media engagement and loneliness, depression, and anxiety</cite>

## Theoretical and Practical Implications
Computational theories of human–computer interaction suggest that AI can be engineered to support social interaction by modeling and responding to cues, but these capabilities must be balanced with safeguards to prevent over-reliance or displacement of human relationships.<cite id="5">AI can be engineered to support human interaction by modeling and responding to social cues</cite> Evidence from longitudinal experiments and field studies indicates that higher daily usage of AI companions can correlate with greater loneliness and reduced socialization, emphasizing the importance of usage patterns and design choices in shaping relational outcomes.<cite id="11">Higher daily usage correlates with higher loneliness and lower socialization</cite> In home environments, domestication frameworks highlight the social dimension of technology adoption, suggesting that robots’ acceptance depends on how they are woven into existing care networks and family routines.<cite id="17">A “social dimension” of domestication is crucial for older adults, caregivers, and robots in the home</cite><cite id="18">Long-term acceptance unfolds through temporal stages of pre-adoption, adoption, adaptation, and use/retention</cite>

## Conclusion
AI interaction has the potential to both support and strain interpersonal relations, depending on design, context, and usage. Empirical evidence shows that AI companions can alleviate loneliness and provide social support, but heavy or poorly designed use can conversely reduce socialization and increase dependence.<cite id="1">AI companions can reduce loneliness and provide social support</cite><cite id="11">Poorly designed or heavy use can increase loneliness and dependence</cite> Algorithmic matchmaking reshapes how people meet and form relationships, while deepfakes and misinformation threaten trust and social cohesion.<cite id="22">Algorithmic matchmaking effectiveness depends on user perceptions of AI</cite><cite id="26">Deepfakes reduce trust without necessarily misleading viewers</cite> Addressing these dual roles will require careful design, ethical governance, and context-sensitive deployment that complements rather than replaces human relationships, while recognizing the global variation in loneliness and the risks of social media for vulnerable populations.<cite id="31">Problematic loneliness is common globally</cite><cite id="36">Loneliness and social anxiety are linked to problematic social media use</cite>
</answer>

However, the bulk of this research has been conducted in the context of social support interventions that specifically address stressful situations or health improvements. Little research has examined social support received from artificial agents in everyday contexts. Objective: Considering that social support manifests in not only crises but also everyday situations and that everyday social support forms the basis of support received during more stressful events, we aimed to investigate the types of everyday social support that can be received from artificial agents. Methods: In Study 1, we examined publicly available user reviews (N=1854) of Replika, a popular companion chatbot. In Study 2, a sample (n=66) of Replika users provided detailed open-ended responses regarding their experiences of using Replika. We conducted thematic analysis on both datasets to gain insight into the kind of everyday social support that users receive through interactions with Replika. Results: Replika provides some level of companionship that can help curtail loneliness, provide a'safe space' in which users can discuss any topic without the fear of judgment or retaliation, increase positive affect through uplifting and nurturing messages, and provide helpful information/advice when normal sources of informational support are not available. Conclusions: Artificial agents may be a promising source of everyday social support, particularly companionship, emotional, informational, and appraisal support, but not as tangible support. Future studies are needed to determine who might benefit from these types of everyday social support the most and why. These results could potentially be used to help address global health issues or other crises early on in everyday situations before they potentially manifest into larger issues.</summary><hostname>ResearchGate</hostname><publisher>Journal of Medical Internet Research</publisher><author_list><author name="Vivian Ta Phd" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /><author name="Caroline Griffith" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /><author name="Carolynn Boatfield" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /><author name="Xinyu Wang" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /><author name="Maria Civitello" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /><author name="Haley Bader Ba" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /><author name="Esther Decero" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /><author name="Alexia Loggarakis" affiliation="Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, IL, United States" /></author_list><url>https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Vivian-Ta-Johnson/publication/339763899_User_Experiences_of_Social_Support_From_Companion_Chatbots_in_Everyday_Contexts_Thematic_Analysis/links/5e679e8292851c7ce05934bd/User-Experiences-of-Social-Support-From-Companion-Chatbots-in-Everyday-Contexts-Thematic-Analysis.pdf</url><publish_time>2020年3月1日0时0分</publish_time></document><document reference_id="<|superscript|>:2"><title>Artificial intelligence chatbots as a source of virtual social support: Implications for loneliness and anxiety management</title><summary>Loneliness, social isolation, and anxiety affect millions of people across the world. Exploratory analyses revealed that those with stronger emotional attachment tendencies and higher trust in the AI chatbot tended to experience greater loneliness and emotional dependence, respectively.
